## **Instructions for companies** 

This is the template for submission of evidence to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) as part of the single technology appraisal (STA) process. Please note that the information requirements for submissions are summarised in this template; full details of the requirements for pharmaceuticals and devices are in the user guide. 

This submission must not be longer than 150 pages, excluding appendices and the pages covered by this template. If it is too long it will not be accepted. 

Companies making evidence submissions to NICE should also refer to the NICE health technology evaluation guidance development manual. 

In this template any information that should be provided in an appendix is listed in a box. 

## **Highlighting in the template (excluding the contents list)** 

Square brackets and grey highlighting are used in this template to indicate text that should be replaced with your own text or deleted. These are set up as form fields, so to replace the prompt text in [grey highlighting] with your own text, click anywhere within the highlighted text and type. Your text will overwrite the highlighted section. 

To delete grey highlighted text, click anywhere within the text and press DELETE. 

Grey highlighted text in the footer does not work as an automatic form field, but serves the same purpose – as prompt text to show where you need to fill in relevant details. Replace the text highlighted in [grey] in the header and footer with appropriate text. (To change the header and footer, double click over the header or footer text. Double click back in the main body text when you have finished.)

## **B.1 Decision problem, description of the technology and clinical care pathway** 

## **B.1.1** _**Decision problem**_ 

The objective of this evaluation is to determine the clinical and cost-effectiveness of durvalumab (1,500 mg; every four weeks [Q4W]) in combination with tremelimumab (300 mg; single dose), hereafter referred to as STRIDE, within its full marketing authorisation for the first-line treatment of adults with advanced or unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).[1, 2] 

First-line treatment options in the United Kingdom (UK) for adults with advanced or unresectable HCC comprise atezolizumab + bevacizumab (the current standard of care [SoC]), and sorafenib or lenvatinib as alternative first-line therapies.[3] Advanced or unresectable HCC is associated with a significant clinical, humanistic and economic burden, imposing a negative impact on patients and caregivers, in addition to the healthcare system and workforce productivity in the UK. This submission explores the unmet need associated with currently available treatments and describes how STRIDE represents an alternative first-line option to address these. By leveraging mature clinical data from the pivotal HIMALAYA trial, conducting indirect treatment comparisons (ITCs) to assess the comparative efficacy of STRIDE vs. comparators followed by an economic analysis, this submission demonstrates the clinical and cost-effectiveness of STRIDE for the treatment of patients with advanced or unresectable HCC in the UK.[4] 

The decision problem addressed within this submission is broadly consistent with the National Institute of Health and Care Excellence (NICE) final scope for this evaluation, and any differences between the decision problem addressed within this submission and the NICE final scope are clearly outlined in Table 1.

## **B.1.3** _**Health condition and position of the technology in the**_ 

## _**treatment pathway**_ 

**Summary of health condition and position of STRIDE in the treatment pathway Disease overview** 

- HCC is the most common form of primary liver cancer, accounting for ~50% of all liver cancer cases[26] (Section B.1.3.1) 

- The National Cancer Registration statistics for England report that 3,557 adults (age 20 and older) were diagnosed with liver cancer (excluding intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma) in 2021.[27] In a study projecting cancer incidence and mortality in the UK until 2035, liver cancer is among the fastest increasing cancers in both incidence and mortality[28] 

- Major risk factors for the development of HCC comprise drivers of cirrhosis, including infection with hepatitis B (HBV) or hepatitis C virus (HCV), chronic alcohol consumption, obesity and diabetes[29, 30] 

- Approximately 41% of cases are identified as advanced or unresectable HCC at first diagnosis.[27, 29] This is partly due to HCC being generally asymptomatic or presenting with non-specific symptoms in the early stages of the disease (Section B.1.3.1) 

## **Disease burden** 

   - Survival for patients with HCC is poor; the five-year survival for HCC in the UK remains below 10%, dropping to 2% in metastatic HCC, representing a significant clinical burden for patients and their families.[3, 29, 31, 32] For patients with advanced or unresectable HCC, average life expectancy is less than two years with treatments currently available in the UK[33] (Section B.1.3.3.1) 

- HCC often presents with non-specific symptoms such as loss of appetite, weight loss, and malaise, similar to symptoms of cirrhosis.[34, 35] Additionally, underlying liver disease and high portal hypertension in advanced or unresectable HCC patients increases the risk of gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding, which means some individuals may not be eligible to receive systemic treatment regimens containing anti-angiogenic agents[7, 36] (Section B.1.3.3.1) 

- • Disease symptoms in individuals with advanced or unresectable HCC have profound 

- Company evidence submission template for durvalumab with tremelimumab for untreated advanced or unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma [ID2725] 

© AstraZeneca (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 24 -->

- humanistic and health-related quality of life (HRQoL) impacts.[37] As such, individuals report significantly lower physical wellbeing and overall HRQoL than the general population, patients with chronic liver disease, and patients with other cancers[29] (Section B.1.3.3.2) 

- • Advanced or unresectable HCC also poses a significant economic burden on both individual patients, caregivers and the National Health Service (NHS).[37, 38] Indirect costs associated with HCC are primarily driven by sick leave, long-term disability days, workers’ compensation and disability among employees.[39] Furthermore, unpaid family members caring for individuals with advanced or unresectable HCC face significant economic and HRQoL burdens, often resigning from their jobs, losing income, depleting savings and experiencing stress from supporting with their family member’s receipt of specialised care[40] (Section B.1.3.3.2 and B.1.3.3.3) 

- **Treatment pathway** • There are no curative treatment options for advanced or unresectable HCC, with systemic therapy being the only current treatment option[29, 37] (Section B.1.3.4) 

- • Atezolizumab + bevacizumab is the current first-choice SoC treatment for patients with advanced or unresectable HCC[3, 10, 41, 42] (Section B.1.3.4.1) 

- • For those who have contraindications or would prefer oral therapy, sorafenib and lenvatinib are alternative first-line therapies[3] (Section B.1.3.4.2) 

- **Unmet need in advanced or unresectable HCC** • The five-year survival for metastatic HCC in the UK is 2%, with an average life expectancy of less than two years despite current treatments.[31, 33] This highlights the significant unmet clinical need for individuals with advanced or unresectable HCC[3, 29, 31, 32] (Section B.1.3.4.4) 

- • There is a considerable unmet need for a treatment that can alleviate the humanistic burden associated with HCC, with patients emphasising the need for improved OS (Section B.1.3.4.4) 

- • Many patients with advanced or unresectable HCC have a high risk of bleeding and are therefore contraindicated to atezolizumab + bevacizumab.[43] For these individuals, there is a significant unmet need for a treatment that can extend survival without increasing toxicity[29] (Section B.1.3.4.4) 

- • Treatment with atezolizumab + bevacizumab also requires an endoscopy ahead of initiation, which increases the NHS resource burden and may introduce a delay to patients receiving life-extending therapy[7, 44] (Section B.1.3.4.4) 

- **Proposed positioning of STRIDE** • STRIDE (Single Tremelimumab Regular Interval Durvalumab) represents a novel treatment option with a favourable administration schedule for patients with advanced or unresectable HCC. The HIMALAYA trial provided unprecedented and highly mature overall survival (OS) data, including an exploratory five-year analysis, representing the longest follow-up for an immunotherapy treatment in this setting. The primary analyses showed a statistically and clinically significant benefit of STRIDE over sorafenib for OS (Section B.1.3.4.5) 

- • STRIDE also demonstrated an acceptable toxicity profile in HIMALAYA, with no meaningful increase in liver toxicity and no treatment-related gastrointestinal or oesophageal varices haemorrhage events observed.[45] The favourable safety profile is particularly beneficial when compared to the currently SoC, atezolizumab + bevacizumab[3] (Section B.1.3.4.5) 

- • Based on expert clinician feedback, the British Society of Gastroenterology (BSG) guidelines and data from the HIMALAYA trial, STRIDE is proposed to be positioned as a first-line treatment option for patients with advanced or unresectable HCC in the UK who are ineligible for locoregional therapy[3] (Section B.1.3.4) 

## **B.1.3.1 Advanced or unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma** 

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common form of primary liver cancer, accounting for ~50% of all liver cancer cases.[26] The National Cancer Registration statistics for England report that 3,557 adults (age 20 and older) were diagnosed with liver cancer (excluding intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma) in 2021.[27] These figures have increased substantially since the 1970s, and Company evidence submission template for durvalumab with tremelimumab for untreated advanced or unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma [ID2725] 

© AstraZeneca (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 25 -->

in a study projecting cancer incidence and mortality in the UK until 2035, liver cancer is among the fastest increasing cancers in both incidence and mortality.[28] 

Cirrhosis, regardless of its cause, is a primary factor contributing to HCC.[37] Accordingly, major risk factors for the development of HCC comprise drivers of cirrhosis, including infection with HBV or HCV, chronic alcohol consumption, obesity and diabetes.[29, 30] Many of these causes are related to lifestyle, an issue recognised by the UK government, leading to the implementation of national policies to limit alcohol intake and encourage healthy living.[3, 46] 

During the early stages of disease, HCC is generally asymptomatic or presents with non-specific symptoms. These include fatigue, weakness, loss of appetite, weight loss, nausea and vomiting, pain around the liver area and malaise.[34, 35] Despite improvements in the screening of patients with known HCC risk factors, including cirrhosis, age and geographic region,[36] patients often receive a delayed diagnosis.[34] Approximately 41% of cases are identified as advanced or unresectable at first diagnosis, whilst 30–50% of patients undergoing surgery experience disease recurrence within two years.[27, 29, 47] For individuals with advanced or unresectable HCC, including those at the intermediate stage who are ineligible for locoregional therapy, systemic therapy remains the only treatment option.[47] As a result, despite potentially curative outcomes for earlystage patients, overall prognosis for patients with HCC remains poor, with the five-year survival remaining below 10% in the UK.[3, 29, 32, 48] For patients with advanced or unresectable HCC, average life expectancy is less than two years with treatments currently available in the UK.[33] 

## **B.1.3.2 Classification of hepatocellular carcinoma** 

Diagnosis of HCC comprises imaging and pathological components, such as computerised tomography (CT), MRI (magnetic resonance imaging), ultrasounds, positron emission tomography (PET), biopsies and blood tests.[49] Once a patient has been diagnosed with HCC, their disease is classified via a process known as staging, which facilitates appropriate treatment selection.[50, 51] The key factors for staging in HCC include tumour characteristics (size, number of tumours, growth rate, spread), liver function and patient health.[50, 51] 

The most widely used system to assess disease stage and treatment options in the UK is the Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) classification.[3, 52, 53] The BCLC staging system assesses the number and size of liver tumours, HCC clinical features (Okuda score), patient health and fitness (Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group [ECOG] performance status [PS]), and liver function (Child-Pugh score).[51] These criteria are used to classify patients, starting from Stage 0 (very early HCC) to Stage D (terminal HCC).[51] The patient populations considered within this evaluation are individuals in Stage B (intermediate HCC) who are ineligible for locoregional therapy, and Stage C (advanced or unresectable HCC). The Cancer Registration Statistic identified that approximately 41% of individuals have advanced or unresectable HCC at the time of diagnosis. This aligns with a prospective study involving 591 individuals in the UK who underwent BCLC stage assessment at diagnosis revealed that around 40% were classified as having advanced or unresectable HCC at the time of diagnosis (Table 3).[47]

## **B.1.3.3 Burden of disease** 

## _**B.1.3.3.1 Clinical burden**_ 

Patients with advanced or unresectable HCC experience a profound clinical burden, from both the symptoms of their condition, the therapies they are treated with, and the dismal survival prospects associated with this disease. 

When symptomatic, HCC is generally associated with non-specific complaints, such as loss of appetite, weight loss and malaise, which are often comparable to symptoms of cirrhosis.[34, 35] Symptoms with increased specificity to HCC are the onset of fluid in the abdomen (ascites), damage to the brain (encephalopathy), skin and eyes turning yellow (jaundice), or variceal bleeding in the GI tract.[34] In certain cases of advanced or unresectable HCC, patients may present with acute onset of severe abdominal pain and distension, low blood pressure (hypotension), tumour rupture and bleeding within the peritoneal cavity (intraperitoneal).[34] 

HCC is a highly fatal cancer, often diagnosed late, with an incidence to mortality ratio approaching one.[3] Despite there being several treatment options available the median OS for patients with late-stage HCC on systemic therapies is 8–19 months.[29] The five-year survival from HCC in the UK remains below 10%, dropping to 2% in individuals with metastatic disease, highlighting the significant unmet clinical need particularly for individuals with advanced or unresectable HCC.[3, 29, 31, 32]

<!-- page 27 -->

There is an additional clinical burden associated with systemic therapies currently available to patients with advanced or unresectable HCC. Firstly, the currently available treatments are associated with toxicities that not only decrease HRQoL but also result in treatment interruptions and dose reductions, which can potentially decrease treatment efficacy.[56] Secondly, the underlying liver disease and high likelihood of portal hypertension in patients with advanced or unresectable stage HCC results in an elevated risk of GI bleeding, particularly with treatments that include anti-angiogenic agents (such as bevacizumab), which inhibit the growth of new blood vessels.[57] Recent interviews with UK HCC clinicians found that some patients are being prescribed atezolizumab + bevacizumab at the discretion of their physician, despite the associated heightened bleeding risk which would typically be a contraindication. Physicians must then monitor patients for bleeding risk while they are on atezolizumab + bevacizumab, as there are no safer alternative systemic treatment options available with comparable efficacy. This highlights the need for alternative, efficacious treatment options that do not heighten the risk of bleeding.[7] Thirdly, given the aforementioned bleeding risks, patients with HCC who are treated with atezolizumab + bevacizumab are required to receive an endoscopy prior to starting treatment to assess their bleeding risk. This procedure can be unpleasant for patients and may delay treatment initiation (further detail is given in Section B.1.3.4.1).[57, 58] 

## _**B.1.3.3.2 Humanistic burden**_ 

Patients with HCC experience a substantial humanistic burden and report significantly lower physical wellbeing and overall HRQoL than the general population, patients with chronic liver disease, and patients with other cancers.[29] In a meta-analysis of 16 studies evaluating HRQoL of HCC patients using the 36-Item Short Form Survey (SF-36), individuals with HCC report substantially poorer scores in several domains: general health (38.2 vs. 70.1), mental health (45.2 vs. 75.2), physical functioning (36.2 vs. 83.0), role–emotional (37.7 vs. 77.9), role–physical (37.7 vs. 77.9), social functioning (38.7 vs. 83.6), and vitality (42.1 vs. 57.0) when compared to the age-adjusted general public.[59] Lower HRQoL scores are associated with a range of liver- and tumour-related factors, with worse Child-Pugh class and increased tumour burden being independently associated with lower HRQoL levels.[29] Wellbeing challenges include poor energy, troubles with sleep, difficulties digesting food, appetite loss, increased pain, decline in physical mobility, decreased ability to perform usual activities and poor mental health and social functioning.[56] Symptoms of diarrhoea, fatigue, skin toxicities and appetite loss are reported to have the largest impact on patients’ HRQoL.[37] 

Whilst there is limited research into HRQoL in patients with advanced or unresectable HCC specifically, these patients report that the most severe symptoms at diagnosis are fatigue and distress, and 90% of patients report pain during and after treatment.[60-62] The abdomen and lower back were the most common sites of pain.[60] Following treatment, fatigue remained the most serious symptom, followed by sleep disturbance, distress, sadness, and lack of appetite.[62] Symptoms of upper GI distress and liver function impairment also remained after treatment.[62] 

Improved patient HRQoL, in particular involvement in life situations involving family, partner relationship, work or household chores, may be independently associated with improved survival in patients with advanced or unresectable HCC.[29] Specifically, a multivariate analysis of the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) Core Quality of Life questionnaire (QLQ-C30) and clinical variables found that higher scores in the physical functioning domain (p=0.0034; hazard ratio [HR] for 10 point decrease=0.911) and the role functioning domain (p=0.0383; HR for 10 point decrease=0.944) were associated with longer survival.[63] Furthermore, poor HRQoL has been shown to be an independent prognostic factor of Company evidence submission template for durvalumab with tremelimumab for untreated advanced or unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma [ID2725] 

© AstraZeneca (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 28 -->

all-cause mortality among advanced stage HCC patients, highlighting that treatment strategies that maintain HRQoL may in turn help to improve survival.[29, 59] 

Patients with advanced or unresectable HCC often require informal caregiving to manage daily living; this is often provided by unpaid family members.[40] A systematic literature review (SLR) conducted by Woodrell et al. investigated the physical and emotional stressors for patients with advanced liver disease and their families.[40] The study found that liver diseases carry a considerable burden, with physiological, psychological, and social complexities posing a threat to the HRQoL experienced by both patients and family caregivers.[40] 

## _**B.1.3.3.3 Economic burden**_ 

HCC imposes a significant economic burden on both individuals and the NHS. A study evaluating the impact of secondary and tertiary healthcare provision for 15,684 individuals diagnosed with HCC in England between 2010 to 2016 determined a total cost of approximately £245 million. Per patient, the median expenditure over a two-year period was £9,065, with an interquartile range of £1,965 to £20,491.[38] Individuals with compensated cirrhosis incurred significantly greater healthcare costs than those with decompensated cirrhosis (£14,038 vs £7,744; p<0.001), highlighting the critical need for effective care and management of those with liver damage. Furthermore, healthcare expenditure for this condition is projected to increase as a result of the continuing upward trend in HCC incidence, as described above.[28] 

HCC is also associated with indirect costs as a result of lost productivity due to morbidity and premature mortality experienced by patients with the disease. As such, indirect costs associated with HCC are driven by sick leave, long-term disability days, workers’ compensation and disability among employees.[39] Furthermore, caregivers experience financial burdens from caregiving responsibilities, with carers of patients with end-stage liver disease reported resigning from their job, losing income, and depleting savings in the last six months of a patient’s life. Carers additionally report stress associated with travel for specialised care, including upheaval of everyday life and a financial impact.[40] 

## **B.1.3.4 Clinical pathway of care** 

The BSG have recently published guidelines with recommendations for the management of patients with HCC, which, alongside NICE recommendations,[8-10, 64, 65] are expected to guide clinical practice within the UK.[3] They were developed by UK-based liver cancer experts, including hepatologists, liver surgeons, radiologists, pathologists, oncologists, palliative care physicians and clinical nurse specialists. Input was also provided by patients who have been diagnosed with and treated for liver cancer. 

According to the BSG guidelines, at the early stages of HCC, treatments include surgical resection, liver transplantation and ablation.[3] As the cancer progresses, locoregional therapy is considered for patients who are ineligible for surgery, or as a bridging therapy to reduce tumour size and number to maintain eligibility criteria for transplantation whilst on the waiting list.[3] However, for individuals at the advanced or unresectable stage, curative treatment is not possible.[66] Currently, systemic therapy is the only treatment option for individuals within the patient population considered in this evaluation, with the goal of extending survival and maintaining patients’ HRQoL for as long as possible.[3, 67]

## _**B.1.3.4.1 Atezolizumab + bevacizumab**_ 

Atezolizumab + bevacizumab is the current first-line SoC treatment for patients with advanced or unresectable HCC in the UK, following its NICE recommendation in December 2020 (TA666).[3, 10, ] 41, 42 This combination is administered intravenously (IV) every three weeks (Q3W) until loss of clinical benefit as assessed by the investigator or until unacceptable toxicity. Both atezolizumab and bevacizumab are monoclonal antibodies, with atezolizumab targeting programmed deathligand 1 (PD-L1) and bevacizumab targeting vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). Clinical evidence supporting atezolizumab + bevacizumab for the treatment of advanced or unresectable HCC was evaluated in the open-label, Phase III IMbrave150 randomised controlled trial (RCT) vs. sorafenib.[44] 

Despite becoming the first-line SoC for patients with advanced or unresectable HCC, there are limitations associated with this treatment. Firstly, the IMbrave150 trial only provided a median follow up of 15.6 months (range: 0–28.6), which increases the uncertainty in the long-term efficacy and safety of this treatment.[33] Secondly, atezolizumab + bevacizumab may not be suitable for a considerable proportion of patients, with clinicians estimating that approximately 25% are contraindicated due to bleeding risk and other comorbidities.[7] As discussed in Section B.1.3.3.1, patients with advanced or unresectable HCC are at an increased risk of GI bleeding, particularly those with cirrhosis.[3, 7, 44] This risk can be exacerbated by anti-angiogenic agents such as bevacizumab. Consequently, an endoscopy is required for all individuals prior to initiation of treatment with atezolizumab + bevacizumab to assess patients for the presence and treatment of oesophageal varices, increasing the NHS resource burden.[57, 68] Furthermore, the need to undergo an endoscopy may not only be distressing for patients but may also delay patients’ initiation of this systemic therapy and subsequently the receipt of any treatment benefit. 

## _**B.1.3.4.2 Sorafenib and lenvatinib**_ 

For patients who have a contraindication to atezolizumab + bevacizumab, or otherwise decline IV therapy in favour of oral therapy, sorafenib and lenvatinib are alternative first-line therapies recommended by NICE for advanced or unresectable HCC.[8, 9] Additionally, both therapies are recommended by the BSG HCC guidelines as second-line therapies for patients who have previously been treated with atezolizumab + bevacizumab in the first-line.[3] This recommendation is also supported by the BlueTeq criteria.[69] Given the non-inferiority of OS for lenvatinib compared with sorafenib, the BSG guidelines advocate that the decision on which of these to use might be influenced by consideration of secondary endpoints such as response rate and progression-free survival (PFS), in addition to toxicity profile.[3] 

Sorafenib is an orally administered multi-receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that exerts antiangiogenic and anti-proliferative effects through the inhibition of multiple protein kinases.[70] It was recommended by NICE in 2017 (TA474) for the treatment of advanced HCC in patients with Child-Pugh class A liver impairment.[9] Treatment with sorafenib is associated with high toxicity, limited long-term survival and worse clinical outcomes for patients with poor liver function, which is common to patients with advanced or unresectable HCC.[71, 72] 

Lenvatinib is an alternative, orally administered multi-receptor TKI which was recommended by NICE in 2018 (TA551).[8] Whilst lenvatinib and sorafenib have comparable OS, lenvatinib has demonstrated increased PFS relative to sorafenib (NCT01761266).[73] Similar to sorafenib, treatment with lenvatinib is associated with high toxicity.[73]

## _**B.1.3.4.3 Selective internal radiation therapies**_ 

Selective internal radiation therapy (SIRT) is an intra-arterial therapy option involving the injection of small radioactive beads into the liver’s blood supply. The beads lodge themselves within the vessels that supply the tumour and emit localised radiation to kill tumour cells.[74] SIRT requires close coordination between nuclear medicine, interventional radiology and oncology, and demands specific equipment and expertise. It is therefore only available in 11 NHS centres in the UK due to its specialised nature.[75] 

Two types of SIRT, SIR-Spheres and SIRT TheraSphere, were recommended by NICE in March 2021 as an option for treating unresectable advanced HCC in patients with Child-Pugh class A.[76] Subsequently, SIRT QuiremSphere was also recommended by NICE in TA985 for unresectable advanced HCC.[77] All three treatments have been proposed as potential comparators to STRIDE in the NICE final scope.[78] However, as described in Table 1, the patient population for this submission excludes candidates eligible for locoregional therapy due to the nature of their liver disease, which renders locoregional therapy unsuitable as a possible result of their tumour burden, liver function, vascular invasion, among other factors.[5] Therefore, since SIRT is a locoregional therapy, it is not considered a relevant comparator for this population. Recent interviews with clinician experts in the UK have reinforced this perspective.[7] They indicated that patients with advanced or unresectable HCC are only considered for systemic therapy if they are no longer eligible for SIRT or other locoregional treatments, or if SIRT is not available to them.[7] Furthermore, clinicians have raised concerns on the limited clinical evidence on SIRT therapies as well as the ambiguous guidelines on when SIRT therapies should be used.[7] 

As mentioned above, available clinical evidence on the efficacy of SIRT treatments in HCC is weak. Studies such as SIR-TACE (comparing SIR-Spheres to TACE) and the PREMIER and Kulik et al. studies (comparing TheraSphere to TACE) did not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in outcomes, nor improved overall survival, and were associated with high levels of uncertainty due to small sample sizes and a high risk of bias.[76] Furthermore, the SARAH and SIRveNIB trials comparing SIR-Spheres with systemic therapy showed no survival advantage over sorafenib.[79, 80] 

The DOSISPHERE open-label Phase II study, which investigated TheraSphere in patients with large solitary tumours (≥7 cm), found that SIRT could be beneficial for patients with large solitary tumours who are not eligible for TACE or systemic therapy.[81] However, this evidence is associated with significant uncertainty, including imbalances in baseline characteristics and the lack of a direct comparison of SIRT to a current first-line treatment option (e.g., sorafenib).[76] UK HCC clinicians interviewed supported the use of SIRT exclusively for patients with large solitary tumours ineligible for TACE or systemic therapy.[7] 

The HEPAR Phase II study investigating the safety and efficacy of QuiremSphere in patients with HCC at BCLC stage B or C found that QuiremSphere has a manageable safety and tolerability profile.[82] As such, NICE have approved QuiremSphere for use based on a cost comparison, with QuiremSphere considered equivalent in cost and efficacy to the other SIRT therapies, SIRSpheres and TheraSphere.[77] However, there are a number of concerns regarding the robustness of QuiremSphere data, given the extremely limited evidence and the lack of high-quality, head-tohead comparisons, which hinder meaningful comparisons with other SIRT therapies. Furthermore, the existing comparative evidence is largely limited to retrospective studies that carry a high risk of bias due to imbalances in baseline characteristics between treatment arms and the absence of adjustments for confounding variables.[83, 84]

In conclusion, all three SIRT therapies are not considered a suitable comparator for individuals with advanced or unresectable HCC who are ineligible for locoregional therapy. In addition, the existing evidence on the survival benefits of SIRT in patients with advanced unresectable HCC who are eligible for locoregional treatment remains limited. 

## _**B.1.3.4.4 Unmet need in advanced or unresectable HCC**_ 

As noted above, atezolizumab + bevacizumab is the current SoC for the first-line treatment of patients with advanced or unresectable HCC in the UK, with lenvatinib and sorafenib offering alternative first-line treatment options.[3] However, the limited long-term follow-up data limits the confidence in survival extrapolation.[33] Furthermore, treatment with atezolizumab + bevacizumab requires an endoscopy ahead of administration, which not only increases NHS resource use burden, but may also introduce a delay in patients receiving potentially life-extending therapy.[7, 44] Furthermore, atezolizumab + bevacizumab may not be suitable for a considerable proportion of patients who are contraindicated to this regimen.[3, 7, 44] Accordingly, there is a significant unmet need for a novel treatment that can extend survival without increasing bleeding risk.[29] There further remains a considerable unmet need for a treatment that can contribute to alleviating the humanistic burden associated with HCC, both for the individual and their carers.[29, 85] Finally, advanced or unresectable HCC imposes a considerable economic cost on society, both directly and indirectly, hence alternative treatments that can help reduce this burden are paramount.[37, 38] 

## _**B.1.3.4.5 STRIDE for advanced or unresectable HCC**_ 

STRIDE represents a novel treatment option for patients with advanced or unresectable HCC that aims to address the unmet need that exists for this condition. STRIDE has been evaluated in the randomised, open-label, multicentre, Phase III HIMALAYA study, in which statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvements in key clinical outcomes relative to sorafenib were observed.[45] Importantly, STRIDE provided the longest follow-up from a Phase III study in this setting, establishing itself as the only approved regimen to demonstrate a survival benefit after five years in an exploratory analysis. This analysis showed that STRIDE demonstrated a 19.6% probability of OS compared to 9.4% in sorafenib after 5 years. 

This combination of two immuno-oncology (IO) therapies was hypothesised to result in complementary, long-lasting immune effects, enhanced anti-tumour activity and ultimately, improved patient outcomes, which is evidenced in the 5-year data cut from HIMALAYA.[24] Relatedly, the mechanism of action of STRIDE offers patients important advantages with regards to risk of bleeding. As described previously, patients with advanced or unresectable HCC are at increased risk of variceal bleeding as a result of conditions such as cirrhosis, portal hypertension and anticoagulant use, among others.[86] As such, treatment regimens that include anti-angiogenic agents may not be suitable for a considerable proportion of patients with advanced or unresectable HCC. No anti-angiogenic agents are included within the STRIDE regimen, making STRIDE suitable for all patients with advanced or unresectable HCC regardless of bleeding risk. 

The administration frequency of STRIDE is also advantageous when compared to current SoC. Both treatment administration and laboratory tests for STRIDE occur every four weeks, whereas with the current SoC, atezolizumab + bevacizumab, these occur every three weeks. Therefore, STRIDE presents a less burdensome treatment pathway, requiring fewer hospital visits. This reduction in visit frequency not only alleviates the burden on the NHS but also contributes to improving HRQoL for patients by reducing the number of hospital visits required.

<!-- page 34 -->

The BSG made a strong recommendation for the use of STRIDE in first-line advanced or unresectable HCC in their recent guidelines. This recommendation is underpinned by highquality clinical evidence demonstrating improved survival compared to sorafenib, a manageable toxicity profile and a reduced risk of variceal bleeding.[3, 78, 87] This recommendation is echoed by the BCLC guidelines, which highlight the superior survival outcomes with STRIDE over sorafenib as a key differentiator.[87] This aligns with the view of experts in the field, who concluded that STRIDE is a suitable first-line treatment. Furthermore, clinicians have highlighted that the unprecedented long-term efficacy data provides confidence in the regimen’s lasting benefits, while also offering particular advantages for patients at risk of GI bleeding and with other comorbidities.[88] 

Furthermore, STRIDE is suitable for some patients with BCLC Stage B, corresponding to intermediate HCC. For individuals with intermediate disease who are ineligible for locoregional therapy or no longer qualify after receiving one or more rounds of locoregional therapy, systemic therapies are offered.[3] STRIDE therefore represents a valuable treatment option for patients with unresectable intermediate HCC for patients who are not amenable to locoregional therapy. 

## **B.1.4** _**Equality considerations**_ 

It is not anticipated that the provision (or non-provision) of STRIDE within its licensed indication would exclude from consideration any people protected by equality legislation, lead to a recommendation that has a different impact on people protected by equality legislation than on the wider population, or lead to recommendations that have an adverse impact on people with a particular disability or disabilities.

## **B.2 Clinical effectiveness** 

## **Summary of clinical effectiveness** 

## **HIMALAYA trial design** 

- HIMALAYA is a randomised, multicentre, open-label, Phase III study that explored the efficacy and safety of STRIDE in patients with advanced or unresectable HCC vs. sorafenib[45] (Section B.2.2) 

- Adult patients with confirmed advanced or unresectable HCC (Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer [BCLC] stage B or C) were enrolled in the trial. Patients ineligible for receipt of locoregional therapy were included (Section B.2.3.1) 

- The primary analysis took place on 27[th] August 2021, once 555 OS events had occurred in the STRIDE and sorafenib treatment arms combined (71% maturity).[89] Two additional exploratory OS data cut-offs (DCOs) took place on 23[rd] January 2023 and 1[st] March 2024, representing four and five years of follow up, respectively 

## **Key primary and secondary endpoints** 

- HIMALAYA met its primary endpoint (DCO: 27[th] August 2021), with STRIDE demonstrating a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in OS vs. sorafenib, with a survival rate of 30.7% for STRIDE vs. 20.2% for sorafenib (HR: 0.76; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.61–0.96) (Section B.2.6.1) 

      - STRIDE consistently demonstrated an improvement in OS compared to sorafenib at all measured timepoints, including at 18, 24, 36 (the primary DCO), 48 and 60 months 

      - At the exploratory five-year analysis, STRIDE demonstrated a survival rate of 19.6% compared to 9.4% for sorafenib[90 ] 

      - These clinically meaningful results are consistent with expectations for the distinct dual immunotherapy (IO) mechanism of action of STRIDE 

      - The maturity of the HIMALAYA OS dataset is unparalleled, representing the longest OS follow-up period of any study in advanced or unresectable HCC to date, providing treating clinicians with confidence in the long-term efficacy of STRIDE 

- At the primary DCO (27[th] August 2021), a greater proportion of patients were progression-free in the STRIDE treatment arm compared with the sorafenib arm (12.5% vs. 4.9%, respectively). The median PFS for STRIDE and sorafenib was comparable (HR: 0.90; 95% CI: 0.77–1.05)[45] 

   - This comparable result between arms aligns with the typical efficacy pattern observed with IO-IO therapies, whereby the indirect mechanism of action results in a delayed treatment effect.[91] As a result, IO-IO therapies often show minor PFS benefits despite clinically significant improvements in OS. Existing literature and clinicians highlight that OS is considered the most reliable endpoint for patients with HCC, and reiterate that weak surrogacy exists between OS and PFS in advanced or unresectable HCC, particularly for treatment with IO-IO therapies[3, 92-94] (Section B.2.6.2) 

- A statistically significantly greater proportion of patients responded to STRIDE compared to sorafenib, with a four-fold increase in objective response rate (ORR), a secondary endpoint, in the STRIDE treatment arm compared to the sorafenib treatment arm (20.1% vs. 5.1%; OR: 4.69; 95% CI: 2.85–8.04; nominal p<0.0001; primary DCO: 27[th] August 2021)[45, 89] (Section B.2.6.2)

**Indirect treatment comparison** 

- The clinical SLR identified 17 studies, which were assessed for inclusion in the network meta-analysis (NMA). Three studies, the HIMALAYA, IMbrave150 and REFLECT trials, were eligible and formed a network of evidence for both OS and PFS, connected via a common sorafenib treatment arm (Section B.2.9.2 and B.2.9.3) 

- • The appropriateness of performing an NMA was assessed. Overall, the trials were generally comparable in terms of study design and patient baseline characteristics (Section B.2.9.4). However, there was a significant disparity in the length of follow-up reported across all three trials, with HIMALAYA having materially longer follow-up compared to IMbrave150 in particular 

- • There was evidence of proportional hazard (PH) assumption violation for HIMALAYA and REFLECT for OS and PFS. Time-varying analyses for REFLECT showed that the HR for lenvatinib vs. sorafenib trended towards 1 over time for both PFS and OS, meaning that the results from an NMA may overpredict survival for lenvatinib. There was no evidence of PH violation for IMbrave150, and therefore the estimate from the NMA of atezolizumab + bevacizumab vs sorafenib was unlikely to be biased 

- • A Bayesian NMA was conducted for OS and PFS to provide estimates of the relative effectiveness of STRIDE, atezolizumab + bevacizumab, lenvatinib and sorafenib. Both fixed effects (FE) and random effects (RE) models were fitted with the most appropriate model selected using the deviance information criterion (Section B.2.9.6)

## **B.2.1** _**Identification and selection of relevant studies**_ 

A systematic literature review (SLR) was conducted to identify and synthesise relevant clinical evidence on the efficacy and safety of durvalumab in combination with tremelimumab (STRIDE regimen) and other first-line treatments in patients with advanced or unresectable HCC. The original SLR was conducted on 31[st] August 2020, and subsequently underwent updates on 26[th] October 2021 and 10[th] April 2024. 

In the recent SLR update, following de-duplication of results, a total of 1,764 publications were screened at the title and abstract stage. Of these, 146 were reviewed at the full-text stage. After excluding publications that did not meet the eligibility criteria, 54 publications were included in the SLR from database searches. Supplementary searches retrieved an additional 16 articles, resulting in a total of 70 articles included from both the electronic database and supplementary searches. Following an evidence prioritisation step, in which studies of direct relevance to the submission decision problem were extracted, 14 of the 70 publications identified in the SLR update were extracted. Additionally, 26 articles were included from the original SLR and first update. Therefore, a total of 40 publications were ultimately extracted.

## **B.2.2** _**List of relevant clinical effectiveness evidence**_ 

Of the unique studies identified, only one trial (HIMALAYA) provided evidence for the clinical efficacy and safety of STRIDE in the patient population of interest for this evaluation (patients with advanced or unresectable HCC). 

## **HIMALAYA** 

The clinical effectiveness and safety of durvalumab in combination with tremelimumab for patients with advanced or unresectable HCC was assessed in HIMALAYA, a randomised, multicentre, open-label, Phase III trial. This study considered patients with advanced or unresectable HCC who were not eligible for locoregional therapy and had not received prior systemic therapy for HCC.[4] 

A total of four treatment arms were analysed: 

- **STRIDE** : A single dose of tremelimumab (300 mg) and durvalumab (1,500 mg Q4W) 

- Durvalumab 1,500 mg monotherapy Q4W 

- **Sorafenib** (400 mg) twice daily (BID) 

- T75+D: A dose of tremelimumab (75 mg Q4W) and durvalumab (1,500 mg Q4W) 

For this submission, only the STRIDE and sorafenib arms are considered relevant (the other two regimens are not licensed nor anticipated to be licensed for the indication of relevance to this submission). Accordingly, results presented within the submission are for these two treatment arms only. Further information on the trial design can be found in Section B.2.3.2. An overview of HIMALAYA is included in Table 4, with the methodology and results of the trial presented in the sections that follow.

## **B.2.3.2 Trial design** 

The trial initially planned to screen approximately 1,600 patients and randomly assign 1,200 patients across each of the four treatment arms in a 1:1:1:1 ratio using an interactive web response system (IWRS).[4, 22] The protocol was altered after the T75+D treatment arm was closed following a risk-benefit assessment. This decision was based on results from a preplanned analysis evaluating tolerability and clinical activity in a Phase II trial (Study 22; NCT02519348), in which the efficacy data for the T75+D regimen did not differentiate from the durvalumab monotherapy arm.[22] As a result, there was insufficient clinical activity observed in Study 22 to warrant continuation of enrolment in the T75+D arm in the HIMALAYA study. Consequently, the planned sample size was increased from 1,200 to 1,310 patients. This included 385 patients allocated to the STRIDE, durvalumab monotherapy and sorafenib arm, as well as 155 to T75+D arm, who were randomly assigned before enrolment closure.[4] 

The key inclusion and exclusion criteria are outlined in Table 5. The following stratification factors were applied during randomisation: MVI (Yes or No), aetiology of liver disease (HBV vs. HCV vs. others) and ECOG performance status (0 or 1). Patients continued their assigned treatment arm until confirmed disease progression, unacceptable toxicity or met any of the trial discontinuation criteria. However, patients with confirmed progressed disease (PD) who, in the Investigator’s opinion, continued to receive benefit from their assigned treatment and met the criteria for treatment in the setting of PD, could continue to receive their assigned treatment regimen. 

The finalised distribution of patients and methodology of drug administration across treatment arms are below, with the two treatment arms relevant to this submission marked in **bold** (Figure 3): 

- **STRIDE** (a single dose of tremelimumab [300 mg] + durvalumab [1,500 mg] Q4W [T300+D]): 393 patients 

- **Sorafenib** (400 mg) BID: 389 patients 

- Durvalumab monotherapy (1,500 mg) Q4W: 389 patients 

- T75+D (tremelimumab [75 mg] Q4W for four doses + durvalumab [1,500 mg] Q4W): 153 patients

## **B.2.3.3 Data cut-offs** 

## **Data cut-offs** 

The key analyses conducted for the HIMALAYA study relevant for this submission are: 

- **Primary analysis:** The primary analysis was performed once 555 OS events occurred in the STRIDE and sorafenib arms combined (representing 71% maturity), 47 months after the first patient was randomised (DCO: 27[th] August 2021). This is the DCO considered for all secondary endpoints[4, 89] 

- **Updated analysis I:** The updated analysis evaluated the OS and safety of STRIDE vs. sorafenib with 4 years of follow-up (DCO: 23[rd] January 2023)[98] 

- **Updated analysis II:** Additional five-year OS analysis has been conducted for STRIDE vs. sorafenib, representing the longest follow up to date in Phase III studies in advanced or unresectable HCC (DCO: 1[st] March 2024) 

It should be noted that the primary analysis was powered for statistical analysis. The updated analyses were exploratory endpoints intended to assess the long-term effectiveness of STRIDE, thus capturing the high level of maturity within the dataset, but they were not powered for statistical analysis.

## **B.2.4** _**Patient characteristics**_ 

The demographic and key baseline characteristics of the overall population of patients included in the HIMALAYA trial are presented in Table 9. The treatment arms were balanced in terms of demographic and baseline characteristics.[4] In addition, the stratification factors comprising aetiology of liver disease (determined by virology laboratory assessments at screening), MVI and ECOG PS were also balanced across treatment arms.[4] 

Both arms of this trial are representative of patients with advanced or unresectable HCC in the UK, as evidenced by a recent prospective, multicentre audit of 361 patients with advanced HCC in the UK.[103] The audit involved 11 UK centres providing specialist care to liver cancer patients, and reported comparable baseline characteristics to the HIMALAYA trial, including a similar percentage of male participants (82%), average age (68, range 21–87), Child-Pugh scores (5 and 6 in 75% and 25% of individuals, respectively) and baseline alpha-fetoprotein (AFP; ≥400 ng/mL in 37% of individuals).[103] The alignment between the HIMALAYA trial and the UK population was validated through clinician interviews. Slight deviations were noted in the baseline populations; for example, a higher incidence of non-viral HCC aetiology is observed in the UK compared to HIMALAYA. This is attributed to increased rates of metabolic dysfunctionassociated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and alcohol consumption, particularly in UK cities. Nonetheless, clinicians expected these variations and still considered this dataset to be generalisable to UK clinical practice.[7]

## **B.2.6** _**Clinical effectiveness results of the relevant studies**_ 

## **B.2.6.1 Primary endpoint: overall survival** 

Overall survival is defined as the time from the date of randomisation until death due to any cause, regardless of whether the patient withdrew from randomised therapy or received another anticancer therapy. Any patient not known to have died at the DCO date was censored based on the last recorded date on which the patient was known to be alive. If the last known date alive or if the date of death was after the DCO date, patients were censored at the DCO date. 

HIMALAYA met its primary endpoint (DCO: 27[th] August 2021), with STRIDE demonstrating a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in OS vs. sorafenib, with a median survival of 16.43 months (95% CI: 14.16–19.58) vs. 13.77 months (95% CI: 12.25–16.13; Appendix M). In the exploratory 4-year updated analysis I (DCO: 23[rd] January 2023), STRIDE maintained improved OS results, with survival probabilities of 25.2% for STRIDE compared to 15.1% for sorafenib (Appendix M).[104] Most recently, in the exploratory 5-year (DCO: 1[st] March 2024) updated analysis II, the survival probabilities were 19.6% for STRIDE compared to 9.4% for sorafenib (Table 11). This represents the most mature OS dataset available for a systemic therapy in advanced or unresectable HCC, thereby enabling clinicians to have confidence in the long-term survival benefits of STRIDE for their patients.[104]

The HIMALAYA outcomes for OS are highly promising for patients with advanced or unresectable HCC in the UK. The mature dataset, which includes three-year primary analysis data along with four and five-year OS exploratory analyses, demonstrates a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in survival relative to sorafenib over the longest follow-up duration observed in this setting. The availability of an alternative therapy that enhances survival compared to current therapies will be of significant value to patients with advanced or unresectable HCC and their families. 

## **B.2.6.2 Secondary endpoints: efficacy** 

Five key secondary endpoints were used to assess the efficacy of STRIDE compared to sorafenib in patients with advanced or unresectable HCC. These included PFS, TTP, ORR, DoR and DCR. At the primary DCO (27[th] August 2021), all five endpoints are assessed in all individuals in the FAS according to RECIST 1.1 by Investigator assessment.

## _**B.2.6.2.1 Progression-free survival**_ 

PFS is defined as the time from the date of randomisation until the date of objective progressive disease (PD) or death by any cause in the absence of PD, regardless of whether the patient withdrew from study treatment or received another anticancer therapy prior to progression. As PFS was not included in multiple testing procedure (MTP), it is not controlled for multiplicity and statistical testing was performed at a nominal 5% significance level (please see Table 7 for more detail on statistical analyses).[89, 98] 

At the primary analysis (DCO: 27[th] August 2021), the Kaplan-Meier estimate for median PFS was similar in both treatment arms. Median PFS was 3.78 months in the STRIDE treatment arm compared with 4.07 months in the sorafenib treatment arm (Table 12 and Figure 6).[4] Despite this, a greater proportion of patients were progression-free at the primary analysis in the STRIDE treatment arm compared with the sorafenib arm (12.5% vs. 4.9%; Table 12).[4] 

This finding of similarity in median PFS for STRIDE relative to sorafenib aligns with the typical efficacy pattern observed with IO-IO therapies, where the indirect mechanism of action, specifically, the inhibition of cellular pathways that down-regulate the immune response, subsequently allowing the upregulation of the immune system to target cancer cells (see Section B.1.2), often results in a delayed treatment effect.[91] As a result, the observed PFS benefit is often minor with IO-IO therapies, whilst a clinically significant improvement in OS is observed.[3, 92-94] 

Recent interviews with UK HCC experts highlighted the importance of the prolongation of OS as a key outcome for patients with HCC and their carers, with one clinical expert emphasising that OS is the most important endpoint for decision-making in advanced or unresectable HCC. Supporting this, Huang et al. published a study in 2024 in which an SLR and meta-regression of Phase I–III clinical trials of IO therapies in unresectable HCC was performed. Meta-regression of OS and surrogate endpoints identified a particularly weak correlation between PFS and OS (R[2] : 0.352, 95% CI: 0.000–0.967) across Phase II and III trials, with the authors concluding that PFS has limited utility as a surrogate endpoint in unresectable HCC. Potential reasons for this offered by the authors were the role of pseudoprogression, in which the tumour may show local enlargement or the appearance of new lesions at the beginning of treatment, but then significant therapeutic effects can appear subsequently, in addition to the role of liver decompensation as a key risk factor for mortality in HCC.[94] 

The clinical experts consulted echoed the findings of this study, highlighting that firstly, the measurement of PFS is challenging, as radiologic progression is a subjective measurement prone to reading errors.[106] Secondly, it was also noted that patients are frequently eligible to continue treatment both within the trial setting and real-world setting even after disease progression.[4] This is crucial for patients with limited subsequent treatment options, as is the case for advanced or unresectable HCC, however, it undermines PFS as a reliable prognostic marker for OS. Collectively, these findings indicate a weak surrogacy between PFS and OS in advanced or unresectable HCC, particularly when IO-IO therapies are used. Overall, OS is considered the most reliable endpoint for evaluation of efficacy in this setting by clinical experts.[7, 93]

## _**B.2.6.2.2 Time to progression**_ 

TTP is defined as the time from randomisation until objective tumour progression in the absence of death. If a patient died without tumour progression, they were censored at the time of death. 

At the primary analyses, the Kaplan-Meier estimate of median TTP was 5.4 months (95% CI: 3.8–5.6) in the STRIDE treatment arm and 5.6 months (95% CI: 5.1–5.8) in the sorafenib treatment arm (Figure 7).[4]

## _**B.2.6.2.3 Response rates**_ 

Upon receipt of cancer treatment, there are four categories of response level that can be achieved: complete response (CR), partial response (PR), stable disease (SD) and progressive disease (PD). ORR is defined as the percentage of patients with at least one unconfirmed visit response of CR or PR. Data obtained up until PD, or the last evaluable assessment in the absence of PD, was included in the assessment of ORR. Patients who discontinued the assigned treatment regimen without PD or received a subsequent therapy and then responded were not included as responders in the ORR. 

At the primary analysis, the ORR based on Investigator assessment according to RECIST 1.1 for confirmed response was 20.1% for the STRIDE treatment arm, and 5.1% for the sorafenib treatment arm.[4] Treatment with STRIDE had a nominally greater likelihood of response *** ***** *** *** ********** ******* ******** compared to sorafenib ( ).[89] Confirmed CRs were only observed in patients in the STRIDE treatment arm (n=12/393, 3.1%), with no complete Company evidence submission for durvalumab with tremelimumab for untreated unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma [ID2725]

## **B.2.6.2.5 Duration of response** 

DoR is defined as the time from the date of first documented response (CR or PR) until the first date of documented PD, or death in the absence of PD. 

At the primary analysis, the median DoR from onset for patients with an objective response was found to be greater for patients in the STRIDE treatment arm (22.3 months) than for patients in the sorafenib treatment arm (18.4 months). At ** ****** following onset of response, the percentage of patients remaining in response was *********** ****** for the ****** treatment arm compared with the ********* treatment arm (***** vs. ****** respectively). This aligns with expectations of the STRIDE mechanism of action, in which a strong and durable stimulation of the immune system to attack cancer cells is elicited. However, it should be noted that the number of responders in the sorafenib treatment arm is low (20 patients achieving PR and no patients achieving CR), leading to uncertainty in the median estimate for this arm.[4, 89] Detailed DoR results are presented in Table 14.

## **B.2.6.3 Patient-reported outcomes** 

## _**B.2.6.3.1 EORTC QLQ-C30 and EORTC QLQ-HCC18**_ 

A secondary objective of the HIMALAYA study was to assess disease-related symptoms, impacts and HRQoL of the STRIDE regimen vs. sorafenib.[89, 107] Two PRO instruments were used to measure patient HRQoL as a secondary objective in the HIMALAYA trial: the EORTC QLQ-C30 and EORTC QLQ-18-item HCC HRQoL questionnaire (EORTC QLQ-HCC18).[107] 

The EORTC QLQ-C30 is a 30-item self-administered questionnaire which reviews five functional scales, three symptom scales and a global health status. The EORTC QLQ-HCC18 is an 18-item self-administered questionnaire developed and validated specifically for HCC. 

Baseline EORTC QLQ-C30 and EORTC QLQ-HCC18 were mostly comparable for patients in the STRIDE and sorafenib treatment arms, and scores were generally towards the higher end of the scale for physical functioning for STRIDE but reduced for GHS/QoL (Table 15). Additionally, there was a trend towards more severe symptoms at baseline in the sorafenib treatment arm, in particular for fatigue, appetite loss, abdominal pain, and shoulder pain.[107]

## **B.2.7** _**Subgroup analysis**_ 

Subgroup analyses were undertaken to assess the consistency of treatment effect across a range of important clinical and demographic characteristics (Figure 13). 

The OS benefit favouring STRIDE treatment vs. sorafenib treatment was consistent across most pre-specified subgroups, evidenced by the fact that the HR point estimate for each subgroup was contained within the 95% CI of the HR for the overall population. Some variability was observed, particularly in the female sex subgroup and the subgroup of patients with confirmed HCV disease. For analysis of the female sex subgroup, this variability is likely due to the small sample size (<100 patients were enrolled in each treatment arm). For HCV, a post-hoc analysis of baseline covariates within the HCV subgroup identified potential imbalances in prognostic factors between the groups. Despite this, the overall subgroup analyses demonstrate that the OS benefit observed in the intention-to-treat (ITT) population was consistent across stratification and prespecified subgroups.[45] This benefit was also seen at the primary DCO (Appendix E).

## **B.2.8** _**Meta-analysis**_ 

A meta-analysis is a common statistical method used to generate aggregate measures of effect from individual trials. As only one trial of STRIDE was performed (i.e. HIMALAYA), no metaanalysis was completed. 

## **B.2.9** _**Indirect and mixed treatment comparisons**_ 

## **Summary of network meta-analysis** 

- The SLR identified 17 studies which were assessed for inclusion in the NMA, of which three studies were determined eligible for inclusion, including the HIMALAYA, IMbrave150 and REFLECT trials (Section B.2.9.2). These studies were used to form a network of evidence for STRIDE, atezolizumab + bevacizumab and lenvatinib, for both OS and PFS, connected via a common sorafenib treatment arm (Section B.2.9.3) 

- The appropriateness of performing an NMA was assessed. Overall, the three trials were generally comparable in terms of study design and patient baseline characteristics (Section B.2.9.4) 

- There was significant disparity in length of follow-up between the three trials. However, NMA models allowing for a time-varying treatment effect were not considered appropriate, as they would be limited in their ability to compare long-term efficacy due to the short follow-up for IMbrave150 in particular 

- There was evidence of proportional hazard (PH) assumption violation for HIMALAYA and REFLECT for OS and PFS. Time-varying analyses conducted for RELFECT suggested a positive treatment effect for lenvatinib at the beginning of the study follow-up that diminishes over time, meaning that the results of the NMA may overpredict survival for lenvatinib 

- There was no evidence of PH violation for IMBrave150, and therefore the estimate from the NMA of atezolizumab + bevacizumab vs sorafenib was unlikely to be biased 

- • A Bayesian NMA was conducted for both OS and PFS to provide estimates of the relative efficacy of STRIDE, atezolizumab + bevacizumab, lenvatinib and sorafenib. Both fixed and 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab with tremelimumab for untreated unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma [ID2725] 

© AstraZeneca (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 65 -->

- random effects models were fitted with the most appropriate model selected using the deviance information criterion (Section B.2.9.6) 

- • For both OS and PFS, the RE model with informative prior was selected (Section B.2.9.7) • For OS, using the ****** OS data-cut from HIMALAYA, the NMA results found that STRIDE and atezolizumab + bevacizumab improved OS compared with sorafenib, with consistent point estimates to those seen in trial results (*** **** **** **** *********** **** **********]; respectively). However, Crls intervals all crossed 1, indicating no statistical differences between all comparators and sorafenib in the RE model with informative prior 

- • For OS, the NMA found that lenvatinib had a HR close to 1 in the comparison to sorafenib, with a similar point estimate to the non-inferiority REFLECT trial (**** ***********) 

- • For investigator-assessed (INV) PFS, the NMA results found that atezolizumab + bevacizumab, lenvatinib and STRIDE all showed improved PFS compared with sorafenib (HR: **** **** **** *********** **** ************ **** **********]; respectively), again reflecting point estimates from trial results but with no statistical differences observed in the RE model with informative prior 

- • The key area of uncertainty in the NMA was related to the significant disparity in the length of follow-up reported across the included trials, with HIMALAYA having materially longer follow-up compared to IMbrave150 in particular 

- • The PH assumption for HIMALAYA and REFLECT was violated. The uncertainty associated with violations of the PH assumption was addressed in the economic model by independently fitting curves for HIMALAYA. For the comparative effectiveness input in the model for lenvatinib vs sorafenib, given the statistical non-inferiority observed in REFLECT between these two treatments, the HR is set to 1 for OS.[73] For PFS, time-varying analyses conducted for REFLECT suggested the positive treatment effect for lenvatinib diminishes over the course of the study, meaning that the application of a constant HR in the model could be considered conservative. The standard NMA results for atezolizumab + bevacizumab vs. sorafenib were not affected by PH assumption violations 

- • Overall, the NMA identified that STRIDE was associated with a comparable improvement in survival vs. sorafenib compared to atezolizumab + bevacizumab, the key comparator in this submission 

## **B.2.9.1 Identification of comparator studies** 

As described in Section B.2.1, a clinical SLR was conducted which identified and synthesised relevant clinical evidence on the efficacy and safety of STRIDE and other first-line treatments in patients with advanced or unresectable HCC. The SLR identified 88 publications on 17 unique studies which were considered for inclusion in the NMA. 

Full details of the SLR are provided in Appendix D. 

## **B.2.9.2 Eligibility for the network meta-analysis** 

Studies identified in the SLR were assessed for their eligibility for inclusion in NMAs. To permit comparisons with STRIDE via the treatment arms in HIMALAYA, studies were eligible if they included as treatment arms only the comparators of interest, as shown in Table 17. Specifically, first-line treatments included were those considered comparators to STRIDE in current UK clinical practice for the treatment of advanced or unresectable HCC and align with the decision problem (Section B.1.1). Nivolumab was not included as a comparator given it has not been recommended in the UK for untreated, unresectable HCC. Otherwise, studies were not excluded on the basis of patient population, outcomes and study design, since the eligibility criteria applied

## **B.2.9.4 Heterogeneity across included trials** 

## _**B.2.9.4.1 Study design**_ 

The study designs of included studies were generally comparable (see Appendix D). All studies were large, international, Phase III RCTs. Eligibility criteria were similar across the studies, particularly in reference to HCC aetiology, ECOG PS, Child Pugh Score and presence of ascites. HIMALAYA and REFLECT both additionally specified BCLC criteria B or C. Notably, there were some differences in eligibility based on tumour location. IMbrave150 included 15% of patients with a tumour thrombus in the main trunk and/or contralateral portal vein (PVT stage VP4) whereas these patients were excluded from both HIMALAYA and REFLECT due to their poor prognosis. 

## _**B.2.9.4.2 Patient characteristics and treatment effect modifiers**_ 

The patient populations of the eligible studies were generally comparable, although there were some differences identified (see Appendix D). The difference in eligibility criteria relating to tumour location contributed to a difference in MVI prevalence in participants at baseline, with IMbrave150 having a higher prevalence than HIMALAYA and REFLECT. 

A number of patient characteristics were identified as potential treatment effect modifiers (TEMs) in HCC, i.e., patient characteristics that impact the relative effect of a treatment. TEMs have the potential to bias analyses if there are notable imbalances across trials. There was some variation identified across three potential TEMs in the included studies (aetiology, MVI/EHS and region), and this was explored further. Other potential TEMs (AFP level, BCLC stage, ECOG score and gender) were found to have little differences in the distribution of characteristics across studies. Further details on all potential TEMs are provided in Appendix D. 

Disease aetiology was investigated by assessing subgroup results across trials from patients with HBV, HCV and nonviral subgroups across HIMALAYA, REFLECT and IMbrave150 (Section B.2.7 for HIMALAYA). No clear conclusions could be drawn on HCV and nonviral subgroups, due to lack of clarity on the direction of bias for HCV subgroups and wide confidence intervals as a result of the relatively small sample sizes in the alcohol (nonviral) subgroup for REFLECT and both the HCV and nonviral subgroups for IMbrave150. However, patients with HBV across 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab with tremelimumab for untreated unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma [ID2725] 

© AstraZeneca (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 68 -->

HIMALAYA, REFLECT and IMbrave150 trials demonstrated improved OS compared with the non-HBV populations in these trials. Based on these results, it was noted that the lower proportion of patients with HBV in HIMALAYA compared to IMbrave150 and REFLECT could lead to the treatment effect of STRIDE being underestimated relative to the two comparator studies. However, while there was some evidence of treatment effect modification in favour of lenvatinib and atezolizumab + bevacizumab based on disease aetiology, as disease aetiology was not a stratification factor during randomisation for either trial, the subgroups may not have been balanced for prognostic factors, and the studies were ultimately not designed to detect subgroup effects for these populations. Patients were stratified for disease aetiology in HIMALAYA. Clinicians interviewed by AstraZeneca further suggested that the role of aetiology as a TEM was not conclusive, and it was therefore decided not to explore more complex methods to adjust for disease aetiology in the NMA. 

Differences in the location and degree of liver invasion across trials were expected due to differences in exclusion criteria for IMbrave150 compared with HIMALAYA and REFLECT highlighted above. As such, this was investigated further using data from Breder _et al._ which excluded patients with PVT stage VP4 from analyses.[111] This analysis found that the OS point estimate for this subgroup of patients in IMbrave150 (0.62 [0.34, 1.11])[111] was similar to that of the rest of the ITT population (0.67 [0.51, 0.88]). Furthermore, subgroup analyses of patients with (0.64 [0.49, 0.81]) and without (0.64 [0.38, 1.10]) MVI/EHS also had similar point estimates for OS, indicating a limited influence of differences in the location and degree of liver invasion in modifying treatment effect. 

Geographical region was not included as a stratification factor for HIMALAYA but was included in REFLECT and IMbrave150. A greater proportion of study centres in REFLECT were in Asia compared with HIMALAYA and IMbrave150. However, OS results from REFLECT for subgroups of patients in both Western and Asia-Pacific regions both did not demonstrate a statistical difference between lenvatinib and sorafenib. OS results from IMbrave150 for a subgroup of patients in centres in Asia (excluding Japan), and centres in the rest of the world demonstrated a statistical difference between atezolizumab + bevacizumab and sorafenib. 

In summary, differences identified in potential TEMs across the trials were not considered to bias the analyses. None of the trials investigated were sized for individual subgroup analyses, and many subgroup results were not based on stratified subgroups. Meta-regression techniques to adjust for these characteristics as sensitivity analyses using aggregate data were infeasible due to a small number of studies (<10) being included in NMAs. Therefore, methods for population adjustment were not considered further and unadjusted NMAs were conducted. 

## _**B.2.9.4.3 Progression-free survival assessor type**_ 

As only investigator-assessed PFS was collected in HIMALAYA, the NMA used investigatorassessed PFS across all studies to ensure alignment with HIMALAYA. Investigator-assessed PFS was available across all included studies, however exact definitions varied. Within HIMALAYA and IMbrave150, investigators assessed PFS according to RECIST 1.1 and in REFLECT, investigators assessed PFS according to the modified response evaluation criteria in solid tumours (mRECIST).[112] No adjustments can be made for the differences between mRECIST and RECIST 1.1, but a study comparing mRECIST to RECIST 1.1 found that the performance of both criteria in assessing disease progression is identical.

There were differences in follow-up across the studies, with HIMALAYA having the longest follow-up of the three studies in the network. Under proportional hazards, the effect of treatment is assumed to be constant over time, and differences in duration of follow-up are unlikely to bias results. Moreover, NMA models allowing for a time-varying treatment effect, such as piecewise parametric, spline or fractional polynomial NMAs were not considered appropriate, as they would nonetheless be limited in their ability to compare long term efficacy due to the short follow-up for IMbrave150 in particular. 

## **B.2.9.5 Proportional hazards** 

The credibility of the PH assumption, which assumes that the relative hazard of the outcome of interest between treatment arms remains constant over time, was assessed for all studies included in the OS and PFS networks. 

The assessment for HIMALAYA was based on the analysis of individual patient data (IPD). For REFLECT and IMbrave150, the published Kaplan-Meier curves were digitised and the IPD reconstructed based on the Guyot algorithm.[113] Each digitised curve was compared to estimates reported in the original publication (including median time to event and HR) to ensure the validity of the digitisation step. The formal assessment of the PH assumption was then based on the visual inspection of the Kaplan-Meier curves, the log-log plot, the Schoenfeld residuals plot and the Grambsh and Therneau test.[114-117]

Results from the assessment of PHs are summarised in Table 20, where evidence of violation is indicated by curves in the log-log plot not being approximately parallel, and/or the p-value of the Schoenfeld test being less than 0.05. Further details of the assessment are given in Appendix D. The assessment indicated that there was no evidence of proportional hazard (PH) violation for IMbrave150, and therefore the estimate from the NMA of atezolizumab + bevacizumab vs sorafenib was unlikely to be biased. However, there was evidence of PH assumption violation for HIMALAYA and REFLECT for OS and PFS. In particular, use of HRs estimated from an NMA for comparisons involving STRIDE and lenvatinib may be biased and are unlikely to be an accurate reflection of hazards over the full follow-up period for OS and PFS. 

For treatment comparisons via sorafenib in the NMA, more advanced methods such as fractional polynomial or piecewise models were deemed unnecessary and overly complex. In particular, complex NMAs would either require strong assumptions or be limited to the follow-up period of the trial with the shortest follow-up, and therefore fail to capture the full treatment effect of STRIDE. While the limited reporting on longer follow-up for IMbrave150 and REFLECT constitutes a limitation for both the standard NMA and potential complex analyses, the comparison between atezolizumab + bevacizumab and sorafenib can be robustly estimated by a standard NMA given that there is no evidence of PH violation for IMbrave150 across PFS and OS endpoints. 

As there was evidence of non-proportional hazards for REFLECT, the HR between lenvatinib and sorafenib may vary over the follow-up time. Therefore, time-varying HR was calculated from REFLECT for OS and PFS (detailed methodology and results in Appendix N). For this analysis, a series of parametric survival models were fit to a data set containing both arms (lenvatinib and sorafenib) of the REFLECT trial, with the inclusion of a treatment covariate (lenvatinib vs. sorafenib) on the shape and scale parameters.[73] The resulting models predict time-varying HRs. The time-varying HRs from the PFS and OS models suggest a positive treatment effect at the beginning of the study follow-up that diminishes over time, leading to convergence of the lenvatinib and sorafenib arms in both the PFS and OS curves; this is consistent with the KaplanMeier plots presented in Appendix N. Therefore, the results of the NMA may overpredict survival for lenvatinib. 

For lenvatinib, given that it is hypothesised that the application of a constant HR for REFLECT may overpredict long-term survival for lenvatinib, results from the REFLECT trial were taken directly to inform the cost-effectiveness model for OS, specifically a HR of 1, capturing the statistical non-inferiority observed in REFLECT between the two treatments. This is viewed as conservative given that the time-varying analysis predicts HR above 1 over time for most models (see Appendix N). Non-inferiority for PFS was not observed in REFLECT, therefore the NMA

The uncertainty associated with violations of the PH assumption for HIMALAYA will be addressed in the economic model by independently fitting curves to the patient-level data from the HIMALAYA study, as recommend in NICE Decision Support Unit (DSU) Technical Support Document (TSD) 14.[118] 

## **B.2.9.6 Methods** 

Bayesian analyses were conducted for both OS and PFS, where input data preparation and models to be fitted were determined by OS and PFS being time-to-event outcomes. In a Bayesian NMA, a ‘statistical difference’ is ascertained by a result in which the 95% CrI does not include the null value (0) in the case of mean differences, and 1 in the case of odds/HRs. 

For the NMAs of OS and PFS, a normal distribution with an identity link was specified, as recommended in the NICE DSU TSD 2 for an NMA of treatment differences, which was modelled using a log HR on the continuous scale.[119] 

Both FE and RE models were fitted. The deviance information criterion (DIC), total residual deviance and effective number of parameters were generated and compared between models. If random effects models failed to converge, an informative prior on the between-study SD parameter τ was considered, using the methods of Turner _et al_ .[120] For each analysis, the most appropriate model was selected by comparing the DIC between the RE and FE models; as the RE model allows for between-study heterogeneity, this was selected in preference to the FE model unless the DIC improved by at least five points in the FE model. 

Each study had only two arms and therefore multi-arm adjustment was not required. No closed loops of evidence were present in the network (Figure 14), so an assessment of inconsistency was not required. 

Model parameters were estimated using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method implemented in OpenBUGS, version 3.2.3 (revision 1012).[121-123] The initial prior distributions used are listed in Table 21. Distribution parameters for each of the vague priors were modified as required if there were truncation or convergence issues. The informative priors used, as recommended by Turner _et al_ . are detailed in Table 22.
