## **B.2.9.8 Uncertainties in the indirect and mixed treatment comparisons** 

The eligibility criteria for inclusion of studies in the NMA required that all evidence considered was from Phase III RCTs, and as such ensured, as far as possible, that each included study provided high quality evidence. 

While patient populations were largely similar across the three included studies, differences in aetiology may have underestimated NMA results for STRIDE due to the relatively low prevalence of HBV in the HIMALAYA population compared with IMbrave150 and REFLECT. However, as there is no conclusive evidence on the role of aetiology as a TEM, this is not considered a key uncertainty within the analyses and is not anticipated to have material impact on the results. 

Follow-up times varied across studies, with a substantially longer follow-up time in HIMALAYA compared to REFLECT and IMbrave150. As a result, the standard NMA approach deployed will not have fully captured changes over time across the studies. However, more complex methods to address the difference in follow-up times were not expected to rectify this issue. 

The violation of the PH assumption for HIMALAYA and REFLECT may have also introduced uncertainty to the results. However, models such as fractional polynomial or piecewise models were deemed unnecessary and overly complex, and would have strong limitations in their ability to compare long term efficacy due to the short follow-up for IMbrave150 in particular. Instead, the uncertainty associated with violations of the PH assumption for HIMALAYA was addressed in the economic model by independently fitting curves to the patient-level data from the HIMALAYA study, as recommend in NICE DSU TSD 14.[118] For lenvatinib, given that it is hypothesised that the application of a constant HR to the sorafenib arm may overpredict long-term survival for lenvatinib, OS results from the REFLECT trial were taken directly to inform the cost-effectiveness model, specifically an HR of 1, capturing the statistical non-inferiority observed between the two treatments in the trial. Given non-inferiority between the two treatments was not observed for PFS in REFLECT, the NMA estimate is used for PFS in the model (Section B.3.3.2). The standard NMA results for atezolizumab + bevacizumab vs. sorafenib were unaffected by PH assumption violations and could therefore be used in the model. 

## **B.2.9.9 Conclusions of the indirect and mixed treatment comparisons** 

The NMA showed that STRIDE is an effective treatment for advanced or unresectable HCC, with numerically improved OS and PFS compared with sorafenib. Overall, the NMA identified that

## **B.2.10** _**Adverse reactions**_ 

STRIDE demonstrated a favourable safety profile, with the overall evaluation of safety and tolerability of the STRIDE regimen was generally consistent with that observed in previous studies with durvalumab and tremelimumab.[89, 124] No new adverse drug reactions were identified for the STRIDE regimen and no new safety findings were observed in patients with HCC.[22] Furthermore, in both arms, AEs were manageable according to toxicity management guidelines.[89, 124]

## **B.2.10.3.2 Haemorrhagic events** 

Due to their underlying liver disease and high incidence of portal hypertension, patients with advanced or unresectable HCC are at a particularly high risk of GI bleeding. This risk may be exacerbated by antiangiogenic agents such as bevacizumab, for which bleeding is a known safety concern.[57, 68] As such, it is recommended that all individuals undergo an endoscopy to assess the presence of gastroesophageal varices before starting treatment with atezolizumab + bevacizumab. However, access to an endoscopy in the NHS can be challenging, potentially delaying or precluding treatment.[3, 57] 

The overall frequency of haemorrhagic-related TRAEs was very low for both total and grade ≥3 events, with the frequency of patients reporting any haemorrhagic TRAE **** **** ***** ** **** in the sorafenib arm (****) compared with the STRIDE arm (***** Table 29).[89] No gastrointestinal or intra-abdominal events were observed with STRIDE, whereas gastrointestinal haemorrhages (n=3, 0.8%) and intra-abdominal haemorrhages (n=1, 0.3%) were observed with sorafenib. No oesophageal varices haemorrhages were seen with either STRIDE or sorafenib (Table 29). Furthermore, no treatment-related deaths due to AEs in the haemorrhage standardised MedDRA queries (SMQs) were reported in the STRIDE arm. In contrast, the sorafenib arm reported *** treatment-related deaths: *** from a cerebral haematoma and *** from haematuria.[89] These findings indicate that STRIDE is not associated with an increased bleeding risk.

## **B.2.11.** _**Ongoing studies**_ 

There are currently no ongoing studies of relevance to this evaluation. 

## **B.2.12.** _**Interpretation of clinical effectiveness and safety evidence**_ 

The clinical effectiveness and safety of durvalumab in combination with tremelimumab for patients with advanced or unresectable HCC was assessed in HIMALAYA, a randomised, multicentre, open-label, Phase III trial. This study considered patients with advanced or unresectable HCC who were ineligible for locoregional therapy and had not received prior systemic therapy for HCC (first-line setting).[4] 

HIMALAYA met its primary endpoint (DCO: 27[th] August 2021), with STRIDE demonstrating a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in OS vs. sorafenib, with a median survival of 16.43 months (95% CI: 14.16–19.58) vs. 13.77 months (95% CI: 12.25–16.13).[4] At all recorded landmarks, a greater number of patients were alive in the STRIDE treatment arm compared with the sorafenib treatment arm; in the primary DCO (three years) OS rates were 30.7% and 20.2% in the STRIDE treatment arm and sorafenib treatment arm, respectively (95% CI: 25.8–35.7);[4] in updated analysis I (four years), 25.2% survival was observed in the STRIDE treatment arm vs. 15.1% for sorafenib;[98 ] most recently, in updated analysis II (five years), the survival probability in the STRIDE arm was 19.6% compared to 9.4% in the sorafenib arm.[90] The maturity of the OS dataset in HIMALAYA is unprecedented, capturing the longest OS follow-up period in any study in advanced or unresectable HCC to date. These sustained, improved OS results can be easily understood by patients and their caregivers, highlighting the crucial role of improved long-term survival in alleviating clinical burden and enhancing health-related quality of life for patients and their carers.[7] 

STRIDE also demonstrated positive results for the secondary outcomes in HIMALAYA. A greater proportion of patients in the STRIDE treatment arm achieved a confirmed ORR compared with patients in the sorafenib treatment arm (20.1% vs. 5.1%, respectively). Additionally, 3.1% of patients in the STRIDE arm achieved a CR, a key surrogate outcome for OS, whereas no patients achieved this in the sorafenib arm.[45] The median DoR based on Investigator assessment was numerically longer in the STRIDE treatment arm than in the sorafenib treatment arm (22.3 months vs. 18.4 months, respectively), with a numerically higher for the STRIDE treatment arm compared with the sorafenib treatment arm (***** vs. ****** respectively).[45] 

At the primary DCO (27[th] August 2021), a greater proportion of patients were progression-free in the STRIDE treatment arm compared with the sorafenib arm (12.5% vs. 4.9%, respectively). The median PFS for STRIDE and sorafenib were comparable (HR: 0.90; 95% CI: 0.77–1.05).[45] As discussed in Section B.2.6.2, this aligns with the typical efficacy pattern of IO-IO therapies, where observed PFS benefits are minor, but OS improvement is clinically and statistically significant. UK HCC experts confirmed that PFS is not a reliable surrogate for OS in advanced or unresectable HCC. This is due to the subjective nature of radiologic progression and the continuation of treatment beyond progression. This finding is further supported by a recent publication by Huang et al., which demonstrated a weak correlation between PFS and OS in 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab with tremelimumab for untreated unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma [ID2725] 

© AstraZeneca (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 86 -->

patients with unresectable HCC.[94] Collectively, these findings indicate weak surrogacy between PFS and OS in HCC, particularly with IO-IO therapies. Therefore, OS is considered the most valuable metric when assessing the efficacy of different treatment options in this disease area.[7] 

STRIDE further resulted in improvements in PROs, including longer median time to deterioration of all EORTC QLQ-C30 and EORTC QLQ-HCC18 scores, including GHS/QoL, physical functioning and disease-related symptoms, except for jaundice, where sorafenib was nominally higher. Furthermore, it well-tolerated from the patient perspective with no meaningful impact on HRQoL compared with treatment with sorafenib.[95] 

Importantly, STRIDE demonstrated a favourable safety profile; all AEs were manageable according to toxicity management guidelines and the overall evaluation of safety and tolerability in HIMALAYA was generally consistent with that observed in previous studies with durvalumab and tremelimumab.[89, 124] STRIDE demonstrated overall lower rates of grade 3/4 treatmentrelated adverse events (TRAEs) and TRAEs leading to discontinuation than sorafenib.[22] Furthermore, haemorrhagic-related TRAEs were lower in STRIDE than sorafenib and hepatotoxicity rates were similar, indicating that STRIDE does not increase the bleeding risk or liver toxicity.[4, 89] This favourable safety profile provides a notable advantage over the current SoC, and is reflected in its recent first-line recommendation in the BSG guidelines.[3] 

Three of the 17 unique studies identified by the SLR were determined eligible for inclusion in the NMA, including the HIMALAYA trial. The appropriateness of performing an NMA was assessed following the methodology outlined in NICE DSU Document 2.[125] Overall, the three trials were generally comparable in terms of study design and patient baseline characteristics. There was evidence of PH assumption violation for HIMALAYA and REFLECT for OS and PFS. However, there was no evidence of PH violation for IMbrallve150. These studies were used to form a network of evidence for both OS and PFS, connected via a common sorafenib treatment arm. The analysis found that STRIDE and atezolizumab + bevacizumab improved OS compared to sorafenib, although no statistical differences were observed (*** **** **** **** *********** **** **********]). The NMA found that lenvatinib had a HR close to 1 in the comparison to sorafenib, with a similar point estimate to the non-inferiority REFLECT trial (**** ***********). Similarly, for PFS, STRIDE, atezolizumab + bevacizumab and lenvatinib showed improvements over sorafenib, yet these results lacked statistical significance (*** **** ************ **** **** **** *********** **** **********], respectively). Overall, the NMA identified that STRIDE was associated with a comparable improvement in survival vs. sorafenib compared to atezolizumab + bevacizumab, the key comparator in this submission 

HIMALAYA was deemed to be of high quality following critical appraisal (Section B.2.5). This RCT recruited a large sample size and randomised stratification by key prognostic factors which led to balanced treatment arms. Patient characteristics were further representative of the advanced or unresectable HCC patient population in the UK, as supported by clinician validation (Section B.2.4). As referred to above, the five-year OS data is a key strength of the evidence base supporting the STRIDE regimen, providing substantial certainty of the long-term clinical benefits associated with this regimen. 

Limitations of HIMALAYA included the open-label design. This was necessary due to the differing drug administration methods of the treatments; STRIDE is administered intravenously while sorafenib is taken orally. Furthermore, despite not having UK centres in this trial, the trial participant characteristics closely align with an advanced HCC patient audit in the UK, ensuring 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab with tremelimumab for untreated unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma [ID2725] 

© AstraZeneca (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 87 -->

the trial is generalisable to patients in the UK.[103] The alignment between the HIMALAYA trial and the UK population was validated through clinician interviews.[7] While slight deviations in baseline populations (such as non-viral HCC, HCV, and HBV) were noted, attributed to higher rates of MASLD and alcohol consumption in UK cities, clinicians anticipated these variations and still deemed the dataset generalisable to UK clinical practice.[7] 

An additional limitation of HIMALAYA was the absence of a direct comparisons to two of the current first-line treatment options: lenvatinib and atezolizumab + bevacizumab, noting that the latter was not reimbursed SoC at the time the trial was designed. However, an NMA was conducted to provide comparative treatment effectiveness estimates.[7] During the NMA feasibility assessment, violation of the PH assumption for HIMALAYA and REFLECT was identified, which may have introduced uncertainty to results. However, models such as fractional polynomial or piecewise models were deemed unnecessary and overly complex, and ultimately did not address the key limitation which is the lack of long-term efficacy published for REFLECT and IMbrave150. Instead, the uncertainty associated with violations of the PH assumption was addressed in the economic model by independently fitting curves for HIMALAYA. For lenvatinib vs sorafenib, as per the results of the REFLECT trial, where statistical non-inferiority between lenvatinib and sorafenib was observed for OS, the HR was set to 1, to indicate equivalence in efficacy. This is viewed as conservative given that the time-varying analysis exploring non-proportionality in REFLECT predicts HRs above 1 over time for most models (see Appendix N). For PFS, the timevarying analysis also concluded that using a constant HR in the economic model was a conservative choice (Section B.3.3.2). The standard NMA results for atezolizumab + bevacizumab vs. sorafenib were not affected by PH assumption violations. 

In summary, the STRIDE regimen demonstrated a significant improvement in OS vs. sorafenib, leading to approximately 20% of patients surviving at least five years.[90] Furthermore, STRIDE demonstrated a favourable safety profile, including a low risk of haemorrhagic and hepatic events,[89] providing confidence in the safety of the regimen and re-enforcing its value as an important treatment alternative for all patients with advanced or unresectable HCC. STRIDE is supported by unprecedented and highly mature evidence demonstrating significant prolongation of survival within this patient population. The unprecedented OS results underscore the critical importance of STRIDE for patients, affirming STRIDE as a well-tolerated and effective treatment alternative for patients with advanced or unresectable HCC ineligible for locoregional therapy in the UK.[57, 68, 126] 

## **B.3 Cost effectiveness** 

## **Summary of the cost effectiveness analysis** 

- A _de novo_ cost-effectiveness model was developed to assess the cost-effectiveness of STRIDE in adult patients with advanced or unresectable HCC, in line with the HIMALAYA patient population, licence and decision problem for this submission (Section B.3.2.1) 

- The comparators to STRIDE considered within the analysis were atezolizumab + bevacizumab, sorafenib and lenvatinib (Section B.3.2.3) 

- The model adopted a partitioned survival approach with three health states: progression free (PF), progressed disease (PD) and dead, over a lifetime time horizon (40 years) (Section B.3.2.2) 

- Parametric survival extrapolations were fit to OS and PFS data for STRIDE and sorafenib from the HIMALAYA trial in order to extrapolate outcomes over the full modelled time horizon (Section B.3.3.2, B.3.3.4 and B.1.1.1) 

- Within HIMALAYA, STRIDE is compared to sorafenib only. Therefore, comparative 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab with tremelimumab for untreated unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma [ID2725] 

© AstraZeneca (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 88 -->

- effectiveness evidence vs. atezolizumab + bevacizumab for OS and PFS was sourced from the NMA (Section B.2.9). In line with the REFLECT trial, which showed statistical noninferiority between lenvatinib and sorafenib, a HR of 1 between lenvatinib and sorafenib was applied in the model for OS. The NMA estimate was used for PFS. HRs for atezolizumab + bevacizumab and lenvatinib vs. sorafenib were applied to the parametric survival extrapolations for OS and PFS for sorafenib in order to generate long-term survival estimates for these two comparators. 

- • Costs included in the model were drug acquisition, drug administration, subsequent treatment, health state resource use, AE and end-of-life costs, adopting an NHS and PSS perspective[127, 128] (Section B.3.5) 

- • Utility values for the PF and PD states were derived from values obtained from the HIMALAYA trial via the EQ-5D-5L questionnaires. These values were cross-walked to the EQ-5D-3L, in line with the methods described in Hernández-Alava et al.,[99] as recommended by NICE (Section B.3.4.5) 

- **Base case cost-effectiveness results** • In the base case, STRIDE was associated with a dominant deterministic incremental costeffectiveness ratio (ICER) relative to atezolizumab + bevacizumab, the principle comparator and current SoC in NHS clinical practice for patients with advanced or unresectable HCC. At a willingness-to-pay (WTP) threshold of £30,000/QALY gained, STRIDE therefore represents a cost-effective use of NHS resources (Section B.3.10) 

- • STRIDE was associated with deterministic, pairwise ICERs of ******* and ******* per QALY, relative to alternative therapies sorafenib and lenvatinib, respectively, which are alternative first-line treatments when IOs cannot be used (Section B.3.10) 

## **Base case cost-effectiveness results** 

## **Sensitivity and scenario analysis** 

- The deterministic and probabilistic base case results show that incremental QALYs for the comparison between STRIDE and atezolizumab + bevacizumab fall either side of zero, indicating, at a minimum, likely clinical equivalence between the two interventions, which is further supported by the results of the NMA. To investigate this equivalence, a cost comparison was conducted, the results of which showed that STRIDE is associated with cost-savings when compared to atezolizumab + bevacizumab 

- • Pairwise probabilistic ICERs for the comparison between STRIDE and sorafenib and STRIDE and lenvatinib were consistent with the deterministic ICERs 

- • A deterministic sensitivity analysis (DSA) was conducted. The model was robust to the variation in the majority of model inputs, however in the comparison of STRIDE to lenvatinib, results were influenced by the PFS HR for lenvatinib vs. sorafenib (Section B.3.11.2) 

- • Scenario analyses were conducted to explore the impact of structural assumptions and alternative inputs on the results of the cost-effectiveness analysis. In the majority of scenarios, STRIDE remains dominant vs. atezolizumab + bevacizumab. The ICERs vs. sorafenib and lenvatinib remain relatively stable between scenarios, illustrating the robustness of the model to uncertainty. (Section B.3.11.4) 

## **Conclusions** 

- There is a significant unmet need in UK clinical practice for an efficacious treatment that leads to improved survival for patients with advanced or unresectable HCC, without an associated increase in bleeding risk (Section B.1.3.3) 

- • STRIDE represents an alternative therapeutic option that is supported by mature, fiveyear OS data that is associated with minimal added bleeding risk compared to current SoC in the UK, atezolizumab + bevacizumab 

- These analyses demonstrate that STRIDE represents a cost-effective use of NHS resources with the potential to reduce the clinical and humanistic burden for adults with advanced or unresectable HCC, as well as the economic burden on the NHS

## **B.3.1** _**Published cost-effectiveness studies**_ 

A SLR was conducted to identify and synthesise relevant economic models, cost and healthcare resource use, and humanistic burden (utilities and HRQoL) of STRIDE and other first-line treatments in adults with advanced or unresectable HCC. The original SLR was conducted in May 2020, and subsequently underwent updates in October 2021 and June 2024. 

In the recent SLR update, following de-duplication of results, a total of 400 publications were screened at the title and abstract stage, of which 29 were reviewed at the full-text stage. After excluding publications that did not meet the eligibility criteria, five (three economic model publications, two HRQoL publications) publications were included in the SLR from database searches. Supplementary searches retrieved an additional two articles (one economic model publication, one HRQoL publication), resulting in a total of seven articles included from both the electronic database and supplementary searches. 

Additionally, 160 articles (104 publications on economic models or cost and resource use, 56 humanistic publications) were included from the original SLR and first update. Therefore, a total of 107 publications comprising economic models and cost and resource use studies and 58 humanistic publications were ultimately included in the SLRs. 

A description of the SLR methodology and results can be found in Appendix G. No prior economic evaluations were identified for STRIDE in the population of relevance to this submission, however, the most applicable economic models to this submission were reported in the previous NICE appraisals for atezolizumab + bevacizumab, lenvatinib and sorafenib, the details of which can be found in Table 32.[8-10]

## **B.3.2** _**Economic analysis**_ 

As described in Section B.3.1, no economic evaluations of STRIDE in advanced or unresectable HCC were identified in the economic SLR. As such, a _de novo_ cost-effectiveness analysis was conducted to inform this evaluation through a model built in Microsoft Excel[®] . 

The objective of this economic evaluation was to assess the cost effectiveness of STRIDE in adult patients with advanced or unresectable HCC relative to atezolizumab + bevacizumab, sorafenib and lenvatinib. 

## **B.3.2.1 Patient population** 

The economic analysis considered patients with advanced or unresectable HCC in line with the HIMALAYA patient population, the licensed indication for STRIDE and the decision problem defined in Section B.1.1. 

## **B.3.2.2 Model structure** 

The cost-effectiveness analysis was conducted using a partitioned survival model (PSM). This model structure was deemed the most appropriate based on the clinical data available. It also aligns with the structure adopted in previous NICE evaluations in advanced or unresectable HCC.[8-10, 129] The model structure directly leverages key time-to-event endpoints in the HIMALAYA study, namely OS and PFS. It reflects the natural disease course and the primary objectives of treatment for patients with advanced or unresectable HCC in the form of delaying progression and in extending survival. 

The three health states included in the PSM are: 

- **PF** : patients who are alive and whose disease has not progressed 

- **PD** : patients who are alive but whose disease has progressed 

- **Death** : patients who have died 

A simplified model schematic is presented in Figure 22, showing the potential transitions between the three health-states. 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab with tremelimumab for untreated unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma [ID2725] 

© AstraZeneca (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 91 -->

**Figure 22: Simplified model schematic** 

**==> picture [452 x 194] intentionally omitted <==**

All patients enter the model in the ‘progression-free’ state, receiving STRIDE or a comparator treatment (atezolizumab + bevacizumab, sorafenib, lenvatinib). Patients may remain progression-free, progress, or die. Patients in the ‘Progressed disease’ health state can either remain alive with progressed disease or die, but the model does not allow for patients to improve their health state. The separation of pre- and post-progression states helps capture differences in both costs and patient HRQoL before and after progression. In line with clinical practice, within the progression-free and progressed health states, patients may either be on or off treatment. The ‘Death’ health state is an absorbing state. 

The proportion of patients within each health state was determined by OS and PFS curves via an area-under-the-curve approach (Figure 23). This ensures that the model closely reflects disease progression and the observed survival profile of patients treatment with STRIDE and comparator therapies.

## **Features of the cost-effectiveness analysis** 

Costs and health state utilities were allocated to each health state and multiplied by state occupancy to calculate the weighted costs and QALYs per cycle, which were totalled at the end of the time horizon. The output of the model was the ICER of STRIDE vs. the relevant comparators. 

In line with the NICE reference case,[130] the perspective on costs and outcomes was that of the NHS and Personal Social Services (PSS). A lifetime time horizon of 40 years was chosen to capture patient outcomes up to a potential age of 100 years. This was considered appropriate as 4% of patients remain alive in the intervention arm after a 20-year period (the time horizon used in previous models)[9, 10] and thus enables the model to capture the full set of accumulated costs and QALYs in all treatment arms. A 1-week cycle length was considered in the base case as this was deemed appropriate given the rate at which clinical events may occur, and the frequency with which treatment regimens are administered. This aligns with the most recent NICE evaluation in advanced HCC (TA666, see below).[10] A half-cycle correction was applied. Costs and effects were discounted at 3.5% annually, in line with the NICE reference case.[130] 

Features of the analysis were based on previous NICE evaluations of HCC including: 

- TA666: atezolizumab + bevacizumab for treating advanced or unresectable HCC[10] 

- TA474: sorafenib for treating advanced HCC[9] 

- TA551: lenvatinib for treating advanced HCC[8] 

A summary of the key features of the evaluations of the three relevant comparators, as well as the economic analysis and justifications for the current evaluation, are provided in Table 32.

## **B.3.2.3 Intervention technology and comparators** 

## **Intervention** 

As discussed in Section B.1.2, the intervention of interest to the cost-effectiveness analysis is STRIDE. As per the SmPC, it is advised that STRIDE is administered until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity occurs.[1, 6] 

## **Comparators** 

As discussed in Section B.1.3, atezolizumab + bevacizumab is the current first-line SoC for patients with advanced or unresectable HCC who are ineligible for locoregional therapy in the UK, however, there is an elevated risk of bleeding associated with this regimen (Section B.1.3.4.1).[44, 126] For those contraindicated to atezolizumab + bevacizumab or those who decline IV therapy in favour of oral therapy, sorafenib and lenvatinib are alternative first-line therapies for advanced or unresectable HCC (Section B.1.3.4.2). Accordingly, three comparators have been included in the model: atezolizumab + bevacizumab, sorafenib and lenvatinib. 

## **B.3.3** _**Clinical parameters and variables**_ 

## **B.3.3.1 Baseline characteristics** 

The baseline characteristics of the modelled patient population were informed by the HIMALAYA trial (Table 33). As noted in Section B.2.4, and confirmed by clinical expert feedback, the baseline characteristics of the HIMALAYA trial were considered to be generally representative of patients in UK clinical practice.[7]

## **B.3.3.2 Survival analyses methodology** 

As discussed in Section B.2.3.3, there are three key DCOs from the HIMALAYA trial: 

- **Primary analysis:** The primary analysis was performed once 555 OS events had occurred in the STRIDE and sorafenib arms combined (representing 71% maturity), 46 months after the first patient was randomised (DCO: 27[th] August 2021)[4, 89] 

- **Updated analysis I:** The updated analysis evaluated the OS and safety of STRIDE vs. sorafenib with 4 years of follow-up (DCO: 23[rd] January 2023)[98] 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab with tremelimumab for untreated advanced or unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma [ID2725] 

© AstraZeneca (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 97 -->

- **Updated analysis II** : An additional five-year OS analysis has been conducted for STRIDE vs. sorafenib, representing the longest follow up period to date in Phase III studies in advanced or unresectable HCC (DCO: 1[st] March 2024). 

Within the model, efficacy data for STRIDE and sorafenib were informed by the most mature DCO available for the outcome in question: OS was informed by the updated analysis II DCO, while PFS and TTD were informed by the primary analysis. 

## **Survival analyses methodology: STRIDE and sorafenib** 

For STRIDE and sorafenib, as presented in Section B.2.6.2.1, individual patient data (IPD) were directly available from the HIMALAYA trial over a median follow-up duration of 5 years for OS, and a median follow-up duration of approximately 2.5 years for PFS and TTD.[90, 137] 

Parametric survival functions were fitted to the Kaplan-Meier data for each arm in HIMALAYA. As recommend in NICE DSU TSD 14 and 21,[89, 118] the following steps were undertaken to select best-fitting and clinically valid parametric survival extrapolations for the STRIDE and sorafenib arms: 

- **Assessment of proportional hazards (PH) assumption** 

   - The PH assumption between treatment arms in HIMALAYA was assessed through visual assessment of Kaplan-Meier curves, log-log plots, plots of the Schoenfeld residual and consideration of time-varying HR, if reported. If the PH assumption holds, as indicated by approximately parallel log-log plots, a Schoenfeld’s residual p- value >0.05 (indicating no autocorrelation among residuals at a 95% confidence interval), or a relatively stable HR over time, joint parametric models accounting for both treatment arms can be considered. Otherwise, independent models may be fit to each treatment arm. Further details on the PH assessments conducted for HIMALAYA are presented in Section B.2.9.5 and Appendix D. 

- **Assessment of observed trial hazards** 

   - The hazards (rates of events) for each treatment arm within the HIMALAYA trial period were assessed through visual inspection of the observed raw and smoothed hazard plots. Assessment of the hazard plots can indicate whether standard parametric survival models such as proportional hazards and accelerated failure time (AFT) models are suitable, or whether models with greater flexibility, such as splinebased models, should be explored. 

   - Within the hazard plots, the within-trial period hazard was also visually compared to the hazards predicted by each parametric model on a long-term basis. Hazards over a 20-year timeframe were considered to confirm that the extrapolated hazards for the chosen base case extrapolations were clinically plausible. 

- **Statistical goodness of fit** 

   - The statistical goodness of fit of each extrapolation was assessed by considering the ranking of the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC). 

- **Visual fit to Kaplan-Meier plots** 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab with tremelimumab for untreated advanced or unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma [ID2725] 

© AstraZeneca (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 98 -->

   - The goodness of fit of the parametric extrapolation to the Kaplan-Meier data was visually assessed, with consideration given to the entire trial period for which data were available. 

- **External validation is desirable in understanding the suitability of the extrapolations** 

   - Although HIMALAYA trial data are highly mature, clinical plausibility in the long-term remains an important consideration. UK clinical expert opinion was therefore sought to understand outcomes that could be expected for both the sorafenib and STRIDE arms in NHS clinical practice. External evidence was also considered and used where appropriate to validate the model extrapolations. 

## **Approach to comparator efficacy: atezolizumab + bevacizumab and lenvatinib** 

In the absence of a direct comparison between STRIDE and each of atezolizumab + bevacizumab and lenvatinib, comparative effectiveness from the NMA described in Section B.2.9 were explored to inform the model. Long-term survival estimates for atezolizumab + bevacizumab and lenvatinib could be generated through the application of the relevant HR from the NMA to the selected parametric survival function for the sorafenib treatment arm, the common comparator arm from the NMA. In order to explore this approach, the assessments of PH between atezolizumab + bevacizumab and sorafenib, and lenvatinib and sorafenib, for both OS and PFS, were reviewed. These assessments are presented in Table 20, Section B.2.9.5 and detailed further in Appendix D. 

With regards to the comparison with lenvatinib, the PH assessment indicated that there was evidence of PH violation within REFLECT for OS and PFS. As such, NMA-derived HRs for comparisons of lenvatinib to sorafenib may be biased; following an assessment of the timevarying HR from REFLECT and the trend towards a HR of 1 for lenvatinib vs. sorafenib, the direction of this bias appears to favour lenvatinib (Section B.2.9.5). Therefore, the application of a constant HR from the NMA for lenvatinib in the economic model may overestimate the long-term effect of lenvatinib treatment (see Section B.2.9.5 and Appendix N). Further to this, the REFLECT study was a non-inferiority study, which concluded that lenvatinib was statistically noninferior compared with sorafenib in terms of OS. Accordingly, a HR for lenvatinib vs. sorafenib of 1 was used in the base case for OS. For PFS, statistical non-inferiority was not observed in REFLECT, and thus the HR from the NMA was used, which may be considered a conservative approach. 

There was no evidence of PH violation for IMBrave150, and therefore the survival estimate for this comparator informed by the NMA-derived HR for atezolizumab + bevacizumab vs sorafenib was unlikely to be biased. 

It is noted that choice of parametric extrapolation for the sorafenib treatment arm (to which relevant HRs would be applied) was not limited to proportional hazards models, but also considered functions such as accelerated failure time (AFT) models and spline-based models. The purpose of this was to maximise choice from a range of potentially clinical valid extrapolations. Whilst the combining of HRs with survival probabilities estimated from an AFT model is technically mixing assumptions on how treatment effects would (theoretically) be applied in the survival model (acting on the time scale for an AFT model) and how they are modelled in the comparative analysis (acting on the hazard scale). However, there is no reason to artificially constrain the comparator curves to the same form. If the estimated curves for the comparators are clinically valid, the conflating of technical assumptions is immaterial.

## **B.3.3.3 Overall survival** 

## _**B.3.3.3.1 Assessment of PH assumption – STRIDE vs sorafenib**_ 

As discussed in Section B.2.9, the PH assessment for the STRIDE and sorafenib OS outcomes was based on IPD from HIMALAYA. The formal assessment of the PH assumption, based on the visual inspection of the Kaplan-Meier curves, the log-log plot, the Schoenfeld residuals plot and the Grambsh and Therneau test, found that the PH assumption was violated.[114-117] Further details of this assessment can be found in Section B.2.9.5. 

Given the PH assumption was violated, it was considered necessary to explore independently fitted models rather joint-fitting models. Additionally, as patient-level data are available for HIMALAYA, it is considered unnecessary to consider a joint approach as fitting separate parametric models to each treatment arm involves fewer assumptions.[118] 

## _**B.3.3.3.2 Assessment of observed trial hazards – STRIDE vs sorafenib**_ 

Plots of the observed raw and smoothed hazards were assessed to judge the complexity of observed trial hazards and determine whether parametric models with greater flexibility should be considered alongside standard parametric models. ## **Observed vs modelled hazard rate** 

The observed hazard of the STRIDE arm from HIMALAYA was compared with the hazards of spline-based survival models in Figure 27, Figure 28 and Figure 29 below. *** ****** ******* ***

## **External validation** 

The HIMALAYA trial provides highly mature OS data from a median follow-up of five years. This represents a significant strength of the evidence base supporting STRIDE, as it substantially reduces uncertainty in the resulting long-term survival extrapolations in the model. In particular, the goodness of fit statistics can be considered particularly informative in the consideration of extrapolation selection, given the long-term Kaplan-Meier data available with which to statistically compare each extrapolation. 

To supplement the mature data from HIMALAYA further, and in line with recommendations from NICE TSD 14, clinical feedback was also sought from UK-based oncologists on survival expectations should patients receive STRIDE in NHS clinical practice, and the long-term clinical validity of the modelled survival extrapolations.[118] 

The consulted oncologists consistently confirmed that a long-term benefit of STRIDE on patient survival was in line with their expectations. In particular, the observation of a “tail” or “plateau” in the long-term survival estimates for STRIDE aligned with their expectations. The clinicians confirmed that this pattern of survival was expected given the dual IO mechanism of action of the STRIDE regimen, and the resulting strong stimulation of the immune system to attack cancer cells. As can be observed in Figure 26, all extrapolations assessed demonstrate a long-term survival benefit of STRIDE, with a “tail” observed in their shape, in line with clinician expectations. Upon presentation of a selection of the better fitting extrapolations (Odds 1 knot, Normal 1 knot and Hazard 1 knot) under assessment to the clinicians, preference was expressed 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab with tremelimumab for untreated advanced or unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma [ID2725] 

© AstraZeneca (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 107 -->

at least once for each of the three extrapolations, and so all extrapolations were considered plausible. 

Considering the combination of factors above, specifically, observed trial hazards, goodness of fit statistics and clinical opinion, the Normal 1 knot model was selected as the base case. When comparing the 1-knot models, which were considered clinically plausible (see Table 34), the Normal 1 knot model provided the middle estimate between the proportion alive at later timepoints: **** estimated by the Hazard model, **** estimated by the Odds model, **** estimated by the Normal model at 20 years). It represents a robust fit to the Kaplan-Meier data from HIMALAYA and captures expected OS in the long-term for patients treated with STRIDE in NHS clinical practice. For completeness, the generalised gamma extrapolation was assessed in a scenario analysis as it was considered a clinically plausible alternative that was one of the bestfitting statistically among the set of standard models assessed (Appendix N).

## **External validation** 

As previously described, the HIMALAYA trial provides highly mature OS data from a median follow-up of five years, thereby minimising uncertainty in the resulting long-term survival extrapolations in the cost-effectiveness model. In particular, the goodness of fit statistics can be considered particularly informative in the consideration of extrapolation selection, given the longterm Kaplan-Meier data available with which to statistically compare each extrapolation. 

To supplement the mature data from HIMALAYA further, and in line with recommendations from NICE TSD 14, clinical feedback was sought from UK-based oncologists on the long-term clinical validity of the modelled parametric survival curves.[118] 

Clinicians noted that survival of patients receiving sorafenib in NHS clinical practice is poor; in contrast to their expectations of STRIDE where a “tail” in the curve is expected (as described in Section B.3.3.4.3). The clinicians’ expectation of the pattern of long-term survival with sorafenib was such that the proportions of patients alive would progressively and successively drop to zero.[7] This pattern of survival is aligned with the shape of all extrapolations presented in Figure 31. Clinicians commented that survival for sorafenib may be overestimated by these extrapolations. One possible reason for this overestimation is the use of subsequent IO in the sorafenib arm in the trial: ***** of patients in the sorafenib arm in the trial received a subsequent IO, compared to just **** in the STRIDE arm. This was made up predominately of nivolumab (******* followed by pembrolizumab (****) and atezolizumab (****). No adjustment was made to the survival data for these subsequent IOs. Given the poor survival expectations associated with sorafenib in NHS clinical practice, among the best fitting extrapolations presented, the oncologists considered the extrapolations predicting the lowest survival expectations to be the most clinically plausible (see Table 35).[118] The three best fitting curves (Odds 1 knot, Hazard 1 knot, Normal 1 knot) identified above through the AIC/BIC statistics all demonstrated comparable long-term survival over the full model time horizon, and given the clinicians’ feedback, Hazard 1 knot was selected in the base case . 

To further support the clinical validity of the chosen base case extrapolation, given that sorafenib has been licensed for the treatment of advanced HCC for a number of years, a targeted literature search for external evidence on survival data with sorafenib was conducted. This search identified two papers - a meta-analysis of randomised trials evaluating sorafenib in advanced HCC by Tan et al (2023) and a retrospective review of electronic prescribing records in advanced HCC patients in Scotland by Peters (2018).[139, 140] The retrospective review found a median survival of 10.4 months, and the meta-analysis estimated a median OS of 10.43 months. The Hazard 1 knot model for sorafenib estimates a median of ~13.8 months, indicating that the curve selection may represent a conservative model choice for the base case.

## **B.3.3.4 Progression-free survival** 

Within each treatment arm, the PFS extrapolations were constrained by the OS extrapolations in the model. This ensured that the PFS extrapolation for each intervention did not exceed the OS extrapolation, maintaining clinically meaningful model outputs. 

The extrapolation selection process for PFS aligned with that taken for OS. 

## _**B.3.3.4.1 Assessment of PH assumption – STRIDE vs sorafenib**_ 

As discussed in Section B.2.9, the PH assessment for the STRIDE and sorafenib PFS outcomes from HIMALAYA was based on IPD from the trial. The formal assessment of the PH assumption, based on the visual inspection of the Kaplan-Meier curves, the log-log plot, the Schoenfeld residuals plot and the Grambsh and Therneau test, found that there was violation of the PH assumption.[114-117] Further details of this assessment can be found in Section B.2.9.5. 

As the PH assumption had been violated, it was considered necessary to explore independently fitted models rather joint-fitting models. 

## _**B.3.3.4.2 Assessment of observed trial hazards – STRIDE vs sorafenib**_ 

Plots of the observed raw and smoothed hazards were assessed to judge the complexity of observed trial hazards and decide whether more flexible parametric models should be considered alongside the standard parametric models. ## **External validation** 

As described for OS, data were extrapolated to provide long-term estimates for PFS for STRIDE and its comparators. In line with recommendations from NICE TSD 14, clinical feedback was sought from UK-based oncologists on the long-term clinical validity of the modelled parametric survival extrapolations.[118] 

The majority of the clinical experts agreed that the Hazard 3 knot extrapolation was the most appropriate choice for the STRIDE arm, justifying this extrapolation as the most clinically plausible. As the Hazard 3 knot extrapolation was also the best fitting extrapolation according to the model fit statistics and showed a good visual fit to the Kaplan-Meier data from HIMALAYA, it was considered the most robust choice of extrapolation. For completeness, the second best fitting standard model, the generalised gamma, was explored in a scenario analysis.

## **External validation** 

As described for OS, data were extrapolated to provide long-term estimates for PFS for STRIDE and its comparators. In line with recommendations from NICE TSD 14, clinical feedback was sought from UK-based oncologists on the long-term clinical validity of the modelled parametric survival extrapolations for sorafenib and STRIDE.[118] Whilst the hazard 2 knot model (the best fitting spline model by AIC/BIC) specifically was not validated with clinical experts (standard models were presented only), of the extrapolations presented, the clinicians deemed the lognormal to be the most clinically plausible model relative to NHS clinical practice. A comparison of the log-normal and hazard 2 knot model illustrates that the PFS predictions are lower with the log-normal model vs. the hazard 2 knot (5-year landmark: 1.49% vs. 5.2%; 10-year landmark: 0.3% vs. 2.0%). 

In order to account for the varying observed hazard in the sorafenib Kaplan-Meier data (Figure 36), the hazard 2 knot model was selected for the base case. This model represented the best fitting model among the spline models assessed. Furthermore, based on the clinical feedback described above, this extrapolation represents a conservative choice as it likely overestimates PFS on sorafenib relative to NHS clinical practice, and as a result likely underestimates the treatment benefit of STRIDE with regards to PFS. For completeness, a scenario analysis using the log-normal curve was conducted.

## **B.3.3.5 Time to treatment discontinuation** 

TTD for STRIDE and sorafenib was modelled consistently with the approach taken for PFS and OS, with parametric survival functions applied to TTD data from the HIMALAYA trial. For STRIDE, only TTD for durvalumab was extrapolated; tremelimumab is administered as a one-off administration and applied as a singular cost at treatment initiation at the start of the model. 

In the absence of TTD data from HIMALAYA for atezolizumab + bevacizumab and lenvatinib, TTD for these interventions was assumed to align with their corresponding extrapolations for PFS (as described in Section B.3.3.4). Since atezolizumab + bevacizumab is recommended for use until loss of clinical benefit or unacceptable toxicity, and lenvatinib is recommended for as long as clinical benefit is observed or until unacceptable toxicity, this can be considered a conservative assumption, as patients may receive treatment beyond progression in clinical practice.[141, 142] 

## _**B.3.3.5.1 Assessment of PH assumption – STRIDE vs sorafenib**_ 

As per OS and PFS, the PH assessment for the STRIDE and sorafenib TTD outcomes from HIMALAYA was based on IPD from the trial. The formal assessment of the PH assumption, based on the visual inspection of the Kaplan-Meier curves, the log-log plot, the Schoenfeld residuals plot and the Grambsh and Therneau test, found that there was violation of the PH assumption demonstrates that the PH assumption does not hold.[114-117] Further detail on the PHA for TTD can be found in Appendix D. 

As the PH assumption had been violated, it was considered necessary to explore independently fitted models rather joint-fitting models.

## **B.3.4.1 Health-related quality-of-life data from clinical trials** 

Within the HIMALAYA trial, data were collected using two PRO measures: EORTC QLQ-C30 and EORTC QLQ-HCC18. EQ-5D-5L and EQ-VAS data were also reported as exploratory endpoints. HRQoL results from HIMALAYA are presented in Section B.2.6.3. 

## **B.3.4.2 Mapping** 

No mapping methods were employed as part of this cost-effectiveness analysis given the availability of the EQ-5D data from the HIMALAYA trial, which aligns with NICE’s preference.[132] As EQ-5D-5L data were collected within the trial, these values were cross-walked to EQ-5D-3L; this is further described in Section B.3.4.5.

## **B.3.4.3 Health-related quality-of-life studies** 

As described in a SLR was conducted to identify relevant economic, cost and healthcare resource use and HRQoL studies in adults with advanced or unresectable HCC. The original SLR was conducted in May 2020, and subsequently updated in September 2021 and June 2024. 

An overview of the SLR methodology and results can be found in Appendix H. In total, 49 studies across 58 publications were identified across the original SLR and two updates, with 2 HRQoL studies identified in the latest update. However, as EQ-5D data were available from the HIMALAYA trial, representing data directly relevant to the patient population under consideration in this submission, these data were used to inform the economic model. 

## **B.3.4.4 Adverse reactions** 

Given that treatment dependent utilities were applied in the model, separate disutilities associated with individual AEs were not applied in the base case. 

## **B.3.4.5 Health-related quality-of-life data used in the cost-effectiveness** 

## **analysis** 

Within the model, utility values were applied based on the treatments patients received. 

EQ-5D-5L utility data were collected in the HIMALAYA trial (FAS; DCO: 27[th] August 2021). Utility values were derived using a mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM) analysis of all the post-baseline scores for each visit to estimate the statistical relationship between utilities and treatment (base case) and separately, utilities and health state (scenario).[145] This method accounts for the autocorrelation in utility score within each patient and is appropriate when handling data that are missing at random. Notably, a random intercept model assuming independent within-subject errors was fitted to account for the subject variability. 

In the model, utilities were treatment-dependent, and it was assumed that atezolizumab + bevacizumab would have the same utility value as STRIDE, and lenvatinib would have the same utility value as sorafenib. This approach was adopted as it was considered to be the most robust way of capturing the impact of adverse events due to TKIs on patients, as evidenced in IMbrave150 and HIMALAYA, and a systematic review and meta-analysis of systemic therapies for advanced HCC which shows that patients treated with TKIs are almost twice as likely as those treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors to experience an adverse event that is Grade 3 or higher (69% vs. 35%).[45, 146] 

The EQ-5D-5L health utility value sets from the HIMALAYA trial were cross-walked to the EQ5D-3L using the algorithm described in Hernández-Alava et al., as recommended by NICE.[99, 130] Utility values in the model were age-adjusted using the age- and sex-matched general population utility values reported in Hernández-Alava et al. Age-adjustment of utility values was performed multiplicatively with the multiplier equal to one in the first cycle and gradually decreasing over time.[119] 

The base case utility values based on the treatment model are provided in Table 50.

## **Subsequent treatment costs** 

In the HIMALAYA trial, ***** of patients received a disease-related anticancer treatment after discontinuing treatment with STRIDE, and ***** after discontinuing treatment with sorafenib.[45] Whilst some of the subsequent treatments received are commonly used in UK clinical practice (e.g., regorafenib), there were also treatments not routinely used in the UK (e.g** ***** of patients received an IO after discontinuation from sorafenib, including ***** who received nivolumab).[64] Therefore, in order to align with UK clinical practice, the subsequent treatments within the model were informed by NICE recommendations and clinical expert feedback.[7-9, 64] 

The distribution of patients progressing to each subsequent treatment, based on the first-line therapy they received, are provided in Table 55. These distributions represent treatments received in the second-line only, as only a small proportion of patients receive third-line treatment for advanced or unresectable HCC as a result of the short disease prognosis and reducing fitness to receive active therapy with each treatment line. ## **B.3.5.2 Health state unit costs and resource use** 

The proportion of patients receiving each healthcare resource use item by treatment and health state are provided in Table 57 and the frequency per week are presented in Table 58. The proportion multiplied by the frequency is presented in Table 59, and this forms the model input. Uncertainty is modelled around proportion multiplied by frequency, rather than separately on the proportion and frequency as individual inputs. These values were calculated based on resource use estimates reported in previous technology appraisals (TA666 and TA551) and adjustments were made based on a validation exercise with clinicians.[7, 8, 10] 

Costs were taken from the NHS Reference Costs 2021/2022 and PSSRU Unit Costs of Health and Social Care 2022/23.[8, 10, 127, 128] The itemised costs for each type of resource use is presented in Table 60. 

Costs were higher for patients who received atezolizumab + bevacizumab in the progression-free health state due to the requirement for every patient to receive an initial endoscopy and treatment and laboratory tests every three weeks. 

Resource use was assumed to be higher for patients in the progressed disease health state who had received sorafenib at first-line, accounting for the high proportion of patients receiving subsequent active treatment as opposed to best supportive care (BSC), and extensive duration of subsequent treatment received (e.g. cabozantinib). Clinicians also provided feedback which suggested that use of TKIs in first-line is typically a second choice to IO, and is most often given if a patient is contraindicated to IO treatment due to comorbidities such as hypertension or cardiovascular/metabolic abnormalities.[7] As such, it is likely that when these patients progress, they will require more monitoring and may be more likely to be hospitalised, compared to patients who receive IO in first-line. 

Finally, the total costs per health state per cycle for the PF and PD health state are presented in Table 61.

## **B.3.5.4 Miscellaneous unit costs and resource use** 

The model includes a cost for end-of-life care, which is applied upon death. Aligned with TA666 and TA551, as well as the findings from Georghiou and Bardsley 2014, it is estimated that this cost amounts to £8,249.15 for individuals with advanced or unresectable HCC.[8, 10, 150] 

## **B.3.6** _**Severity**_ 

Survival for patients with advanced or unresectable HCC is poor, with an average life expectancy is less than two years despite the treatments currently available in the UK.[33] Disease symptoms in individuals with advanced or unresectable HCC have profound humanistic and HRQoL impacts.[37] As such, individuals report significantly lower physical wellbeing and overall HRQoL than the general population, patients with chronic liver disease, and patients with other cancers.[29] 

The severity modifier tool developed by ScHAAR and Lumanity was used to calculate the absolute and proportional severity modifiers, using the reference case Measurement of Valuation of Health (MVH) value set and Health Survey for England (HSE) 2014 Adjusted Limited Dependent Variable Mixture Model (ALDVMM).[151] A summary of the features of the QALY shortfall analysis is provided in Table 64. Based on this QALY shortfall analysis, the proportional QALY shortfall for the base case meets the threshold for applying a severity modifier of x1.2 to the incremental QALYs for the comparisons against lenvatinib and sorafenib. 

The model predicts median OS is ~22 months for atezolizumab + bevacizumab, and ~13 months for sorafenib and lenvatinib. Therefore, advanced or unresectable HCC would have previously met end of life criteria. As highlighted by the external evidence cited in Section B.3.3.3.4, median OS for patients treated with sorafenib may be even lower (~10 months).

## **B.3.7** _**Uncertainty**_ 

Comprehensive five-year overall survival data is available from the HIMALAYA trial. With the availability of highly mature data, long-term survival extrapolations can be generated with greater certainty. Any remaining uncertainty has been mitigated through detailed consultations with UK specialists regarding the anticipated long-term survival of adults with advanced or unresectable HCC in the UK. 

## **B.3.8** _**Managed access proposal**_ 

The HIMALAYA trial provides highly mature OS data from a median follow-up of 5 years, thereby minimising uncertainty in the resulting long-term survival extrapolations. In line with recommendations from NICE TSD 14, clinical feedback was sought from UK-based oncologists on the long-term clinical validity of the modelled parametric survival extrapolations for sorafenib and STRIDE.[118] Given the availability of mature, long-term survival data, validated by clinicians, decision uncertainty for this evaluation is greatly minimised. As a result, AstraZeneca do not intend to submit a managed access proposal.

## **B.3.10** _**Base-case results**_ 

## **B.3.10.1 Base-case incremental cost-effectiveness analysis results** 

The base case deterministic and probabilistic cost-effectiveness results for STRIDE vs. atezolizumab + bevacizumab, sorafenib and lenvatinib are presented in Table 68 and Table 69, respectively. The fully incremental results for the deterministic and probabilistic analyses are presented in Table 70 and Table 71, respectively. In the deterministic base case, STRIDE dominated atezolizumab + bevacizumab, accumulating fewer costs and greater QALYs over a lifetime horizon. Relative to sorafenib and lenvatinib, STRIDE was associated with deterministic, pairwise ICERs of ******* and ******* per QALY, respectively; this also includes the application of a 1.2x severity modifier to the incremental QALYs for these two comparisons (see Section B.3.6) 

In the probabilistic analysis, the NHB results are similar to those in the deterministic analyses. Pairwise probabilistic ICERs for the comparison between STRIDE and sorafenib and STRIDE and lenvatinib were consistent with the deterministic ICERs. For the comparison of STRIDE and atezolizumab + bevacizumab, the incremental QALYs are close to zero for both the deterministic and probabilistic analysis, but for the probabilistic analysis the ICERs fall in the southwest (SW) quadrant of the cost-effectiveness plane, meaning that the results show cost saved per QALY forgone. 

At a willingness-to-pay (WTP) threshold of £30,000/QALY gained, STRIDE represents a costeffective use of NHS resources vs. the principal comparator, and SoC in NHS clinical practice, atezolizumab + bevacizumab, in both the deterministic and probabilistic analysis.

## **B.3.11** _**Exploring uncertainty**_ 

Parameter uncertainty in the model was assessed via both probabilistic and deterministic sensitivity analyses, the results of which are presented in Sections B.3.11.1 and B.3.11.2, respectively. In addition, key assumptions in the model were explored in several probabilistic scenario analyses, the results of which are presented in Section B.3.11.4. Overall, it is considered that all relevant uncertainties included in the analyses have been adequately accounted for, and the base case results were found to be robust to uncertainty in the key model inputs and assumptions. 

## **B.3.11.1 Probabilistic sensitivity analysis** 

Probabilistic sensitivity analyses (PSA) were run with 1,000 iterations, with estimates of model parameters based on the uncertainty in the source data (where data availability permitted). Beta distributions were assumed for uncertain parameters bound by zero and one, including utilities, proportions, and probabilities. Log-normal distributions were assumed for hazard ratios. Gamma distributions were assumed for costs. Normal distributions were assumed for other uncertain parameters including resource use frequencies, with capping in place to ensure positivity for parameters which must be non-negative. 

The probabilistic pairwise cost-effectiveness planes for STRIDE vs. relevant comparators are presented in Figure 54 to Figure 56. The cost-effectiveness acceptability curve is presented in Figure 57.

## **B.3.11.2 Cost comparison vs. atezolizumab + bevacizumab** 

The deterministic and probabilistic base case results show that incremental QALYs for the comparison between STRIDE and atezolizumab + bevacizumab fall either side of zero. ## **B.3.12** _**Subgroup analysis**_ 

No subgroup analyses were considered relevant to this appraisal and as such no subgroup analyses were included in the cost-effectiveness analysis. 

## **B.3.13** _**Benefits not captured in the QALY calculation**_ 

Although this evaluation considers the cost-saving advantage of STRIDE not requiring endoscopy compared to atezolizumab + bevacizumab, it does not capture the benefits of reduced amount of time before a patient can commence starting life-extending treatment, nor the reduced capacity burden for the NHS that would be realised if STRIDE was recommended through reduced endoscopy, reduced dosing admin and laboratory tests and monitoring. 

Furthermore, the potential positive impact on carers and/or relatives associated with the improved outcomes of patients that receive treatment with STRIDE is not considered in the economic analysis. The impact of improved outcomes on the productivity of patients, carers and/or relatives is also not considered. 

Given the highly mature long-term survival data available for STRIDE, clinicians can have greater confidence in the long-term efficacy of STIDE for their patients. 

## **B.3.14** _**Validation**_ 

## **B.3.14.1 Validation of cost-effectiveness analysis** 

## **Internal validation** 

A thorough quality control check and technical validation was conducted by health economic modellers, in line with Drummond et al. (2015),[152] Philips et al. (2004),[153] and TECH-VER.[154] 

These checks include, but are not limited to the following criteria: 

- A manual review of all programming using formulae within Microsoft Excel and code in Visual Basis for Applications (VBA) 

- Confirmation that the mathematical calculations, programming, and formulae are consistent with the specification and are logically applied 

- A review of the patient flow sheets, scope, results, and sensitivity analysis functionality 

- Validity checks to ensure consistency between the clinical trial data and model outcomes 

- Extreme value testing (setting in zero values to parameters and stress testing the model in general) to assess whether the outcomes, and changes in outcomes, make intuitive sense for the options selected – in addition to editorial checks (text descriptions, referencing, navigation and graphical outputs) within the model 

## **External validation** 

Long-term survival expectations in advanced or unresectable HCC are detailed in Section B.3.2.2. It demonstrates that the extrapolations have reasonable visual fit to the short-term observed trial Kaplan-Meyer data for the FAS population.

Clinical feedback was also used to validate the inputs and results from the model, including the treatment pathway and validation of long-term survival extrapolations. Where possible, UK sources were used for model inputs to ensure the outputs are representative of NHS clinical practice. 

## **B.3.15** _**Interpretation and conclusions of economic evidence**_ 

## **Principal results from economic analysis** 

To assess the cost-effectiveness of STRIDE vs. relevant comparators in patients with advanced or unresectable HCC, a _de novo_ cost-effectiveness analysis was conducted from the perspective of the NHS and PSS in England. 

In the deterministic base case, STRIDE dominated atezolizumab + bevacizumab, accumulating fewer costs and greater QALYs over a lifetime horizon. Relative to sorafenib and lenvatinib, STRIDE was associated with deterministic, pairwise ICERs of ******* and ******* per QALY, respectively. At a willingness-to-pay (WTP) threshold of £30,000/QALY gained, STRIDE therefore represents a cost-effective use of NHS resources vs. the principal comparator, and SoC in NHS clinical practice, atezolizumab + bevacizumab. The probabilistic base case analysis supports this conclusion, with average results being close to the deterministic base case outcomes and therefore sufficiently robust to uncertainty in parameter estimates. The results of an exploratory cost comparison demonstrate that STRIDE still remains cost-saving when compared to atezolizumab + bevacizumab when assuming equal efficacy across the two treatments. 

The results of the deterministic sensitivity analyses identified respective treatment acquisition costs and NMA-derived hazard rations for OS and PFS, where applicable, as the main drivers of the model outcomes (i.e. INHB); these parameters were therefore also further tested as part of additional scenario analyses, by varying assumptions around vial sharing and RDI, as well as different survival extrapolations. Results remained overall stable across all tested scenarios, with STRIDE remaining dominant across the majority of scenarios, or otherwise cost-effective, against atezolizumab + bevacizumab in particular. 

## **Strengths and limitations** 

Efficacy data for the model was sourced from the HIMALAYA trial, a methodologically robust Phase III RCT in the patient population of interest to this evaluation. The HIMALAYA trial provides long-term data for STRIDE as well as one of the relevant comparators (sorafenib); most notably providing highly mature five-year OS data. Extrapolations were fit directly to these data which, due to the maturity of the data, reduces ambiguity in efficacy extrapolations and as such, is anticipated to significantly minimise decision uncertainty for the NICE Committee. However, the comparator trials spanned a shorter time period and as such, there is increased uncertainty in the long-term survival extrapolations for these comparators. 

Comprehensive clinical validation was performed to validate long-term survival estimates as well as the key assumptions made in the analysis. Baseline characteristics of patients within the HIMALAYA trial are used within the model have been validated by UK clinical experts to be representative of UK clinical practice. 

As the HIMALAYA trial compared STRIDE to sorafenib, an NMA was required to obtain comparative efficacy evidence for the remaining two comparators (atezolizumab + bevacizumab Company evidence submission for durvalumab with tremelimumab for untreated advanced or unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma [ID2725] 

© AstraZeneca (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 172 -->

and lenvatinib). Trials included in the NMA had notably different lengths of follow-up, with comparator trials spanning a much shorter duration relative to HIMALAYA. Therefore, although the NMA used robust methodologies, there is inherent and unavoidable uncertainty in the model outputs for the long-term efficacy of the comparators. Furthermore, the PH assumption was violated for HIMALAYA and REFLECT. For HIMALAYA, this was addressed in the economic model by independently fitting curves to the patient-level data from the HIMALAYA study, as recommended in NICE DSU TSD 14.[118] For REFLECT, an analysis investigating a time-varying treatment effect for the efficacy of lenvatinib vs. sorafenib was conducted to evaluate the impact of the PH violation identified, which found that use of the NMA results within the model was a conservative choice (Section B.3.3.2). As explained above, lenvatinib and sorafenib were considered to have equivalent OS efficacy given the result of the REFLECT study, which showed that lenvatinib was non-inferior to sorafenib but that superiority could not be established. This equivalence was achieved through setting the HR equivalent to 1. There was no violation of the PH assumption for IMbrave150. 

The model closely aligns to the NICE reference case, adopting an NHS and PSS perspective as well as utilising a lifetime horizon of 40 years to ensure all costs and QALY gains associated with the interventions are fully captured and discounting costs and benefits at a rate of 3.5% per annum. Furthermore, learnings and committee preferences were adopted from previous evaluations in this disease area to ensure the trial and evaluation are reflective of current best practices. 

The results of the economic analysis are therefore considered highly relevant to decision-making on the introduction of STRIDE into NHS clinical practice for adults with advanced or unresectable HCC.[8-10] 

## **Overall conclusions** 

There remains a significant unmet need for an efficacious and tolerable treatment option for adults with advanced or unresectable HCC that does not carry an associated increase in bleeding risk. STRIDE offers an efficacious and safe alternative to atezolizumab + bevacizumab, sorafenib and lenvatinib, and is supported by unprecedented, highly mature OS data, which aid in the minimisation of uncertainty associated with the long-term extrapolation of survival outcomes. In the base case, STRIDE was associated with a dominant deterministic incremental ICER relative to atezolizumab + bevacizumab, the principal comparator and current SoC in NHS clinical practice (Section B.3.10). STRIDE can therefore be considered a cost-effective use of NHS resources, whilst fulfilling a significant unmet need for patients with advanced or unresectable HCC in the UK for an effective treatment that does not increase risk of bleeding.

## **Summary of Information for Patients (SIP):** 

## **The pharmaceutical company perspective** 

## **What is the SIP?** 

The Summary of Information for Patients (SIP) is written by the company who is seeking approval from **National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)** for their treatment to be sold to the **National Health Service (NHS)** for use in England.  It is a plain English summary of their submission written for patients participating in the evaluation.  It is not independently checked, although members of the public involvement team at NICE will have read it to doublecheck for marketing and promotional content before it is sent to you. 

The **Summary of Information for Patients** template has been adapted for use at NICE from the Health Technology Assessment International – Patient & Citizens Involvement Group (HTAi PCIG). Information about the development is available in an open-access IJTAHC journal article 

## **SECTION 1: Submission summary** 

## **1a) Name of the medicine** (generic and brand name): 

**Generic name** : durvalumab in combination with tremelimumab. The combined name for this treatment is called **STRIDE** , which is short for Single Tremelimumab Regular Interval Durvalumab 

**Brand name** : IMFINZI[®] in combination with IMJUDO[®] 

**1b) Population this treatment will be used by:** Please outline the main patient population that is being appraised by NICE: 

The population that this treatment will be used for is adults with **advanced** or **unresectable** hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). These individuals must be ineligible for **locoregional** therapy and have not undergone **systemic therapy** during their current disease **stage** . 

**Please note:** Further explanations for the words and phrases highlighted in **blue bold text** are provided in the glossary ( **Section 4b** ). Cross-references to other sections or documents are highlighted in **orange** . 

**1c) Authorisation:** Please provide marketing authorisation information, date of approval and link to the regulatory agency approval. If the marketing authorisation is pending, please state

Durvalumab in combination with tremelimumab currently holds a marketing authorisation for the treatment of adults with advanced or unresectable HCC, which was granted by the **European Medicines Agency (EMA)** .[1] 

A marketing authorisation application was subsequently approved by the United Kingdom (UK) **Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA)** on the 6[th] June 2023 for the use of durvalumab in combination with tremelimumab in patients with advanced with advanced or unresectable HCC.[2] This is the indication under consideration for this evaluation.

## **STRIDE is intended to treat advanced or unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)** 

## **What is hepatocellular carcinoma?** 

Hepatocellular carcinoma, also called HCC, is a type of liver cancer that develops from liver cells called hepatocytes.[3] HCC accounts for about 50% of all liver cancer cases and is the most common type of primary liver cancer, i.e. where the cancer originates within the liver itself.[4] In the UK, approximately 6,100 people are diagnosed with HCC each year, and nearly 6,000 people die from it annually. This means HCC makes up 3% of all cancer deaths in the UK.[5, 6] 

## **What are the signs and symptoms of HCC?** 

For patients in the early stages of HCC, there might not be any symptoms, or they might be hard to spot. Some common symptoms include:[7] 

- Extreme tiredness 

- Weakness 

- Loss of appetite 

- Unintended weight loss 

- Nausea or vomiting 

- Pain in the area of the liver 

- General feeling of being unwell 

Because these symptoms are so general, HCC is often diagnosed late. About 41% of patients are diagnosed when the cancer is already advanced or cannot be removed with surgery.[8, 9] Furthermore, up to half of the patients who do have surgery to remove the cancer find that it comes back within two years.[10] 

## **What causes HCC?** 

HCC often develops in people who have **cirrhosis** , a condition where the liver becomes severely scarred. There are many risk factors that contribute to developing cirrhosis, including: 

- Infections with hepatitis B or C viruses 

- Long-term heavy drinking 

- Obesity 

- Diabetes 

There are also additional factors that can increase the likelihood of have HCC. For instance, individuals aged over 60 (especially those over 85), men, and those with a family history of primary liver cancer are at higher risk. Additionally, individuals with medical conditions such as

gallstones, liver flukes (parasites in the liver), or human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) also have an increased likelihood of developing HCC.[11] 

## **What is advanced or unresectable HCC?** 

HCC initially progresses slowly.[12] In its early stages, it can often be treated effectively with surgery to remove the tumour or through a liver transplant.[7] However, symptoms of HCC are typically scarce and non-specific, which means many people may not realise they have liver cancer until it has advanced. 

As the cancer progresses, it can become more challenging to treat and it may spread to other parts of the liver or to other organs. Doctors use the **Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) Staging System** to describe how far the cancer has progressed, from very early (Stage 0) to terminal (Stage D). You can find more details about staging in **Section 2b** . When HCC reaches an advanced stage (Stage C), it may no longer be possible to remove the tumour surgically. This stage is referred to as advanced or unresectable HCC. At this point, treatment options focus on managing symptoms and trying to slow the progression of the disease, often involving systemic therapies such as targeted treatments, immunotherapy, or chemotherapy. 

## **What is the impact of advanced or unresectable HCC (disease burden)?** 

Physically, advanced or unresectable HCC can cause severe symptoms that make everyday activities difficult, with symptoms like diarrhoea, fatigue, skin toxicity and appetite loss reported to have a significant impact.[13] 

Emotionally, both patients and caregivers often experience stress, anxiety, and depression due to the diagnosis and ongoing treatment. Frequent medical visits and treatments can disrupt daily routines, making it challenging for patients to engage in social activities or maintain their independence.[8] 

Families and caregivers also bear considerable emotional and financial stress. Balancing work, personal life, and caregiving duties can lead to neglecting their own care and reduced well-being.[14] The financial strain of caregiving, such as lost income and extra expenses, can further impact family resources and everyone’s **quality of life.** 

## **What is the personal, financial and societal cost of advanced or unresectable HCC?** 

HCC has significant costs that affect patients, caregivers, and society as a whole. For patients, living with HCC means dealing with symptoms like pain, fatigue, and liver problems, which can disrupt daily life and frequently lead to time off work or long-term disability. **[15]** Caregivers also face financial challenges, often providing unpaid assistance in managing their loved one’s health.[14] 

Treating HCC is also expensive. In England, the cost to treat 15,684 patients over six years was about £245 million, with an average cost of around £9,065 per patient over two years. **[16]** The NHS bears a significant financial burden due to the rising number of HCC cases, which in turn affects the overall economy and workforce. Besides these direct medical costs, there are also indirect costs such as lost income and additional expenses for travel and caregiving responsibilities. **[14]**
