## **2b) Diagnosis of the condition (in relation to the medicine being evaluated)** 

Please briefly explain how the condition is currently diagnosed and how this impacts patients. Are there any additional diagnostic tests required with the new treatment? 

## **How is HCC diagnosed?** 

When diagnosing HCC, doctors use various methods to assess the liver function. Imaging tests, such as **computerised tomography (CT)** , **magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), ultrasounds** and **PET (positron emission tomography)** scans, can be used to look for any tumours within the liver. Tissue **biopsies** can be examined under a microscope for signs of damage or disease. Blood tests can also be taken to look for tumour **markers** , which doctors can look for to diagnose cancers.[11, 17] 

## **Staging** 

Once diagnosed, the next important step is determining the stage of the cancer. The stage of a cancer describes its size and whether it has spread from where it first started. By analysing the stage, clinicians can discuss the best treatment options available for patients. In the UK, the staging depends on factors such as:[7] 

- Where the cancer is in the liver 

- The size of the tumour or tumours 

- How many tumours there are 

- Whether the cancer has spread outside the liver 

- Whether any important **blood vessels** in the liver are affected 

- How well your liver is working 

- Yor general health 

These evaluations use the BCLC staging system to categorise patients, from Stage 0 (very early HCC) to Stage D ( **terminal** HCC), and can inform the type of treatments patients are likely to be recommended. In this evaluation, we are particularly focussed on intermediate (Stage B) and advanced or unresectable (Stage C) HCC. 

Intermediate HCC (Stage B) means there are multiple tumours in the liver, but they haven’t spread outside the liver or into major blood vessels.[18, 19] Advanced HCC (Stage C) is when tumours have started to invade blood vessels or spread beyond the liver to other parts of the body.[18, 19] Patients at this stage might have more severe symptoms and may need treatments like targeted therapies or immunotherapy to help control the disease and improve their quality of life. Understanding these stages is crucial as it helps doctors choose the optimal treatment options for different patients.

## **What are the current treatment options for advanced or unresectable HCC?** 

In England and Wales, three **first-line therapies** are currently recommended by NICE for the systemic treatment of adults with advanced or unresectable HCC.[20-23] 

## **Atezolizumab + bevacizumab** 

The **combination therapy** atezolizumab + bevacizumab is the preferred treatment option for individuals with advanced or unresectable HCC. It is given to patients every three weeks through an **intravenous** (IV) line, which is where the medicine is administered directly into the vein.[21] These medicines help the **immune system** fight cancer and can slow down the growth of blood vessels that feed tumours.[24] 

Since bevacizumab can increase the risk of bleeding, all patients need to have an endoscopy before starting the treatment.[25, 26] This test helps doctors check for any potential bleeding risks. Unfortunately, the procedure can be uncomfortable for patients, it might delay the start of cancer treatment and may put a strain on the healthcare services. 

## **Sorafenib and lenvatinib** 

Some people might not be able to take atezolizumab + bevacizumab. This could be because the treatment needs to be given through an IV or because they are allergic to some of the ingredients. For these individuals, there are two alternative therapies that can be taken: sorafenib or lenvatinib. 

Sorafenib and lenvatinib are both administered orally, with sorafenib taken twice a day and lenvatinib taken once a day.[22, 23] They work by blocking **proteins** needed for cancer **cell** growth and creating new blood vessels.[27-29] Both medications are recommended by NICE for those with advanced HCC and good liver function. 

## **Unmet need** 

Although atezolizumab + bevacizumab is often the first systemic treatment offered to patients with HCC, the requirement for an endoscopy can delay the start of therapy and put extra strain on healthcare services. Additionally, some patients may not be suitable for this treatment due to risks like treatment-related bleeding, other co-existing limiting conditions or allergies to the 

Summary of information for patients for durvalumab with tremelimumab for untreated advanced or unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma [ID2725]

ingredients. Therefore, there is a significant need for more treatment options that can help a large number of patients live longer. 

## **STRIDE** 

STRIDE is a new combination treatment of durvalumab and tremelimumab. Tremelimumab is given as a one-off dose, administered to patients via IV. Durvalumab is administered to patients via IV every four weeks. This combination therapy works by improving the immune system's ability to attack cancer cells without increasing the risk of treatment-related bleeding.[30] 

Recent treatment guidelines developed by experts in liver disease support the use of STRIDE as a first-line treatment alongside atezolizumab + bevacizumab for patients with advanced or unresectable HCC.[5] Alternative options, for example if patients do not want an IV treatment or have an allergy to one of the first-line treatment options, include lenvatinib or sorafenib.[5] This positioning has also been supported by feedback from UK clinical experts.

## **HCC from the patient perspective** 

**Integrating the patient voice with clinician reports to identify hepatocellular carcinomaspecific treatment-related symptomatic adverse events[31]** 

A study was conducted to improve how patients report side effects during clinical trials for HCC. The study used a special system called the **Patient-Reported Outcomes version of the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (PRO-CTCAE)** to gather side effect information from both patients and doctors. Five medical oncologists from different countries and 17 patients with HCC participated. They worked together to identify the most important side effects to monitor during these trials. Doctors highlighted serious side effects like handfoot syndrome, diarrhoea, fatigue, decreased appetite, rash, vomiting, and weight loss. They also noted concerns such as chills, difficulty swallowing, and loss of bowel control. Patients pointed out that loss of appetite, pain at injection sites, fatigue, nausea, and hair loss were particularly bothersome. The study concluded that combining patient and doctor perspectives is crucial. This helps create a useful list of side effects to monitor, making treatments more tolerable for patients. 

## **Unmet need and value of STRIDE** 

Patients with HCC face significant unmet needs, including insufficient information at diagnosis and treatments that often impair their quality of life. Common side effects such as fatigue, nausea, and hair loss are major concerns. There is a need for better communication and more accessible information, as well as treatments that prioritise maintaining and improving quality of life. 

## **How STRIDE addresses these needs** 

STRIDE shows great promise in addressing the needs of patients with HCC. In the HIMALAYA trial, patients answered quality of life and health questions using special questionnaires.[32] Patients on STRIDE experienced longer times before symptoms worsened and showed better overall health, physical functioning, and improvements in specific symptoms like fatigue, nausea, and appetite loss compared to those on sorafenib. STRIDE also improved abdominal pain and swelling more effectively. 

Additionally, patients reported better daily functioning, emotions, and social interactions. Quality of life remained stable and even slightly improved over time for STRIDE patients. Overall, STRIDE leads to better health outcomes and significantly improves the quality of life for patients with HCC, effectively addressing the key areas where patients had highlighted the need for improvement. 

## **SECTION 3: The treatment** 

## **3a) How does the new treatment work?** 

What are the important features of this treatment? 

Please outline as clearly as possible important details that you consider relevant to patients relating 

Summary of information for patients for durvalumab with tremelimumab for untreated advanced or unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma [ID2725] 

© Astra Zeneca (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 193 -->

to the mechanism of action and how the medicine interacts with the body 

Where possible, please describe how you feel the medicine is innovative or novel, and how this might be important to patients and their communities. 

If there are relevant documents which have been produced to support your regulatory submission such as a summary of product characteristics or patient information leaflet, please provide a link to these. 

STRIDE is a combination therapy consisting of two treatments: durvalumab and tremelimumab. 

Durvalumab is a specially designed **antibody** that helps your immune system fight cancer by blocking a protein called **PD-L1** . PD-L1 is a protein that some cancer cells use to hide from your immune cells. By blocking PD-L1, durvalumab enables your immune system's white blood cells to recognise and attack the cancer cells more effectively.[33-35] 

Tremelimumab is another antibody that supports your immune system by targeting a different protein known as **CTLA-4,** which is found on activated **T-cells** . Normally, CTLA-4 can inhibit white blood cell activation, which can limit your **immune response** . By blocking CTLA-4, tremelimumab keeps white blood cells activated and enhances their ability to combat cancer cells.[36, 37] 

When used together, these two treatments offer a complementary approach to combating cancer. Durvalumab stops cancer cells from hiding by inhibiting PD-L1, while tremelimumab ensures that white blood cells stay activated by blocking CTLA-4. Compared to using either treatment alone, this combination results in a stronger and more prolonged immune response against the cancer cells, improving the chances of stopping the cancer.[30] 

Importantly, this treatment avoids using drugs that affect the growth of new blood vessel, and avoiding such drugs can reduce the risk of serious treatment-related bleeding. This is particularly beneficial for patients with advanced liver cancer, who are more likely to experience bleeding complications.[5]

## **3c) Administration and dosing**

## **How is STRIDE taken?** 

The STRIDE regimen involves two medicines: tremelimumab and durvalumab. Treatment begins with a single dose of 300 mg of tremelimumab given through an IV. This happens on the first day of the first treatment cycle ( **Cycle** 1, Day 1). Immediately after, patients receive 1,500 mg of durvalumab, also given through an IV infusion on the same day. After the initial treatment, patients continue to receive 1,500 mg durvalumab alone every four weeks via an IV infusion.[32] The treatment typically continues long-term, but the exact duration will be determined by the doctor based on how the cancer responds to the treatment and if the patient experiences any adverse events. 

Further details on the administration and dosing requirements for STRIDE can be found in the **Summary of Product Characteristics (SmPC)** for STRIDE for the treatment of advanced or unresectable HCC.[38, 39]

## **Studies of STRIDE in advanced or unresectable HCC** 

The key **clinical trial** providing clinical evidence for STRIDE in patients with advanced or unresectable HCC is the **Phase III** HIMALAYA trial.[32, 40] 

The HIMALAYA trial assesses how well STRIDE worked to improve patient survival and reduce or stop tumour growth compared to sorafenib. More details on the exact measurements used can be found in **Section 3e** . The trial also assesses the safety and tolerability of STRIDE compared to sorafenib, including the frequency and severity of side effects, and whether patients had to stop treatment. Finally, the trial considers the impact of STRIDE on patients’ quality of life. 

The HIMALAYA trial is being conducted in 170 countries and includes 1,324 participants. The initial phase of the trial was completed on August 27, 2021, and the entire study is expected to be finished by August 27, 2024. Data collected from HIMALAYA has been reported in the New England Journal of Medicine by Abou-Alfa 2022, and the latest information on the trial is available at ClinicalTrials.gov.[32, 40]

## **Trial results** 

There are six key clinical outcomes that were used to assess the efficacy of STRIDE compared to sorafenib. The outcomes used, their respective definitions, and the results from the HIMALAYA trial are listed below: 

- **Overall survival (OS)** : the duration from the start of the trial until death of any cause 

- **Progression-free survival (PFS):** the time from the start of the trial until the tumour progresses or until death of any cause 

- **Time to progression (TTP):** the time from the start of the trial until the tumour progresses 

- **Objective response rate (ORR):** the number of patients showing **complete** or **partial response** from the treatment 

- **Disease control rate (DCR)** : the number of individuals who had a complete or partial response, or whose disease had stabilised 

- **Duration of response (DoR)** : the percentage of patients still responding to treatment

|---|---|---|
|OSa, months|16.4|13.8|
|PFSa, months|3.8b|4.1b|
|TTPa, months|5.4|5.6|
|ORR, %|20.1|5.1|
|DCR, %|60.1|60.7|
|DoRa, months|22.3|18.4|



**Footnote** :[a] The OS, PFS, TTP and DoR efficacy measures refer to the **median** value;[b] A higher percentage of patients in the STRIDE group (12.5%) remained progression-free compared to the sorafenib group (4.9%), indicating that there is a benefit of the STRIDE treatment to patient despite having similar PFS values. 

In summary, STRIDE demonstrated a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in OS compared to sorafenib, which was the main clinical outcome assessed. Additionally, improvements were observed in ORR and DCR, with comparable PFS, TTP, and DCR to sorafenib. 

## **Indirect treatment comparison** 

No data are available for **direct comparisons** of STRIDE versus atezolizumab + bevacizumab and lenvatinib from the HIMALAYA trial. Therefore, an analysis called an **indirect comparison** was used. This method allows researchers to compare data from different clinical trials by using a common treatment that was assessed in both trials, in this case sorafenib. 

This analysis revealed that OS and PFS were improved for STRIDE, atezolizumab + bevacizumab, and lenvatinib compared to sorafenib. It also revealed that there was no significant difference in effectiveness between STRIDE and atezolizumab + bevacizumab, which is currently the treatment option that offers patients the best chance of survival.

## **Quality of life impact of STRIDE** 

During HIMALAYA, patients were asked to answer questions about their quality of life and health, using the three questionnaires below: 

- **EORTC QLQ-C30** : This is a questionnaire designed to evaluate the overall quality of life of patients with cancer participating in clinical trials. The questionnaire addresses a wide range of health and well-being aspects 

- **EORTC QLQ-HCC18** : This is a specialised questionnaire aimed at assessing the quality of life specifically in patients with HCC involved in clinical trials 

- **EQ-5D-5L** : This is a standardised questionnaire that is non-specific to any disease area which provides a general measure of health and well-being by examining five key areas of daily functioning and health status 

Before treatment began, patients in both the STRIDE and sorafenib groups had similar health scores, but there were some small differences. STRIDE patients had high physical functioning scores but lower overall health and quality of life scores. On the other hand, those starting on sorafenib reported more severe symptoms, including fatigue, loss of appetite, abdominal pain, and shoulder pain. 

Treatment with STRIDE resulted in a longer amount of time before symptoms worsened compared to sorafenib. Patients who received STRIDE showed better results in overall health, physical functioning, and specific symptoms such as fatigue, nausea, and appetite loss. STRIDE also led to greater improvements in abdominal pain and swelling compared to sorafenib. Moreover, patients on STRIDE experienced greater improvements in daily roles, cognitive abilities, emotions and social interactions.[41] 

Quality of life, measured by the EQ-5D-5L questionnaire, remained stable and even improved slightly over time for patients who received STRIDE, compared to patients who received sorafenib. Additionally, patients on STRIDE reported fewer severe problems compared to those on sorafenib, even after stopping treatment. 

Overall, all three questionnaires indicated that STRIDE leads to better health outcomes and improved quality of life for patients. Additionally, treatment with STRIDE allowed patients to maintain their daily functioning and manage disease symptoms for a longer period compared to those who were treated with sorafenib.[41]

## **3g) Safety of the medicine and side effects** 

When NICE appraises a treatment, it will pay close attention to the balance of the benefits of the treatment in relation to its potential risks and any side effects. Therefore, please outline the main side effects (as opposed to a complete list) of this treatment and include details of a benefit/risk assessment where possible. This will support patient reviewers to consider the potential overall benefits and side effects that the medicine can offer. 

Based on available data, please outline the most common side effects, how frequently they happen compared with standard treatment, how they could potentially be managed and how many people had treatment adjustments or stopped treatment. Where it will add value or context for patient readers, please include references to the Summary of Product Characteristics from regulatory agencies etc. 

Every medicine has its own **side effects** and the same medicine can produce different reactions in different people. The SmPC for STRIDE reports side effects which are categorised as very common (occurring in more than 1 in 10 people) and common (occurring in more than 1 in 100 but less than 1 in 10 people).[38, 39] Detailed information about any side effects can be found in the patient leaflets on the EMC website.[42, 43] 

In HIMALAYA, STRIDE was generally well **tolerated** . No new side effects were discovered for STRIDE compared to the already known side effects for the two medicines within the regimen.[44] 

When compared to sorafenib, a similar number of patients experienced serious side effects: 196 patients (50.5%) who received STRIDE and 196 patients (52.4%) who received sorafenib. Additionally, 53 patients (13.7%) receiving STRIDE and 63 patients (16.8%) receiving sorafenib had to stop treatment due to side effects. This suggests that STRIDE and sorafenib have similar safety profiles. 

The most common side effects seen in patients receiving STRIDE were rashes (22.4%), itching (22.9%) and diarrhoea (26.5%). Importantly, there were low levels of bleeding-related side effects in patients treated with STRIDE.[32] There was also no difference in liver-related side effects between STRIDE and sorafenib, indicating that treatment with STRIDE is not associated with increased liver problems.[32]

**3i) Value and economic considerations** 

## **Introduction for patients:** 

Health services want to get the most value from their budget and therefore need to decide whether a new treatment provides good value compared with other treatments. To do this they consider the costs of treating patients and how patients’ health will improve, from feeling better and/or living longer, compared with the treatments already in use. The drug manufacturer provides this information, often presented using a health economic model. 

In completing your input to the NICE appraisal process for the medicine, you may wish to reflect on: 

- The extent to which you agree/disagree with the value arguments presented below (e.g., whether you feel these are the relevant health outcomes, addressing the unmet needs and issues faced by patients; were any improvements that would be important to you missed out, not tested or not proven?) 

- If you feel the benefits or side effects of the medicine, including how and when it is given or taken, would have positive or negative financial implications for patients or their families (e.g., travel costs, time-off work)? 

- How the condition, taking the new treatment compared with current treatments affects your quality of life. 

Healthcare administrators need to get the best value from their limited budgets. To do this, they want to know whether a new medicine provides ‘good value for money’ compared to existing medicines. They will look at the costs of the new medicine and how the health of patients is likely to improve if they take it. The pharmaceutical company that develops the medicine provides this information to healthcare administrators using a **health economic model** . The health economic model developed for this NICE submission will be used to perform an analysis comparing the costs and benefits of the new treatment (STRIDE) with each of the three existing therapies offered as a first-choice therapy to patients: atezolizumab + bevacizumab, lenvatinib and sorafenib. 

## **How the model reflects advanced or unresectable HCC** 

The economic model was designed to reflect the key features of advanced or unresectable HCC and **clinical practice** in the UK. To do this, a model structure called a **partitioned survival model** was chosen, as it best fits the clinical data and matches the methods used in similar analyses. The partitioned survival model was used to model the experience of having advanced or unresectable HCC over time and compares treatment with STRIDE versus atezolizumab + bevacizumab, lenvatinib and sorafenib. 

## **Modelling the impact of STRIDE on quality of life in advanced or unresectable HCC** 

Data from the HIMALAYA trial and the indirect treatment comparison were used to compare STRIDE, atezolizumab + bevacizumab, lenvatinib and sorafenib in a health economic model.[29, 45] The economic analysis considers by how much STRIDE is likely to extend both survival (OS) and the amount of time patients can live without their tumour progressing (PFS). The economic analysis is modelled over a total of 40 years, far beyond the trial period. This is because the HIMALAYA results span four years, but patients can live longer and continue treatment. 

Summary of information for patients for durvalumab with tremelimumab for untreated advanced or unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma [ID2725] 

© Astra Zeneca (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 201 -->

Quality of life and time spent alive is captured by **quality-adjusted life years (QALYs)** . Data on the quality of life of patients in the HIMALAYA were taken from a questionnaire called the EQ-5D-5L ( **Section 3f** ). In the economic model, the quality of life is captured using **utility values** . Utility values are generally a number between 0, which represents death, and 1, which represents perfect health. QALYs are a health outcome measure that considers both the length and the quality of life provided by a treatment. A year spent in perfect health (i.e. a utility score of 1) represents one QALY. In the model, each treatment was assigned a utility value, which reflected the impact adverse events associated with that particular treatment may have on patient quality of life. 

STRIDE is expected to offer better quality of life benefits for patients with advanced or unresectable HCC compared to the lenvatinib and sorafenib, whilst showing similar results to atezolizumab + bevacizumab. The model showed this by modelling evaluating how helpful each treatment is in improving patients' overall well-being. 

Furthermore, STRIDE is likely to help patients live longer compared to lenvatinib and sorafenib, and it is expected to have similar survival results to atezolizumab + bevacizumab. 

## **Modelling the costs of treatments** 

Various different costs are included in the model for the different advanced or unresectable HCC treatments. These costs include: 

- The cost of the medicine itself and how much it costs to administer the medicine 

- The cost of monitoring the patients during treatment 

- The cost of side effects that happen during treatment 

- The costs of end-of-life care 

## **Uncertainty** 

There was some uncertainty about the estimated treatment effects within the model, which quality of life measures should be used, and whether sharing vials of the medicine should be included in the model. However, analyses varying these factors found that the overall conclusion remained unchanged. 

Variations of other inputs in the model were also tested, the results of these tests are explained in **Document B, Section B.3.11.** 

## **Cost effectiveness results** 

Based on the modelling inputs and assumptions from AstraZeneca, treatment with STRIDE was associated with similar health benefits (or ‘ **quality-adjusted life years’ [QALYs]** ) at a reduced cost compared to atezolizumab + bevacizumab, the principle treatment used for advanced or unresectable HCC in the UK, based on AstraZeneca’s calculations. 

Summary of information for patients for durvalumab with tremelimumab for untreated advanced or unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma [ID2725] 

© Astra Zeneca (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 202 -->

## **Benefits of STRIDE not captured in the economic analysis** 

Treatment with STRIDE may have many different positive impacts for people with advanced or unresectable HCC. The model aims to capture as many of these benefits as possible, but there are other benefits that could not be fully captured. For example: 

- While this evaluation highlights that STRIDE saves money by not needing endoscopy compared to atezolizumab + bevacizumab, it doesn't account for other benefits like reduced time to treatment initiation, or reduced strain on the NHS if STRIDE is recommended. 

- The evaluation also doesn't consider the positive effects on carers and relatives due to better patient outcomes with STRIDE. It overlooks how these improved outcomes could boost the productivity of patients, carers, and relatives. 

## **3j) Innovation** 

NICE considers how innovative a new treatment is when making its recommendations. 

If the company considers the new treatment to be innovative please explain how it represents a ‘step change’ in treatment and/ or effectiveness compared with current treatments. Are there any QALY benefits that have not been captured in the economic model that also need to be considered (see section 3f) 

## **STRIDE is an innovative treatment which would represent an important advancement in the treatment of advanced or unresectable HCC** 

STRIDE is an innovative treatment option that consists of two immune system-based therapies, durvalumab and tremelimumab. By bringing together these two therapies, the treatment leverages their unique strengths in enhancing the immune system's ability to fight cancer.[30] 

STRIDE is the first treatment for advanced or unresectable HCC that has strong evidence showing it is effective in patients without resulting in an increased risk of treatment-related bleeding. Therefore, STRIDE stands out as an effective treatment with manageable side effects, making it particularly beneficial for individuals who are not eligible for other treatments. 

Advanced or unresectable HCC can greatly impact a patient’s mental, emotional well-being, and quality of life. Unfortunately, current treatments often come with uncomfortable side effects or may not be suitable for all patients. STRIDE, however, has a manageable safety profile and serves as an alternative clinical option that can improve patients' quality of life compared to other treatments. 

The treatment burden with STRIDE is lower compared to other options, as it requires less frequent treatment sessions. Additionally, unlike other treatments, not all patients need an endoscopy before starting STRIDE. This means patients will spend less time in hospital and experience fewer delays before beginning treatment, thereby improving their overall wellbeing.

## **B.1 Addendum** 

## _**20[th] December 2024**_ 

## **B.1.1** _**Description of survival curves in the submission**_ 

- Company submission Document B, Figure 35: Base case overall survival (OS) parametric survival extrapolations (STRIDE, atezolizumab + bevacizumab, sorafenib and lenvatinib) 

   - The plot depicts the OS Kaplan Meier (KM) curves for STRIDE and sorafenib from the HIMALAYA trial, with the independently fit base case models extrapolated over the model time horizon. Also included on the plot are lenvatinib and atezolizumab + bevacizumab. 

   - The atezolizumab + bevacizumab curve initially sits above the STRIDE curve, up to ~6.5 years, before falling below the STRIDE curve, as a result of applying the hazard ratio (HR) calculated in the indirect treatment comparison (ITC) presented in the Company submission to the sorafenib reference curve for atezolizumab + bevacizumab and using independently fit models for HIMALAYA.  This is an appropriate approach given that the proportional hazards assumption holds within IMBRAVE150 between atezolizumab + bevacizumab and sorafenib, but does not hold within HIMALAYA for STRIDE and sorafenib. 

   - The lenvatinib curve was generated by applying a HR of 1 to the sorafenib arm, reflecting the REFLECT study's conclusion that lenvatinib was statistically noninferior to sorafenib in terms of OS. 

- Company submission Document B, Figure 47: Base case progression-free survival (OFS) parametric survival extrapolations (STRIDE, atezolizumab + bevacizumab, sorafenib and lenvatinib) 

   - The plot depicts the PFS KM curves for STRIDE and sorafenib from the HIMALAYA trial, with the independently fit base case models extrapolated over the model time horizon. Also included on the plot are lenvatinib and atezolizumab + bevacizumab. 

   - The atezolizumab + bevacizumab curve initially sits above the STRIDE curve, up to ~9 years, before falling below the STRIDE curve, as a result of applying the HR calculated in the ITC to the sorafenib reference curve for atezolizumab + bevacizumab, and using independently fit models for HIMALAYA.  This is an appropriate approach given that the proportional hazards assumption holds within IMBRAVE150 between atezolizumab + bevacizumab and sorafenib, but does not hold within HIMALAYA for STRIDE and sorafenib. 

   - Similarly, the lenvatinib curve initially sits above the STRIDE curve, up to ~3 years, before falling below the STRIDE curve, as a result of applying the HR calculated in the ITC to the sorafenib reference curve for lenvatinib, and using independently fit models for HIMALAYA. This is a pragmatic and conservative approach – although the proportional hazards assumption is violated in REFLECT between lenvatinib and sorafenib, time-varying analyses conducted for RELFECT suggested a positive treatment effect for lenvatinib at the beginning of the study follow-up that diminishes over time, meaning that the results of the NMA may overpredict survival for lenvatinib.

## **B.1.2.2 Exploring uncertainty** 

Parameter uncertainty in the model was assessed via both probabilistic and deterministic sensitivity analyses, the results of which are presented in Sections B.1.2.1 and B.1.2.2, respectively. In addition, key assumptions in the model were explored in several probabilistic scenario analyses, the results of which are presented in Section B.1.2.4. Overall, it is considered that all relevant uncertainties included in the analyses have been adequately accounted for, and the base case results were found to be robust to uncertainty in the key model inputs and assumptions. 

## _**B.1.2.2.1 Probabilistic sensitivity analysis**_ 

Probabilistic sensitivity analyses (PSA) were run with 1,000 iterations, with estimates of model parameters based on the uncertainty in the source data (where data availability permitted). Beta distributions were assumed for uncertain parameters bound by zero and one, including utilities, proportions, and probabilities. Log-normal distributions were assumed for hazard ratios. Gamma distributions were assumed for costs. Normal distributions were assumed for other uncertain parameters including resource use frequencies, with capping in place to ensure positivity for parameters which must be non-negative. 

The probabilistic pairwise cost-effectiveness planes for STRIDE vs. relevant comparators are presented in Figure 1 to Figure 3. The cost-effectiveness acceptability curve is presented in Figure 4.

## _**B.1.2.2.3 Deterministic sensitivity analysis**_ 

To assess the robustness of the base case cost-effectiveness results, deterministic sensitivity analyses (DSA) were conducted. The tornado diagrams for STRIDE vs. relevant comparators are presented in Figure 5, Figure 6 and Figure 7. The top 10 most influential parameters on the base case are presented in each case. In the comparison of STRIDE vs. sorafenib, the model was robust to variation in inputs. In the comparison of STRIDE vs. lenvatinib, results were most influenced by the PFS HR. Given PFS informs treatment duration for lenvatinib, and therefore drug costs, this likely explains the level of influence of this input. In the comparison of STRIDE vs. atezolizumab + bevacizumab, the PFS HR was again influential, and otherwise the model was robust to input variation.

## **A6. Priority question. CS, Document B, Figure 19. In Figure 19, the company presented data on serious adverse events that are treatment-related and not treatment-related. Please provide a definition, and a list of adverse events considered not treatment-related, along with their numerical input and analysis results.** 

Causality of AEs was collected in the HIMALAYA trial. AEs were considered as possibly related to any study treatment as assessed by the investigator. Treatmentrelated AEs were reported as possibly related with durvalumab, tremelimumab or sorafenib. A guide to interpreting the causality question was included in the HIMALAYA Clinical Study Protocol.[4] 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 232 -->

The factors to consider when deciding if there is a “reasonable possibility” that an AE may have been caused by the drug include: time course and exposure to suspect drug, consistency with known drug profile, de-challenge experience, no alternative cause, rechallenge experience, laboratory test, overdose of the drug or known mechanism. Missing responses were counted as related.[3] 

For serious adverse events (SAEs), investigators were also required to provide an assessment of the relationship of SAEs to protocol procedures on the SAE report form. This includes both non-treatment-emergent (ie, SAEs that occur prior to the administration of study drug[s]) and treatment emergent SAEs. 

There were no treatment-related SAEs by Preferred Term reported by ≥ 5% patients.[3] The most common SAEs that were not treatment-related are related to the underlying disease progression, such as XXXXXXXXX and XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.[4] 

Table 20 in Appendix I summarises common not treatment-related SAEs from the HIMALAYA trial.

An AE was considered as an “AE on treatment” or “treatment-emergent AE” if it started after dosing or prior to dosing and it worsens following exposure to the treatment.[1] 

Investigators were required to provide an assessment of causality of the AEs. In areas characterized by a high prevalence of HCC (such as Asia and Africa), the primary risk factors are chronic HBV infection and exposure to aflatoxin B1. With reference to: 

1. Sex female 

2. Age at randomisation 

3. Programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression (both positive and negative) 

4. Hepatitis C virus (HCV) as the aetiology of liver disease 

5. Yes macrovascular invasion (MVI) 

6. No extrahepatic spread (EHS)

8. Barcelona Clinical Liver Cancer (BCLC) score B 

Prior to initiating discussion on HRs from the HIMALAYA OS subgroup analysis, it is important to note that this subgroup analysis was not powered for formal comparisons; no multiplicity adjustments were made. This applies for both the primary subgroup analysis as well as the updated analysis I (DCO: 23[rd] January 2023), from the perspective of subgroup data. 

1. Sex female: Upper CI crosses 1. The confidence interval range (HR 1.02 [0.68-1.56]) is large. Not powered for formal analysis. 

2. Age at randomisation: Upper CI crosses 1 however HR is still <1 for patients aged <65. Age was not a stratification factor. Not powered for formal analysis. 

3. Programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression (both positive and negative): The predictive value of PD-L1 status for the efficacy of PD-L1 and PD-1 inhibitors or combination therapies has not been clearly shown in the case of HCC. There is a notable spacial and cellular heterogeneity of PD-L1 expression in HCC samples, which could limit predictive capabilities. PD-L1 status is also known to change over time, therefore a simple biopsy specimen is insufficient for determining long term treatment.[10] In the case of STRIDE, 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 237 -->

based on the subgroup analysis there is no indication to suggest PD-L1 status may have an impact on OS. PD-L1 was not a stratification factor. Not powered for formal analysis. 

4. Hepatitis C virus (HCV) as the aetiology of liver disease: As confirmed by post-hoc multivariate analysis, there was an imbalance observed across treatment arms in the HCV subgroup which was not present in other aetiology subgroups which may have contributed to the HRs observed. Extrahepatic spread (EHS) was more frequent in the STRIDE arm than in the durvalumab and sorafenib arms, and albumin-bilirubin (ALBI) score 2 was more frequent for STRIDE and durvalumab than for sorafenib. A stratified Cox proportional hazards model accounting for the imbalances in EHS and ALBI of the HCV subgroup was applied to all subgroups and resulted in an adjusted OS HR that favoured STRIDE versus sorafenib in the HCV subgroup (HR, 0.89 [0.631.25]).[11] Not powered for formal analysis. 

5. Yes macrovascular invasion (MVI): Upper CI crosses 1 however HR is still <1, not powered for formal analysis. 

6. No extrahepatic spread (EHS): Upper CI crosses 1 however HR is still <1. EHS was not a stratification factor. Not powered for formal analysis. 

7. Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) at baseline <400 ng/mL Upper CI crosses 1 however HR is still <1, not powered for formal analysis. 

8. Barcelona Clinical Liver Cancer (BCLC) score B: Upper CI crosses 1 however HR is still <1. BCLC was not a stratification factor. Not powered for formal analysis. Very small number of patients leading to a very wide range.

## **A18. Priority question. CS, Document B, Figure 24. In Figure 24 (p98), the company presented the observed raw and smoothed hazards from the HIMALAYA trial.** 

## **a) Please clarify how the raw hazard was generated.** 

The raw hazards were generated using the pehaz function in R. These represent the piecewise exponential hazard function. Time is split into equal segments, and the function calculates the hazard as the total number of events divided by the total follow up time in that segments. This is an approximation for the observed hazard. 

## **b) Please explain the purpose of undertaking this analysis in the context of the cost-effectiveness model that was developed.** 

The hazards for each treatment arm within the HIMALAYA trial period were assessed through visual inspection of the observed raw and smoothed hazard plots. Assessment of the hazard plots can indicate whether standard parametric survival models such as proportional hazards and accelerated failure time (AFT) models are suitable, or whether models with greater flexibility to captured changes in the direction of the hazard, such as spline-based models, should be explored.

## **b. Please clarify why an AFT approach was not explored.** 

Standard AFT models (e.g., lognormal and loglogistic) were explored and presented in Appendix O (incorrectly referenced as Appendix N in Document B).

## **c. If spline-based models are favoured by the company, then the EAG suggest that an AFT approach should be explored using methods described by Crowther Royston and Clements in Biostatistics (2023) 24, 3, pp. 811–831 (https://doi.org/10.1093/biostatistics/kxac009) since these accommodate the use of splines.** 

The fitting of spline models to patient level data in the HIMALAYA trial was performed using the flexsurvspline function in the R package, flexsurv. This included the fitting of Royston Parmar restricted cubic spline models on the “hazard”, “odds” 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 251 -->

and “normal” scale, with specifications of 1 to 3 knots. This yielded a total of 9 fitted models per arm, providing an extensive range of extrapolations for the economic model. 

When no knots are specified, the “hazard”, “odds” and “normal” spline models are equivalent to the standard distributions of Weibull, log-logistic and log-normal, respectively. Beyond the last knot, the splines behave in a similar manner to their related standard distribution, i.e., a spline normal behaves like a log-normal distribution. The spline “normal” models fitted to HIMALAYA would therefore produce long-term extrapolations that are consistent with the hazard profile predicted by an accelerated failure time model, such as the log-normal distribution. The spline normal 1 knot was selected in the Company base case to extrapolate STRIDE OS. Spline based normal and odds models for 1-3 knots are also explored and presented for OS and PFS in the CS in Document B Section B.3.3.3 (OS) and B.3.3.4 (PFS). 

The method proposed by the EAG is available through the rstpm2 package in R.[16] As stated in the help files of this package, the rstpm2 function will yield different spline estimates to flexsurv due to the use of a different natural spline basis. If however, the knot placement is the same across packages, as expected, the authors state that “predictions and coefficients are expected to be very similar”.[16]

## **b. In view of the change of observed hazard seen in years 0 to 3 versus years 3 to 6, please clarify whether the company has explored piecewise models.**

The restricted cubic spline models (Royston and Parmer)[19] explored by the Company permit estimation of a continuous function and allow more complex shapes to be modelled. A cubic spline is a piecewise cubic polynomial, where the number of “pieces” is dictated by the number of knots used, ensuring that notable changes in the trial hazard are captured. The Company believe that the spline-based models 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 254 -->

sufficiently capture the observed trial hazard from year 0 to 5, and benefit from not being overly influenced by the trend in the hazard observed at the end of the followup period which is based on a small number of patients as described in response to Question A21a. These models provide a robust fit to the KM probabilities and were explored following guidelines from the NICE DSU TSD 21.[20] 

‘Piecewise models’ as described in NICE DSU TSD 21[20] were not explored, and there are some noteworthy drawbacks of piecewise models which are described in the NICE DSU TSD 21.[20] Splitting data into sections according to time means that sample sizes are reduced, especially in the later segments of the curve, where patient numbers at risk may be very small and the number of observed events may be low, leading to large standard errors and uncertainty when fitting survival models. This is particularly important as it is the model fitted to the latest section of the curve that is used for extrapolation. The modeller also has to decide at which points the new models are fitted, which could introduce bias.

The EAG’s assumption that “pre-progression (on treatment) and pre-progression (off treatment) correspond to the progression-free health state, while progressed (on treatment) and progressed (off treatment) correspond to the progressed disease health state” is correct. However, patients in progressed (off treatment) are not receiving the first-line treatments durvalumab and tremelimumab and sorafenib. 

Subsequent treatments are modelled in the progressed disease health state as a weighted one-off cost applied upon entering the state. This is consistent with the modelling approaches used in previous NICE technology appraisals in advanced HCC.[23,24] 

## **b) What is the main outcome or next health state for patients undergoing subsequent treatment? Is it death? Additionally, what proportion of patients received third-line treatments?** 

A proportion of patients progressing from the progression-free to the progressed disease health state receive a subsequent treatment, which is a one-off cost applied upon entering the progressed disease health state. From this point, patients can either stay in the progressed disease health state or move to the death state. 

Only second-line subsequent treatments are modelled, as only a small proportion of patients receive active therapy beyond first-line treatment for advanced or unresectable HCC. Very few patients receive third-line treatment as a result of the poor disease prognosis, worsening of liver function and reduced patient fitness impacting the potential benefits from further lines of active therapy. This is consistent with the modelling approaches used in previous technology appraisals in advanced HCC.[23] 

**c) It appears that people who received subsequent treatment or in the preprogression (off-treatment) or progressed (off-treatment) health states have different characteristics to those who progressed (on-treatment) and pre-progression (on-treatment) health states, particularly regarding outcomes and resource use. Please provide further justification why separate health states were not used.** 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 260 -->

The model is a 3-state model consisting of progression-free, progressed disease, and death. This model structure was deemed the most appropriate based on the clinical data available. It also aligns with the structure adopted in previous NICE evaluations in advanced or unresectable HCC.[23-25] 

It is unclear where the assertion that patients on-treatment in the pre-progression health state have different outcomes and resource use from those off-treatment in the pre-progression health state originated from, given that no evidence has been provided to support this. Similarly, it is unclear where the assertion that patients ontreatment in the post-progression health state have different outcomes and resource use from those off-treatment in the post-progression health state originated from. The data are not available to model these groups independently. As all treatments have treat-to-progress protocols, a significant majority of patients receive the initial therapies until the point of transitioning into the progressed disease health state. 

Non-treatment related costs and resource use differ depending on the health state the patient is in, but not by on/off treatment status. Utility values were derived from the HIMALAYA trial and do not differ by health state but is dependent upon first-line treatment received, but not by on/off treatment status. Subsequent treatment costs were applied as a weighted one-off cost upon entering the progressed disease health state, and there were no utility values explicitly ascribed to the subsequent treatments received. 

Separate health states for on- and off- treatment in the progression-free and progressed disease, respectively, were not considered necessary, particularly given the data requirements for this technology appraisal, as well as the highly mature HIMALAYA data.

The NICE decision problem and CADTH decision problem are distinctly different. The approaches to modelling reflect the different requirements by each HTA body. - B7. CS, Document B, section B.3.2.2. The company stated _"Patients in the ‘Progressed disease’ health state can either remain alive with progressed disease or die, but the model does not allow for patients to improve their health state."_ (p89). Based on this, it appears that patients in the progression- 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 262 -->

free survival health state have a better health condition than those in a progressed disease health state. However, in Figure 23 (p90), the company showed that the proportion of patients in the "Progressed disease (PD)" health state is assumed to be the difference between the OS and PFS health states. Please provide further clarification on this. Specifically, please explain how this aligns with the health conditions and utility values of patients in the PD health state compared to those in the PFS health state. 

The EAG understanding is correct. 

NICE DSU TSD 19 describes that a partitioned survival model (PSM) with three health states requires two survival curves to estimate state membership: 

1. PFS:  describes time from model entry to exiting the progression-free state via progression or death (a composite outcome); 

2. OS: time from model entry to death. 

The first survival curve (PFS) directly provides the proportion of patients remaining in the first health state – progression-free – over time. State membership for the dead state is simply 1 minus the OS curve at each time point. For the progressed health state, state membership is derived as the difference between the OS and the PFS curve at each time point, as this provides the proportion of patients who are alive but not progression-free. 

The benefits of this approach is that the model structure directly leverages key timeto-event endpoints in the HIMALAYA study, namely OS and PFS. This reflects the natural disease course and the primary objectives of treatment for patients with advanced or unresectable HCC in the form of delaying progression. 

Utility values were derived using a mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM) analysis of all the post-baseline scores for each visit from the HIMALAYA trial to estimate the statistical relationship between utilities and randomised treatment. Deriving utility values from the primary trial informing the efficacy and in the population of interest in the model is aligned with the NICE reference case.[26] In the model, utilities were assigned based on treatment received, and it was assumed that atezolizumab + bevacizumab would have the same utility value as STRIDE, and 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 263 -->

lenvatinib would have the same utility value as sorafenib. This approach was adopted as it was considered to be the most robust way of capturing the impact of AEs due to TKIs on patients, as evidenced in IMbrave150 and HIMALAYA, and a systematic review and meta-analysis of systemic therapies for advanced HCC which shows that patients treated with TKIs are almost twice as likely as those treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors to experience an AE that is Grade 3 or higher (69% vs. 35%).[27,28] Utility values were also age-adjusted using the age- and sex-matched general population utility values reported in Hernández-Alava et al. 

An alternative utility approach has been provided in response to Question B12. This demonstrates consistent results to the Company base case. 

## **B8. Priority question. CS, Document B, section B.3.2.2. The company stated** _**“In line with clinical practice, within the progression-free and**_ 

- _**progressed health states, patients may either be on or off treatment.” (p89).**_ **However, the CS Model 'Model Structure' worksheet indicates that** _**“Time to Treatment Discontinuation (TTD) data is used to separate the progression-free and progressed health states.”**_ **It appears that TTD might be used to distinguish between on-treatment and off-treatment status within both progression-free and progressed health states. Please clarify these 2 statements and provide more details on the role of TTD.** 

The statement that “within the progression-free and progressed health states, patients may either be on or off treatment” is correct. Time on treatment is modelled using TTD data, as this is the most accurate approach to model this parameter. Time on treatment is independent of progression status. This approach was used when individual patient data were available for TTD (i.e., for sorafenib and STRIDE from HIMALAYA). When TTD data were not available (i.e., for atezolizumab plus bevacizumab and lenvatinib), an assumption was made that TTD is equivalent to PFS.

<!-- page 265 -->

adopted as captures the totality of the quality of life data by treatment arm and was considered to be the most robust way of capturing the impact of AEs due to TKIs on patients, as evidenced in IMbrave150 and HIMALAYA, and a systematic review and meta-analysis of systemic therapies for advanced HCC.[27,28] Utility values were also age-adjusted using the age- and sex-matched general population utility values reported in Hernández-Alava et al.[29] 

Overall survival has been established as an unquestionable, unbiased primary endpoint in oncology and in all randomized studies testing systemic first- and second-line therapies in advanced HCC, and weak surrogacy exists between OS and PFS in advanced or unresectable HCC, particularly for IO-IO therapies.[30-33] Given that PFS is a less clinically relevant endpoint, the Company believes that applying the same utility value in both health states is appropriate.

**B12. Priority question. CS, Document B, section B.3.9.2. Table 67 outlines the assumptions used in the company’s economic analysis. The EAG notes the company’s rationale about HRQoL is treatment dependent. Please provide further information to support this approach. The company stated,** _**“this approach was selected as it was considered to be the most robust way of capturing the impact of adverse events due to TKIs on patients.”**_ **(p159). Please provide a model that allows other approaches to be used.** 

As noted by the EAG, treatment dependent utilities were used in order to capture the impact of AEs due to TKIs on patients. 

The EAG has requested a model that allows other approaches to be used. The Company considered NICE TA666 (atezolizumab with bevacizumab in advanced or unresectable HCC) which used a time to death approach for utilities.[23] The Company has performed a similar analysis using the HIMALAYA data and implemented it in the cost-effectiveness model. The methodology and results are detailed here. 

UK utility values were derived from the EQ-5D-5L profiles in HIMALAYA using the UK value set by Hernandez et al. as per the original CS.[29] The statistical relationship between EQ-5D utility and time to death was assessed using regression analysis. To account for the repeated measurements in the study, a MMRM method was used to model EQ-5D utilities.[34] This method accounts for the autocorrelation in utility score within each patient and is appropriate when handling data that are missing at 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 267 -->

random. Notably, a random intercept model assuming independent within-subject errors was fitted to account for the subject variability. 

The analysis set comprised all patients in the full analysis set with an observed death prior to the Updated analysis I DCO date (August 2021), as well as observations from patients who were censored for death, recorded > 30 weeks from their date of censoring. The EQ-5D time-to-death analysis uses the August 2021 DCO, whilst the OS data used in the model uses the latest 5-year OS DCO (March 2024). This is a limitation in the analysis as the censoring/deaths driving the utility analysis have a different DCO (August 2021 DCO) versus the survival data in the CS (March 2024). This cannot be addressed because EQ-5D data were not collected beyond August 2021. 

Observations were categorized according to the proximity to a patient’s death, using the following categories: ≤5 weeks, >5-≤15 weeks, >15-≤30 weeks and >30 weeks from death date. These cut-offs were selected as they align with what was used in TA666. 

Observations from patients who were censored for death, that were recorded >30 weeks from date of censoring, were included in the > 30 week category only. Although these patients hadn’t experienced a death event whilst on the trial, we know death will occur at some point in the future, thereby verifying these as observations > 30 weeks from death. Observations from censored patients that were recorded < 30 weeks from their date of censoring were not included. As the death date for these patients is unknown, we are unable to classify these observations under any of the bounded time intervals. 

Table 9 provides a summary of the marginal means from the time-to-death utility analysis.

**B15. Priority question. CS, Document B, sections B.3.5.1 and B.3.5.2. Table 55 indicates that the majority of patients receiving different treatments after discontinuing first-line treatments are placed on BSC as their subsequent treatment. The EAG assumes that the resource use data by treatment and health state provided in Table 57 (p146) are related to BSC and apply to all patients in the progression-free and progressed disease health states, regardless of prior first-line treatments.** 

## **a) Please clarify the role and features of BSC in this context.** 

Palliative/best supportive care is offered to patients with end-stage liver disease to alleviate symptom burden and is employed when no active treatment options are 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 271 -->

deemed to bring benefit.[35] There is a holistic focus on management of pain, nutrition and psychological support. End-stage liver disease has further implications from the perspective of pharmacokinetics/metabolising medications such as analgesics and anti-anxiety treatments leading to use with caution, with non-pharmacological approaches often preferred. These patients are still monitored (costs included) – resource use items reflected in Table 57. 

- **b) The EAG considers that patients having BSC, as well as those receiving other subsequent treatments, may require medications to improve quality of life and manage symptoms, such as opioids, ondansetron, and metoclopramide. It is unclear how these supportive care medications are incorporated into the subsequent treatments or management of adverse reactions. Please provide clarification on how these supportive care measures are addressed in the model.** 

Monitoring, healthcare professional and hospitalisation costs are included for patients in the progressed disease health states, which make up the majority of the costs for BSC. Opioids, ondansetron, and metoclopramide are all low-cost drugs and are not anticipated to result in a notable additional cost to this health state. These costs were not included in recent technology appraisals in advanced HCC.[23,24] 

The costs of AEs is believed to be adequately captured using the NHS reference costs, and this aligned with previous appraisals in advanced HCC.[23,24]

|**6. What is it like to live**<br>**with the condition? What**<br>**do carers experience**<br>**when caring for someone**<br>**with the condition?**|Liver cancer is the fastest-rising cause of cancer related deaths. Around 6,200 people are diagnosed with liver<br>cancer each year. Incidence of liver cancer has increased by 50% over the past decade and is expected to<br>continue to rise. The most common form of liver cancer is hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), making up around<br>80% of all liver cancers. Only around 20% of liver cancers are diagnosed early (stage 1 or 2). The biggest risk<br>factor for HCC is pre-existing liver disease, with liver cirrhosis being present in 80-90% of people with HCC. Risk<br>factors include Hep B, Hep C, ARLD, MASLD. There are strong links with deprivation (including: homelessness,<br>heavy alcohol and drug use, obesity).<br>Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) is complex, varied and fluctuates, meaning that no one person’s experience is<br>the same as another. A diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma usually comes as a huge shock.<br>Many patients with HCC (approx. 80%) also have underlying liver cirrhosis, which not only makes treatment<br>difficult but also means that they may have other complications. Often the patient is diagnosed with cancer whilst<br>at the same time being told that they have a liver condition with cirrhosis. They live with uncertainty,<br>hopelessness and often stigma and isolation due to the image of liver cancer. The diagnostic process can be<br>protracted. Patients and carers are fearful of the future, the prognosis is extremely poor with only around 13%<br>living for 5 years. Patients often express frustration that they have been diagnosed too late for curative options.<br>Patients and carers worry about whether there will be any treatment options, whether those options will be<br>available in their area, how will family life/finances be impacted by the diagnosis and treatment. What will their<br>quality of life be like and how long are they likely to live for.<br>Primary liver cancer in adults has a poor outlook because it tends to be diagnosed late (only between10% and<br>20% of people are diagnosed at a point when surgery can help). For people where surgery is not an option, the<br>prognosis is particularly poor, and it is rare for people to live more than three years. The lack of other<br>chemotherapeutic drugs particularly affects this group as well as those awaiting a transplant. The British Liver<br>Trust has been working with NHSE to improve early diagnosis on three main workstreams: HCC surveillance,<br>community liver health checks, and piloting primary care case finding. In particular, it is hoped that the HCC<br>surveillance standards will improve early detection and reduce variation in care.<br>Because patients with advanced HCC have such a poor prognosis and there are so few treatment options they<br>are usually completely devastated. Patients are often relatively young and are completely shell shocked. Patients<br>also report feeling extremely unwell, very tired and weak. Some quotes from a focus group and one to one<br>interviewswithpatients and carersinclude:|

"Emotionally it was tough. I felt like I couldn't cope, and it all just caught up with me. I felt like every time I put my head up above water I got shot down." "Immediately after diagnosis I was shell shocked. I took my house in order, made my will. But I made changes to things. Death was imminent in my mind. Having a transplant makes me realise how lucky I am but I wish there had been another option. Liver disease doesn't seem to get the attention of other cancers." "We were just devastated. My husband was prescribed medication and underwent a radiofrequency ablation procedure. He was extremely tired and in pain. He was put on the waiting list, then he had to be taken off the list as the cancer had grown whilst waiting. He was 42 years old, had never drunk in his life and we were told he would die in about six weeks. The rug was completely taken from under my feet … my whole life crumbled and ten years on I am still in pain." Relatives have described the condition as "Brutal - the worst possible way to go". When patients are diagnosed with HCC, they often experience depression from the poor prognosis and a range of symptoms including severe pain that cannot be treated without worsening their liver condition. Other severe symptoms include ascites, fluid in the abdomen that can press on the stomach making it difficult to eat and even to breathe. Hepatic encephalopathy can make everyday functions including conversation, writing and staying awake difficult. Only a very few patients are offered curative treatment, and even then, many live with the uncertainty about whether they will receive a liver transplant before the tumour spreads, or whether they will die as a complication of surgery (liver resection has a relatively high mortality rate). Patients with HCC are often many years younger than those with other cancers, and extra time is of particular importance to people who may have young families and working lives to put in order before death. Buying extra time for such patients not only can positively impact those individuals but can also have a huge positive impact on families and the wider community, with unquantifiable downstream benefits that can bring. There is also wide variation of care across England and Wales with patients experiencing different standards of care depending on where they live. Our survey of 127 patients with HCC revealed • 90% wanted more information after they left their first appointment at the hospital

The majority of patients calling the helpline have Stage BCLC B or C HCC. The B group are offered TACE, or SIRT and C group systemic therapy if they have preserved liver function. Many patients are diagnosed with a liver condition, cirrhosis and liver cancer at the same time. Additional HCC treatments are urgently needed.

Guidelines from the<br>Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer group and from ESMO are generally followed,<br>although access to certain therapies is restricted in the UK.<br>Current systemic therapy options in first line include atezolizumab plus<br>bevacizumab, Lenvatinib and sorafenib. ## **Executive Summary** 

The summary provides an overview of the key issues identified by the Evidence Assessment Group (EAG) as being potentially important for decision making. It also includes the EAG’s preferred assumptions and the resulting incremental costeffectiveness ratios (ICERs). 

Section 1.1 provides an overview of the key issues. Section 1.2 provides an overview of key model outcomes and the modelling assumptions that have the greatest effect on the ICER. Sections 1.2.1 and 1.2.2 explain the key issues in more detail. Background information on the condition, technology and evidence and information on non-key issues are in the main EAG report. 

All issues identified represent the view of the EAG, not the opinion of NICE.

## **Common key issues: clinical effectiveness evidence** 

Here we outline our key concerns with the clinical effectiveness evidence submitted by the company. These include 

- Limitations in the generalisability of the HIMALAYA trial population to the UK NHS HCC patient population. 

- Appropriateness of the company NMA and the clarity of its presentation, together with a failure to consider published NMAs addressing the same issues as the company NMA. 

## **Common key issues: cost-effectiveness evidence** 

Here, we outline our key concerns with the cost-effectiveness evidence submitted by the company. These include: 

- Inconsistent use of individual patient data and hazard ratios across treatments results in unrealistic overall survival projections, especially for STRIDE. 

- The method used for modelling OS and PFS for STRIDE is different from that used for atezolizumab + bevacizumab and for lenvatinib, where NMA HRs associated with substantial uncertainty are used to estimate the impact. The EAG considers there to be a lack of equity in the modelling of STRIDE compared to that for atezolizumab + bevacizumab and lenvatinib. 

16 



<!-- page 345 -->

Warwick Evidence EAG STA and HST Report Template post February 2022 

- In the absence of time to discontinuation of treatment information for atezolizumab + bevacizumab and an assumed lack of information for lenvatinib, the company has assumed that TTD for these is equivalent to the company-developed models for progression-free survival (PFS). However, there are high levels of imprecision associated with PFS models (employing NMA output HRs) in the case of atezolizumab + bevacizumab bears little resemblance to what is seen in the IMbrave150 trial used for NMA input. The company’s NMA output for atezolizumab + bevacizumab PFS is an outsider relative to values in many published NMAs. The EAG is unconvinced that the equivalence of TTD and PFS is a sensible assumption for modelling. The EAG notes that the company states that clinical experts consulted highlighted that the measurement of PFS is challenging, as radiologic progression is a subjective measurement prone to reading errors. And that patients are frequently eligible to continue treatment both within the trial setting and realworld setting even after disease progression. Thus, using PFS as a proxy for TTD is particularly worrying. 

- The company assigned the same utility values for patients receiving first-line treatments (e.g., STRIDE) as for those subsequent treatments (e.g., sorafenib). This is inconsistent with the company’s treatment-related utility assumptions and neglects the impact of treatment-specific adverse events. 

- The source of age-adjustment coefficients for utilities is unclear and these appear overly optimistic. 

- The company's use of a QALY weight of 1.2, based on sorafenib, but the QALY weight should have reflected other established treatments (e.g., atezolizumab + bevacizumab) currently available in NHS practice. 

The key differences between the company’s preferred assumptions and the EAG’s preferred assumptions:

## **1.2 Overview of key model outcomes** 

NICE technology appraisals compare how much a new technology improves length (overall survival) and quality of life represented as quality-adjusted life year (QALY). An ICER is the ratio of the extra cost for every QALY gained. 

Overall, the technology is modelled to affect QALYs by: 

- By changing the overall survival 

- By changing the progression-free survival 

- By changing the incidence of treatment-related adverse events 

Overall, the technology is modelled to affect costs by: 

19 



<!-- page 348 -->

Warwick Evidence EAG STA and HST Report Template post February 2022 

- Drug acquisition, drug administration, and subsequent treatment costs 

- Health state management costs 

- End-of-life care costs and adverse event costs 

The modelling assumptions that have the greatest effect on the ICER are: 

- The assumption of using progression-free survival as a proxy of time-to-treatment discontinuation 

- Using the generalised gamma parametric model (based on the HIMALAYA trial) for sorafenib overall survival 

- Using the constant hazard ratio for overall survival and progression-free survival derived from a network meta-analysis and applied to STRIDE, atezolizumab + bevacizumab, and lenvatinib.

## **1.2.3 Other issues/remaining uncertainty** 

## **Other issues: decision problem** 

- The decision problem population is narrower than NICE scope. 

## **Other issues: clinical effectiveness evidence** 

- Concerns regarding potential long-term immune-related adverse effects and immunogenicity from STRIDE. 

## **Other issues: cost-effectiveness evidence** 

- Previous assessments typically used a 14 to 20-year time horizon, while the company's 40-year proposal was deemed overly optimistic by EAG clinical advisors, especially since only a very small proportion of patients survive beyond 20 years. 

- The company’s  half-cycle correction method for tremelimumab costs overestimates total expenses by misallocating costs, and inflating figures beyond the actual drug cost. 

26 



<!-- page 355 -->

## **1.3 Summary of EAG preferred assumptions and impact to the company ICER (pairwise comparison)** 

The EAG made the following changes to the company's model to form the EAG's base-case (see Table 2). The results show the impact of each change to the pairwise incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs).
