## **2 INTRODUCTION AND BACKGROUND** 

## **2.1 Introduction** 

## **2.1.1 Background** 

## _**Remit/evaluation objectives**_ 

To evaluate the clinical and cost-effectiveness of durvalumab combined with tremelimumab (as Single tremelimumab regular interval durvalumab) hereafter referred to as STRIDE for the first-line treatment of advanced or unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma in adults, within its marketing authorisation. 

## _**Condition, symptoms, and incidence**_ 

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a primary liver malignancy that predominantly affects patients with chronic liver disease and cirrhosis, though up to 25% of cases occur without these risk factors. The global incidence of HCC has been rising over the past 20 years and is expected to continue increasing in many countries. HCC incidence is highest in Asia and Africa due to the high prevalence of hepatitis B and C, both major risk factors for HCC. The incidence of advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) specifically is rarely reported separately to overall liver cancer statistics; liver cancer incidence in the UK has increased by 177% since the early 1990s, with projections indicating a further 6% rise by 2038-2040.[3] Approximately 6,600 new liver cancer cases are diagnosed annually, with higher prevalence in males and older adults. 

HCC patients often present with symptoms of advanced cirrhosis, including jaundice, splenomegaly, and hepatic encephalopathy[4, 5] and approximately 41% of HCC cases are estimated to be diagnosed at an advanced or unresectable stage.[3, 6] 

## _**Mechanism of action**_ 

Durvalumab, a human IgG1 kappa monoclonal antibody, blocks PD-L1 from binding to PD-1 and CD80, enhancing T-cell activation without causing antibody-dependent cytotoxicity. It has a half-life of 21 days and reaches a steady state in 16 weeks. Tremelimumab, a human IgG2 monoclonal antibody, inhibits CTLA-4, releasing T- 

35 



<!-- page 364 -->

Warwick Evidence EAG STA and HST Report Template post February 2022 

cell activation. Both are administered separately via intravenous infusion.[7-9] The EAG notes that the mechanism reported in CS Table 2 matches their findings. 

## _**Treatment pathway**_ 

In the UK, the standard of care for HCC has evolved with advancements in treatment options. Sorafenib was the standard treatment for advanced HCC for many years, having been approved by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) in 2017.[6, 10, 11] 

The combination of atezolizumab and bevacizumab became the new standard of care for advanced or unresectable HCC in the UK following its approval by NICE in December 2020. This combination showed superior overall survival and progressionfree survival compared to sorafenib, based on the results of the IMbrave150 study.[12-] 14 

This combination therapy was approved by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) in late 2020 and is recommended by the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO). For patients who do not respond to this first-line treatment, second-line options are considered based on individual patient factors and disease progression. Additionally, the British Society of Gastroenterology (BSG) provides guidelines for the management of HCC, which include evidence-based recommendations for assessment and treatment (CS, Document B, section B.1.3).[6] 

Selective internal radiation therapy (SIRT) with QuiremSpheres is recommended by NICE (2021)[15] for patients with Child-Pugh grade A liver impairment when transarterial therapies (TACE) are unsuitable. SIRT, administered via a catheter to the hepatic artery, is particularly considered for patients with large solitary tumours or those with local macrovascular invasion, where systemic therapy tolerance is a concern. Despite limited evidence from randomized controlled trials comparing SIRT and TACE for intermediate-stage HCC, SIRT is an option for treating unresectable advanced HCC in adults with compensated chronic liver disease.[15, 16] 

The systemic treatment algorithm for advanced HCC at BCLC stage C includes several first-line options: atezolizumab/bevacizumab, durvalumab/tremelimumab, sorafenib, and lenvatinib. Atezolizumab plus bevacizumab is recommended for patients with advanced HCC, Child-Pugh class A liver disease, and ECOG performance status 0-1, following management of oesophageal varices. If 

36 



<!-- page 365 -->

Warwick Evidence EAG STA and HST Report Template post February 2022 

contraindications exist, sorafenib or lenvatinib may be offered. Sorafenib is also considered for selected patients with Child-Pugh B liver disease.[17-20] 

Second-line treatments include sorafenib, lenvatinib, regorafenib, nivolumab, pembrolizumab, cabozantinib, and ramucirumab. Tyrosine kinase inhibitors are recommended for patients progressing on first-line atezolizumab plus bevacizumab. Regorafenib is specifically recommended for those who have had sorafenib, with Child-Pugh class A liver impairment and ECOG performance status 0 or 1. 

Durvalumab (Imfinzi, AstraZeneca) in combination with tremelimumab has a marketing authorisation for the first-line treatment of adults with advanced or unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma. 

## **2.2 Critique of company’s definition of decision problem** 

## **2.2.1 Population** 

The NICE final scope defined the population as “People with advanced or unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma”.[21] The population in the CS decision problem (CS Document B, Table 1) is the same as in the NICE scope but only includes those who are ineligible for locoregional therapy and have not undergone systemic treatment. Specifically, it refers to “Individuals with advanced or unresectable HCC who are ineligible for locoregional therapy and have not undergone systemic therapy” (CS Document B, Table 1). 

The criteria for ineligibility for locoregional therapy and lack of prior systemic treatment were added to align with the eligibility criteria of the HIMALAYA trial[22, 23] (CS Document B, Section B.2.3.1, Table 5). Additionally, the company clarifies that “all individuals have HCC that is either advanced, meaning it has spread extensively, or unresectable, meaning it cannot be surgically removed” (CS Document B, Table 1). 

The EAG highlights that NICE’s final scope includes a broader population of patients with advanced or unresectable HCC, whereas the company presents evidence of a narrower population. 

The EAG clinical expert advised that the HIMALYA trial was designed to benefit patients most likely to respond to the STRIDE regimen as the first line of systemic therapy. This includes patients with advanced or unresectable HCC who are 

37 



<!-- page 366 -->

Warwick Evidence EAG STA and HST Report Template post February 2022 

ineligible for locoregional treatment due to disease progression. STRIDE is recommended as the first line of systemic therapy, justifying the lack of prior systemic therapy for these patients. The criteria for ineligibility for locoregional therapy and the absence of prior systemic therapy are supported by the EAG’s clinical advisor. The EAG agrees with this recommendation. 

## **2.2.2 Intervention** 

The company’s decision problem intervention(s) aligns with the NICE final scope.[21] The company also describes the technology and mechanism of action of durvalumab and tremelimumab (CS Document B, Section B.1.2, Table 2), which is consistent with the summary of product characteristics (SmPC). 

## **2.2.3 Comparators** 

The company’s decision problem comparators were narrower than the NICE final scope.[21] 

The company's decision problem includes only atezolizumab + bevacizumab, lenvatinib, and sorafenib (CS Document B, pg. 15). 

Based on BSG guidelines and the company’s clinical expert opinions, the company explains that atezolizumab combined with bevacizumab is considered the standard of care (SoC) for first-line treatment in NHS clinical practice (see AstraZeneca Data on File. HIMALAYA Clinician Validation Interviews, supplied in the CS reference pack).[16] Therefore, it is the main comparator in the company's submission. For patients who cannot use atezolizumab plus bevacizumab or prefer oral treatment over intravenous therapy, the BSG guidelines recommend lenvatinib and sorafenib as alternative first-line options.[10, 14, 16, 24] The EAG supports this view, citing the BMJ Best Practice (2024) for hepatocellular carcinoma.[19] Specifically, 

atezolizumab/bevacizumab is the SoC for first-line treatment according to the treatment algorithm for BCLC stage C (advanced disease). 

The company notes that their comparators differ from NICE’s scope because the patient population is ineligible for locoregional therapies like selective internal radiation therapy (SIRT). They argue that best supportive care (BSC) should complement main treatments rather than serve as a standalone comparator. The EAG clinical experts highlighted that while evidence for locoregional therapy is limited, it is administered before systemic treatment. Additionally, BSC is provided for 

38 



<!-- page 367 -->

Warwick Evidence EAG STA and HST Report Template post February 2022 

all patients as part of NHS practice and is not considered a separate comparator. The EAG agrees. 

## **2.2.4 Outcomes** 

The company’s decision problem outcomes align with the NICE final scope.[21] 

## **2.2.5 Other relevant factors** 

The company’s decision problem (CS Document B, section B.2.7) states that clinical efficacy subgroup analyses show the efficacy of STRIDE across various patient characteristics, including: 

- HCC aetiologies 

- ECOG Performance Status (PS) 

- Presence of macrovascular invasion (MVI) 

- The specific subgroups reported are: 

   - Sex 

   - Age at randomisation 

   - PD-L1 expression 

   - Aetiology of liver disease 

   - ECOG PS at baseline 

   - MVI 

   - Extrahepatic spread (EHS) 

   - Region 

   - Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) at baseline 

   - BCLC score 

These details can be found in CS Document B, Table 1. 

The EAG agrees with the company. NICE has not considered any subgroups for this population. However, based on the literature[25-27] and EAG clinical expert, there are subgroups and prognostic factors that affect the treatment and prognosis of patients that should be considered. 

## **2.2.6 Summary section** 

The company’s decision problem specifies a population with advanced or unresectable HCC who are ineligible for locoregional therapy and have not undergone systemic treatment, aligning with the HIMALAYA trial criteria. The EAG 

39 



<!-- page 368 -->

Warwick Evidence EAG STA and HST Report Template post February 2022 

agrees with the provided justification although the population is narrower than NICE final scope. The intervention, STRIDE, aligns with the NICE final scope. However, the company’s comparators (atezolizumab + bevacizumab, lenvatinib, and sorafenib) are narrower than the NICE final scope. The EAG finds the company’s justifications for excluding locoregional therapies and BSC sufficient. The outcomes align with the NICE final scope, and the company presents subgroup analyses across various patient characteristics. The EAG notes that NICE has not considered subgroups.

## **3 CLINICAL EFFECTIVENESS** 

## **3.1 Critique of the methods of review(s)** 

The CS presents a systematic literature review (SLR) of clinical trials on patients with advanced or unresectable HCC. The scope of the SLR has evolved over time. 

## **3.1.1 Searches** 

The bibliographic searches were conducted at three different times, with initial searches missing some key terms, potentially overlooking earlier studies. Subsequent updates improved the comprehensiveness and sensitivity of the searches by including a broader range of terms. All searches were restricted to the English language and specific study types. Additional searches included clinical trial registries and conference abstracts, though details on some methods were 

limited. No searches of health technology assessment (HTA) sources were reported. Supplementary bibliography searches were conducted to address some of the initial search limitations but concerns about the overall sensitivity of the searches remain. For a detailed critique of bibliographic searches, please refer to Appendix 9.1. 

## **3.1.2 Systematic literature review methods** 

A summary of the EAG critique for each step of the SLR and cross-references to the relevant section in the CS is presented in Table 9. 

The full EAG assessment using the modified ROBIS[30] can be found in the Appendix 9.2. Overall, the EAG found the risk of bias in the company’s SLR to be of high concern. 

**Table 9: Summary of the EAG's critique of company SLR** 

|**Method step**|**Section(s) of CS of**<br>**relevance**|**EAG overall assessment**|
|---|---|---|
|Eligibility criteria|CS Appendix D, Table 14|High concern|
|Searches and selection of<br>studies|CS Appendix D, Sections<br>D.1.1-D1.2 and D.1.3<br>CS Document B, section<br>B.2.9|Unclear concern|
|Data extraction and risk of<br>bias assessment|CS Appendix D, Sections<br>D.1.3, D.1.5, D.1.6, D.1.7|Low risk of bias|
|Evidence synthesis|CS Document B, section<br>B.2.9|High concern|



46 



<!-- page 375 -->

Warwick Evidence EAG STA and HST Report Template post February 2022 

CS Appendix D, Sections D.1.5-D.1.10 and D.3 

The EAG conducted a quality appraisal of the company’s SLR using the ROBIS tool.[30] The review’s objectives were clearly defined but evolved over time. The predefined eligibility criteria were broader than the NICE final scope, and later have been adjusted to better align with NICE’s requirements. These criteria were used to select studies for a network meta-analysis (NMA), focusing on overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS), while other outcomes such as objective response rates (ORR), tolerability, or safety were not reported. 

The eligibility criteria were unclear. The company’s inclusion/exclusion criteria for the NMA lacked detail and proper justification, making it difficult to determine the appropriateness of excluded studies. 

The bibliography searches for SLRs and NMAs were incomplete. The original SLR searches missed important synonyms for hepatocellular carcinoma, potentially overlooking relevant studies. Although updated searches improved term variety, they still excluded terms for SLRs and NMAs, potentially missing some relevant studies useful for reference checking. Database searches covered the period from 2016 to April 2024. 

Study characteristics and results were adequately reported. The RoB assessment used by the company was the NICE STA template, also reported in the guidance by the Centre for Reviews and Dissemination (CRD) at the University of York.[31] The EAG has asked the company to clarify (A14) the RoB tool that has been used. The company responded that it was Cochrane RoB2. The company’s claim doesn’t align with the statement in the CS, section D.1.3, Appendix D. 

The company's unclear inclusion/exclusion criteria for the NMA led to limited data, resulting in wide confidence intervals and no statistically significant OS comparisons. The synthesis used only three studies with two interventions each, neglecting additional evidence and resulting in imprecise outputs unsuitable for extrapolation. The EAG noted the lack of steps to address heterogeneity, the absence of funnel plots, limited sensitivity analyses, and low precision in NMA results. Bias was not incorporated, and methodological inadequacies were present.

## **3.2 Critique of trials of the technology of interest, the company’s analysis and interpretation (and any standard meta-analyses of these)** 

## **3.2.1 Overview of key points in the EAG’s critique of key trial - HIMALAYA** 

## _Design_ 

The HIMALAYA trial was a phase III, open-label, multicentre, RCT sponsored by AstraZeneca. The 181 sites were distributed globally across 170 centres with patients enrolled from North America, South America, Asia and Europe. There were no sites in the UK and no patients from the UK, and consequently, the 

generalisability of findings from HIMALAYA to the UK HCC population is questionable. 

## _Intervention_ 

Patients were randomised 1:1:1:1 to one of four treatment arms: 

- A. Orally administered Sorafenib (400 mg twice daily), 

- B. IV administered durvalumab (1,500 mg every four weeks) 

- C. IV administered a combination of a single dose of tremelimumab (300 mg) plus IV durvalumab (1,500 mg every four weeks); a treatment regimen labelled STRIDE. 

- D. IV administered combination therapy of tremelimumab (75 mg) every four weeks for four doses plus IV durvalumab at 1,500 mg every four weeks; a treatment labelled T75+D 

The T75+D treatment arm was discontinued early (with 153 patients randomised) because an interim analysis indicated a lack of efficacy versus durvalumab alone. The EAG is unsure if these patients subsequently received second-line therapy (e.g. oral sorafenib or IV atezolizumab + bevacizumab) or became eligible for reallocation of treatment within HIMALAYA, although the former seems more likely. The company submission does not present data for the durvalumab only arm or interim results for the T75D arm. 

48 



<!-- page 377 -->

Warwick Evidence EAG STA and HST Report Template post February 2022 

## _Population_ 

The company states that the trial is representative of the UK population with advanced or unresectable HCC, supported by a multicentre audit of 361 patients across 11 UK centres.[32] 

The EAG think the recruited population in HIMALAYA was unlikely to reflect the generality of UK HCC patients in several respects: 

- A. Ethnicity (proportion of Asian, Japanese and Chinese patients); 

- B. Age at diagnosis (HIMALAYA recruited some adults diagnosed with HCC at age ≥18 years whereas guidelines from the British Society of 

   - Gastroenterology[16] (see Figure 1) indicate that diagnosis in the UK at age < 

   - 30 years is very rare; median age at diagnosis in HIMALAYA is lower than in the UK); 

**==> picture [452 x 247] intentionally omitted <==**

**Figure 1: Incidence of liver cancer, by age and sex in the UK** 

The EAG’s clinical advisor concurred with this EAG assessment. 

## C. Gender imbalance 

HCC is more common amongst men than women. Gender dimorphism of the liver may render males more susceptible to develop HCC.[33] 

HIMALAYA was weighted heavily with male participants, the ratio men to women was 5.66:1. UK HCC incidence per 100,000 people reported by Cancer Research 

49 



<!-- page 378 -->

Warwick Evidence EAG STA and HST Report Template post February 2022 

UK was 6.2 for women and 14.3 for men, equating to 30.5% female,[16] a ratio of 2.28:1, less than half that in HIMALAYA. This gender imbalance between UK and HIMALAYA populations may limit the generalisability of HIMALAYA findings to the UK clinical setting. 

Sexual dimorphism of the liver and gender dependent immunological differences infer it is feasible that gender differences in response to HCC treatments may exist. Since HIMILAYA is more heavily weighted with men relative to women than the UK HCC population, gender differences in response would skew outcomes in HIMALAYA relative to those expected in the UK clinical setting. 

The company’s exploratory subgroup analysis of overall survival suggests that, in contrast to men, in women sorafenib and STRIDE are equally effective. This analysis is severely underpowered because of low recruitment of women. Balcar et al., 2024 34 used five Phase III “landmark” RCTs in random effects meta-analysis to investigate possible gender differences in overall survival response to first line treatments; they reported pooled estimates suggestive of marginally better response in men (HR 0.79; 0.73, 0.86 || versus HR 0.85; 0.7, 1.03). In all included RCTs women were under-represented; lack of gender data resulted in exclusion of most RCTs. 

Balcar et al., 2024[34] also reported results from a retrospective real-world analysis of overall survival after atezolizumab + bevacizumab; patients from North America, Europe and Asia were included. The study lacked a control arm, the results suggest no gender difference in response. Real world studies for other interventions are lacking. 

In Summary, gender differences in response to first line treatments are feasible. As such the imbalance in gender ratio in HIMALAYA relative to the UK setting would skew outcome estimates. Evidence for differing gender response is weak because trials heavily weight recruitment toward males so that response estimates for women are very uncertain. 

## D. ECOG PS 

In the UK audit the company provided, patients with the ECOG PS ≥ 1 are above 79% while in the HIMALAYA trial only has 37% in both arms. HIMALAYA may not have included any participants with ECOG PS ≥ 1. 

50 



<!-- page 379 -->

Warwick Evidence EAG STA and HST Report Template post February 2022 

## E. Body mass index (BMI) 

Only 14.2% and 12.3% of STRIDE and sorafenib recipients respectively in 

HIMALAYA have BMI above 30, while our clinical advisors said that most patients have BMI above 30. This seems relevant to the fitness of patients and their response to treatments. 

- F. Demographic profile: inclusion and exclusion criteria exercised during recruitment result in a demographically narrower population than in the UK. 

The EAG notes that a recent real-world study of UK HCC that included 2160 patients suggests that more than half of the patients receive no specific cancer therapy.[35] 

## _Randomisation and allocation of treatment_ 

Randomisation was not completely random. Patients were stratified using three demographic factors deemed important influencers of outcome and randomisation used a block system to guard against imbalance in the number of patients recruited to each trial arm. Randomisation was implemented using an Interactive Web Response System (IWRS); allocation of treatment was determined by IWRS and communicated to the centres that recruited patients. EAG assume that investigators then correctly allocated treatment; according to company data on file, only a limited number of patients received the wrong treatment. 

## _Concealment of allocation_ 

HIMALAYA was an open-label trial and as such no attempt was made to conceal treatment received by patients from either patients or the treatment team. Many decisions taken by the treatment teams and/or by patients, such as whether progression has occurred, whether treatment should continue or stop, 

and responses by patients to questions for patient-reported outcomes will potentially be influenced by knowledge of the treatment received. The EAG considers that this introduces a definite risk of bias in outcome results from the trial including any patient-reported outcomes about quality of life. 

## _Comparators_ 

Discounting the discontinued T75+D arm, HIMALAYA encompassed three interventions, two of which, sorafenib and durvalumab, were available for comparison with the STRIDE regimen. The company only reported on STRIDE 

51 



<!-- page 380 -->

Warwick Evidence EAG STA and HST Report Template post February 2022 

versus sorafenib. The EAG consider one remit of the submission to be the estimation of the clinical effectiveness of STRIDE versus alternative first-line treatments. In this respect, EAG would welcome data for durvalumab at the latest cut-off (DCO March 1’st 2024). EAG recognise that durvalumab may not be a UK-approved first-line intervention for HCC, but thinks it reflects a decision by the company not to pursue that option with licensing authorities. The EAG notes that published meta-analyses and network meta-analyses aimed at comparing first-line treatments for HCC include durvalumab as a first-line option; in EAG's opinion, the company’s handling of comparators reflects an over-narrow interpretation of the submission’s remit. 

## _Outcomes_ 

The company specified that the key outcome was overall survival, and this was identified as the “primary objective” of the trial. The company’s first submission (dated 13’th August 2024) presented a CIC analysis of overall survival using the latest cutoff (March 1, 2024) encompassing 6 years (approximately 72 months) maximum follow-up. In a follow-up submission (dated 30th September 2024) the same data was presented but no longer CIC (referenced as Rimassa et al., 2024 ESMO Barcelona 2024). Both submissions lacked analysis of durvalumab, considered by EAG to be an omission of data. 

Five key secondary outcomes were identified. Two of these, progression-free survival (PFS) and time to discontinuation of treatment (TTD) are used in the company’s economic analysis. 

The EAG notes that the company presented a PFS analysis derived from an earlier cut-off (i.e., 27th August 2021 with a maximum follow-up of approximately 42 months) than that was used for overall survival. The EAG are unclear on the reason for using early data cut-off and considers this a potential omission of relevant data. No PFS data for durvalumab was presented. The public domain (Sangro et al., 2024)[22] has OS data from a later cutoff (23 January 2023) than 27th August 2021 but PFS analysis was not presented. The EAG are unclear why no PFS analysis appears to have been undertaken after the cut-off of January 2021 but think it may relate to multiple testing strategies for the trial. The company stated that their clinical experts highlighted that the measurement of PFS is challenging as radiologic progression is a subjective measurement prone to reading errors and that they noted 

52 



<!-- page 381 -->

Warwick Evidence EAG STA and HST Report Template post February 2022 

that patients are frequently eligible to continue treatment both within the trial setting and real-world setting even after disease progression. These statements bring into question the reliability of estimates of this outcome, and since economic modelling PFS is used as a proxy for TTD this also brings into question results for TTD.

## **3.2.3 Patient characteristics** 

The baseline characteristics of the HIMALAYA trial, detailed in CS Document B, section B.2.4, show balanced treatment arms regarding demographics and general characteristics. The company states that the trial is representative of the UK population with advanced or unresectable HCC, supported by a multicentre audit of 361 patients across 11 UK centres.[32] 

The EAG notes that the submission’s UK audit and the HIMALAYA trial have several key differences. HIMALAYA includes younger patients and more people with HBV and HCV. The audit also shows that UK patients have a more severe disease status profile. The audit lacks data on ethnicity, BCLC stage, and other factors. These differences threaten the validity of applying the trial results to the UK population.

## **3.2.3.1 Key differences in patient characteristics between the HIMALAYA trial and the UK audit** 

In the UK, nearly 43% of new HCC cases are diagnosed in individuals aged 75 and over. The HIMALAYA trial population is younger, with a median age of 65. 

The audit includes PS 0 (21%), PS 1 (62%), and PS 2 (17%), while the HIMALAYA consists of only PS 0 and PS 1, with about 62% in PS 0.[32] These differences highlight the lack of comparability between the audit and RCT. 

The UK audit lacks baseline data on 

************************************************************, and PD-L1, so it was not possible to compare these factors with the HIMALAYA trial. Additionally, the UK audit[32] does not capture the BCLC staging system. In terms of these specific factors, it is not possible to draw firm conclusions about the generalisability of the HIMALAYA trial to the UK population reflected by the audit data. 

The EAG’s clinical expert noted that the HIMALAYA trial population is unlikely to fully represent the UK. Regional variations in the UK include older, predominantly white, overweight (BMI >30), and a lower prevalence of viral aetiology. Based on some studies found by the EAG, almost 55% of the UK population with HCC are over 69 years old.

## **3.2.4 Risk of bias in HIMALAYA** 

In CS Document B Table 10, the company provided a summary of its view of the quality of the HIMALAYA trial. The company stated that _“the trial may be considered at low risk of bias”._ However, two entries in Table 10 contradict this: [a] _“no details were provided about allocation concealment”;_ [b] _“high risk”_ of bias because the trial was open-label and investigator assessed. 

The EAG agrees with the entries in CS Document B Table 10 and consequently considers HIMALAYA at substantial risk of bias. 

The EAG independently assessed the HIMALAYA trial using Cochrane RoB version 2, available in Appendix 9.3. 

Although the baseline characteristics (section 3.2.3) do not show significant imbalances between STRIDE and sorafenib, and the cumulative impact of several key prognostic factors in favour of STRIDE, raises concerns that stratification may not have identified the most appropriate factors for randomisation to avoid bias. Bias due to HIMALAYA’s open-label unblinded design presents an appreciable risk of bias, particularly for patient-reported outcomes and from unblinded assessors of progression, time-to-discontinuation of treatment and overall response rate (ORR). The blinded independent central review (BICR) evaluated the exploratory analysis and outcomes, but no data or further information on BICR was reported in the company submission. Therefore, the extent and direction of bias between investigator assessment and BICR assessment cannot be determined. ITT analysis was used and there was no risk of bias from missing data. 

The EAG requested the tabulation of all safety and adverse event data for the 5-year data cut-off (DCO) and beyond. In response, the company presented an overview of serious TRAEs and AEs that were not treatment-related from the updated analysis II (1[st] March 2024). However, no further information on delayed treatment events after five years or beyond was provided. The EAG finds the overview with general results and frequencies inadequate and insufficient. Concerns about long-term TRAEs remain. 

In conclusion, the EAG considers the HIMALAYA trial to have an appreciable risk of bias.

## **3.2.5 Clinical effectiveness results of the HIMALAYA trial** 

## **3.2.5.1 Primary outcome (overall survival; OS)** 

CS Document B, Figure 4 provided the OS Kaplan-Meier results to the maximum follow-up of 60 months; median survival was 16.43 months and 13.77 months respectively for STRIDE and sorafenib. 

Median overall survival results are also reported in the main publication of the trial by Abou-Alfa et al[36] as 16.43 months (95% confidence interval [CI], 14.16 to 19.58) for STRIDE, and 13.77 months (95% CI, 12.25 to 16.13) for sorafenib. 

The CS reports percentage survival for each arm at 18, 24, 36, 48, and 60 months: at 18 months, 24 months and 36 months stating that OS rate ratios for STRIDE compared to sorafenib are 1.17, 1.24, and 1.54 respectively. Survival rates for STRIDE and sorafenib respectively were reported by Abou-Alfa et al[36] as 48.7% (95%CI, 43.6, 53.5) and 41.5% (95%CI, 36.5, 46.4) at 18 months, 40.5% (95%CI, 35.6, 45.3) and 32.6% (95%CI, 27.9, 37.4) at 24 months, and 30.7% (95%CI, 25.8, 35.7) and 20.2% (95%CI, 15.8, 25.1) at 36 months, respectively, demonstrating a statistically significant survival benefit for STRIDE versus sorafenib at 36 months. Irrespective of maximum follow-up the tail of the OS SRIDE plot exhibited many censorings but few events. 

## **3.2.5.2 Secondary outcomes** 

The CS and Abou-Alfa et al.[36] reported on five secondary endpoints: PFS, TTP, ORR, DoR, and DCR. 

## **3.2.5.2.1 Progression-free survival (PFS)** 

CS Document B Figure 6 showed the Kaplan-Meier plot for PFS at maximum followup of approximately 42 months based on Abou-Alfa et al.[36] The median PFS for STRIDE was 3.78 (95%CI:3.68, 5.32) months and for sorafenib was 4.07 (95%CI: 3.75, 5.49) months with hazard ratio reported as 0.90 (95%CI:0.77, 1.05) for STRIDE versus sorafenib. 

## **3.2.5.2.2 Time-to-progression (TTP)** 

CS Figure 7 provided a Kaplan-Meier plot for time to progression (CS Document B, section B.2.6.2.2). Median TTP was similar for each arm. 

58 



<!-- page 387 -->

Warwick Evidence EAG STA and HST Report Template post February 2022 

## **3.2.5.2.3 Response rates (ORR, CR, DOR, DCR)** 

CS Document B, section B.2.6.2.3 reports response rates classified into four levels: complete response (CR), partial response (PR), stable disease (SD), and progressive disease (PD). 

The objective response rate (ORR), assessed by the investigator using RECIST 1.1 criteria, was significantly higher in the STRIDE treatment arm (20.1%) compared to the sorafenib arm (5.1%), with an odds ratio (OR) of 4.69 suggesting patients given STRIDE were approximately 4.69 times more likely to respond than those given sorafenib treatment (<0.0001). 

Abou-Alfa et al.[36] report that the proportion of patients remaining in response at 12 months was 65.8% for STRIDE and 63.2% for sorafenib. 

CR was observed in 3.1% of patients (12 out of 393) in the STRIDE treatment arm and none in the sorafenib treatment arm. 

The company suggests that achieving a CR is strongly associated with longer OS in patients although this is achieved by a relatively small proportion of patients, an interpretation reported in a systematic review and meta-analysis (R² = 0.905).[45] 

At the final data cut-off, the STRIDE arm had a median duration of response (DoR) of 22.3 months compared to 18.4 months for sorafenib, with the STRIDE arm showing a quicker median time to onset of response. However, the low numbers of responders introduce uncertainty in these median estimates. 

## **3.2.5.3 Patient-reported Outcomes (PRO)** 

The HIMALAYA trial included several Patient-Reported Outcome (PRO) tools, such as EORTC QLQ-C30, EORTC QLQ-HCC18, EQ-5D-5L, PRO-CTCAE, and Patient global impression change (PGIC). 

The EORTC instruments aimed to assess disease-related symptoms and quality of life, with STRIDE showing higher physical functioning but lower global health status scores than sorafenib. STRIDE resulted in a longer median time to deterioration in most PRO measures, except jaundice. The EQ-5D-5L, used to determine health state utility values, was detailed in the trial protocol but not extensively covered in the CS Document. Mean EQ-5D-5L and EQ-VAS scores by treatment status taken from the CS are summarised by the EAG (Table 13 and Table 14).

## **3.2.7 Adverse effects** 

The company concluded (CS Document B, section B.2.10) that in the HIMALAYA trial, the STRIDE regimen exhibited a favourable safety profile. The EAG discusses some uncertainties in the interpretation of adverse events findings below. 

## **3.2.7.1 Dose interruptions, reductions and discontinuations** 

The CS Document B, section B.2.10.2 reports that dose delays and infusion interruptions caused dose interruptions in the HIMALAYA. In CS document B, section B.2.10.2, the company states that durvalumab-related dose delays in the STRIDE treatment affected ********************. In CS document B, section B.2.10.3, the company reports that ********** discontinuations due to any adverse event leading to the discontinuation of the study treatment. The company only considers ********* of these cases as possibly related to treatment, which the EAG finds not justified. The reported proportions are calculated and captured by investigators who were not blinded, making the results prone to bias. Therefore, the EAG cannot fully agree that all of these AEs leading to discontinuation are possibly treatment-related. 

## **3.2.7.2 Treatment-related adverse events** 

In Table 28 of CS Document B, section B.2.10.3, the company summarises treatment-related adverse effects (TRAEs) for the HIMALAYA trial, categorising them as “TRAEs of any cause” and “TRAEs”. The EAG requested definitions and lists of AEs in these categories for clarification (A7). The company provided a brief explanation of how AEs were interpreted by the investigators, however, details anticipated by the EAG were not provided. 

The CS reports that patients in the STRIDE arm suffered a higher incidence of adverse events in both categories of TRAE compared to sorafenib, although the Abou-Alfa et al paper[36] based on much shorter maximum follow-up reported that Grade 3/4 treatment-emergent adverse events occurred for 50.5% of patients with STRIDE, and 52.4% with sorafenib. Relative to sorafenib, STRIDE exhibited higher rates of serious TRAEs, immune-mediated TRAEs requiring high-dose steroids, and grade 3 or 4 immune-mediated TRAEs, raising the EAG’s concerns. Immunemediated TRAEs leading to death were observed in STRIDE but not in sorafenib. STRIDE also had a higher incidence of grade 3 or 4 hepatic TRAEs.

While most irAEs manifest during or shortly after treatment, some autoimmune complications, such as colitis, hepatitis, pneumonitis, and endocrine disorders, may arise a year or more later.

## **3.2.7.4 Hepatic events** 

Based on the CS B.2.10.3.3, Tables 30 and 31, the hepatic AEs and hepatic treatment-related AEs, as captured by hepatic Standardised MedDRA queries (SMQs), were comparable between STRIDE and sorafenib. In HIMALAYA (clarification response A5), hepatic AEs were defined as any worsening of Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grades from the start of treatment until 90 days after the last dose or until the initiation of subsequent therapy (see HIMALAYA Clinical Study Protocol (2019) supplied in the CS reference pack).[59, 60] Consequently, irAEs occurring beyond this period or overlapping with subsequent treatments were not captured.[61, 62] The company asserts that these hepatic AEs were tolerable for STRIDE. The EAG notes that STRIDE has a higher overall incidence of hepatic AEs than sorafenib. Severe hepatic AEs (Grade ≥ 3) are more frequent for STRIDE than sorafenib (refer to the additional hepatic AEs in Table 1 and Table 19 based on the CTCAE grade in response to (clarification question A5). 

Overall, sorafenib demonstrates better tolerability regarding hepatic AEs, with lower percentages in most categories, particularly in severe cases and specific conditions like hepatitis.

## **3.2.8 Ongoing studies** 

The company asserts that there are currently no ongoing studies of relevance to this evaluation. The EAG searched and did not identify any further ongoing studies. In particular, the EAG investigated whether the company had discovered any further relevant studies or NMAs had been published. 

## **3.2.8.1 Conclusion of the clinical effectiveness section** 

The HIMALAYA trial faced several limitations, particularly due to its strict eligibility criteria, which may affect the generalisability of its results to the UK population. The NICE final scope was broader and more representative of the UK’s population compared to the company’s narrower scope, making the NICE scope more relevant for the UK context. The HIMALAYA trial’s criteria focus on cancer progression, favouring fitter and younger patients compared to the UK’s population. However these approaches are standard in trials, the EAG raised concerns about the trial’s participant characteristics and baseline differences compared to the UK audit, challenging the company’s claim of generalisability. The EAG clinical advisor mentioned that oncologists may hesitate to treat older patients not represented in trials, but if these patients are fit and without significant comorbidities, they may still be considered for treatment as clinicians become more familiar over time with the regimen. 

There are concerns about safety. Tolerability and TRAEs, associated with STRIDE. especially irAEs, which can be recurrent and life-threatening. Given the evolving nature of this field, patients on STRIDE need close monitoring. Adverse events have been tracked by the company only up to 90 days post-treatment or until subsequent therapy begins, which may not capture all irAEs or those overlapping with new treatments. The company’s responses to the EAG’s safety concerns were not adequate. However, the EAG’s clinical expert commented that, given the poor prognosis of patients, the survival benefits of STRIDE outweigh the risks of long-term side effects. 

While the STRIDE regimen improved overall survival compared to sorafenib, and most adverse events were tolerable and manageable, concerns remain about its generalisability to the UK population and long-term irAEs.

None of the graphics in CS Document B have associated 95%CIs or 95%CrIs. The Appendix Figures 15 and 17 show 95%CIs for reconstructed KM plots for PFS and OS in the REFLECT RCT of lenvatinib versus sorafenib, but this data does not appear to have been utilised in modelling. 

The method used for modelling OS and PFS for STRIDE (using IPD from HIMALAYA possibly at different DCO for OS and PFS) is different to that used for comparators (atezolizumab + bevacizumab and lenvatinib) where NMA HRs associated with very substantial uncertainty are employed. There is a lack of equity in the handling of STRIDE versus atezolizumab + bevacizumab and lenvatinib. 

The KM plot for TTD of STRIDE has an unusual trajectory that appears to be influenced by visit times. Using precise dates for discontinuation that should be available to the investigators would represent an improvement. 

The company states that in the absence of TTD information for atezolizumab + bevacizumab and for lenvatinib, they have assumed that TTD for these is equivalent to the PFS the company developed. However, the PFS models (employing NMA output HRs) are associated with severe imprecision and in the case of atezolizumab + bevacizumab bears little resemblance to what is seen in the IMbrave150 trial used for NMA input. The EAG is unconvinced that the equivalence of TTD and PFS is a sensible assumption for modelling. 

The EAG is not convinced that there is a complete lack of information about TTD for the comparators atezolizumab + bevacizumab and lenvatinib. 

## **3.2.8.2 Summary of clinical effectiveness** 

- The HIMALAYA trial population is a doubtful match for the UK HCC population eligible for first-line treatment making generalisability of findings from the trial outcomes doubtful. 

- The open-label design of HIMALAYA results in an appreciable risk of bias particularly applying to the mutual decisions between patients and investigators and the responses of patients to questionnaires regarding health-related quality of life (HRQoL). 

- Decisions regarding progression and discontinuation of treatment were dependent on trial investigators rather than an independent body.

## **3.2.9 Company NMA and their sources of information** 

The submission itemises analyses of OS and PFS at several different cutoff dates. The relevant information is summarised in Table 16 using data in CS Appendix M Tables 55, 56, and CS Document B Table 11. CS Appendix D Table 20 provides references to studies included in the company’s NMA. Several analyses report a 0.76 HR with various 95%CIs.[35] From information provided in the submission the EAG is unclear which HR and associated 95%CIs were used for the company’s NMA and what justified this choice. The HIMALAYA study Abou-Alfa 2022 (maximum follow-up 40 months) was specified as the relevant study (CS Appendix D Table 2), the HR input for OS appears to have come from a later cutoff analysis of HIMALAYA. Because the company's NMA diagram specifies selected interventions (i.e. only sorafenib and STRIDE) from HIMALAYA (CS Document B Figure 4) the date of cut-off used for data extraction remains unclear. 

In the EAG’s opinion, this statement conflates the distinction between studies and interventions and is confusing. Inclusion for the company’s NMA appears to be based on “ _studies_ ”, but the resulting NMA analyses are based on the company’s selection of _interventions_ used in those studies. For example, for the HIMALAYA trial, data from the durvalumab arm were excluded from the NMA. The company’s exclusion of durvalumab was based on the fact that it is unlicenced in the UK and on clinical advice that because of lack of license it was unused in UK clinical practice. 

The available evidence from HIMALAYA is based exclusively on non-UK patients and the company’s exploratory subgroup analysis of HIMALAYA suggests that the outcome depends on the geographical location of participants. However, the EAG notes that a recent study estimated that more than 50% of HCC cases in England receive no cancer-specific treatment at all.[35] Patient mix of treatments receivers and non-treatment receivers is unknown. In the HIMALAYA trial, virtually all participants receive treatment; so there is a much broader mismatch between the RCT and realworld treatment in the UK. (Please section 3.2.3) 

70 



<!-- page 399 -->

Warwick Evidence EAG STA and HST Report Template post February 2022 

Several recently published NMAs include much more data than the company’s NMA. Consequently, most of these HR estimates have a narrower 95%CrI estimate.[66-77] All except Celsa et al. and Leigh et al. reported HRs with CrIs. 

The EAG suggests that the NMA should include all the available data from the included studies and that the results relevant to the economic model and decision problem should then be selected for input to the economic model. The NMA appears to ignore potentially relevant evidence and may have missed the purpose of the NMA, namely, to synthesise all evidence bearing on the performance of first-line interventions in studies for the defined population. 

In agreement with the EAG for TA666, we consider that it is not unreasonable to conduct an NMA of HRs for the purpose of answering the question whether there is evidence of an average treatment effect ignoring any treatment-by-time interaction over the duration of the observed studies. However, using HRs from NMAs in the context of an economic evaluation is inappropriate in order to estimate population mean benefit. 

The CS Document B lacks any mention of the potentially relevant published NMAs. The company did not specifically search for NMAs. The absence of any consideration of previous NMAs may overlook the existence of potentially important evidence. Given the number of published NMAs and the wider number of 

interventions they have included, the EAG considers this an omission. In conducting the NMA, the EAG suspect that the decision problem has been over-narrowly interpreted. 

## **3.2.10 EAG’s selection and use of published NMAs** 

Considering the limitations addressed in sections 3.1.2 and 3.2.8.1, and after further evaluations, the EAG decided to consider a substitute NMA instead of the company’s. The EAG undertook a targeted search of the epistemonikos database (https://www.epistemonikos.org/) on 24/09/2024 to identify NMAs that included the intervention and comparators of interest. See Appendix 9.4 for the search strategy. Of the 52 records identified in the search, 12 were selected as potentially relevant and checked against pre-specified inclusion/exclusion criteria.[66-77]

## **Summary of EAG issues regarding the company’s NMA** 

1. Reporting of the methodology used to conduct the company NMA was lacking detail and was incomplete. The company’s justification for the inclusion and 

79 



<!-- page 408 -->

Warwick Evidence EAG STA and HST Report Template post February 2022 

exclusion criteria for studies lacked detail and justification. It would be difficult to replicate the NMA. 

2. No literature searches were conducted for published NMAs on this topic. Consequently, no comparison was undertaken between the company’s NMA and those published on the same topic; there was no mention of the existence of other NMAs. 

3. The data used in the NMA was very sparse and all pairwise comparisons resulted in HRs that were not statistically significant; any modelling undertaken with these NMA results will be associated with considerable uncertainty. 

4. Some data from the HIMALAYA trial was not included in the NMA. 

## **3.2.11 Conduct of the company’s NMA** 

In Table 23 lists EAG concerns regarding the conduct of the company’s NMA. 

## **Table 23: EAG points of concern for the company’s NMA** 

_Study type_ 

The use of Phase III RCTs ensures a high level of evidence quality. However, the company did not clearly justify why they limited only to Phase III RCTs. Differences between the study variables such as region (% Asia-Pacific), HBV aetiology, and macrovascular liver invasion may introduce variability that impacts the comparability of outcomes across studies. The company did not justify omitting the durvalumab arm of the HIMALAYA. 

_Treatment effect modifiers (TEMs)_ 

The company acknowledge and explore potential TEMs; however, the inability to adjust for TEMs due to a small number of studies limits the robustness of the NMA. Variations in HBV prevalence, MVI, and regional representation across trials may have introduced bias. The decision not to conduct more complex adjustments, like meta-regression or population adjustment methods, leaves some residual confounding unaddressed. 

_Proportional hazards (PH) assumption_ 

The proportional hazard assumption was violated for REFLECT and HIMALAYA. For REFLECT, the exploration of time-varying hazards as undertaken by the company showed that the application of a constant HR for lenvatinib in the economic model may overestimate the long-term effect of treatment, and therefore yields conservative cost-effectiveness estimates when compared to STRIDE. The company found the proportional hazard violation for STRIDE versus sorafenib (from HIMALAYA) for PFS and OS, and for lenvatinib vs sorafenib (from REFLECT) for PFS and OS. There was no evidence of a proportional hazard 

80 



<!-- page 409 -->

Warwick Evidence EAG STA and HST Report Template post February 2022 

violation for atezolizumab plus bevacizumab versus sorafenib (from IMBrave150). As there was evidence of non-proportional hazards for REFLECT, the company presented an analysis in which a time-varying treatment effect for the efficacy of lenvatinib versus sorafenib was explored (Appendix N). This showed that the application of a constant HR for lenvatinib in the economic model may overestimate the long-term effect of treatment, and therefore yields conservative cost-effectiveness estimates when compared with STRIDE. _PFS assessment consistency_ 

The company used investigator-assessed PFS across all studies to align with the data from HIMALAYA, to ensure consistency. However, the use of different criteria for PFS assessment (RECIST 1.1 versus mRECIST) across studies could still affect comparability. While RECIST and mRECIST may have similar performance, mRECIST includes extra factors that could potentially impact the results. Furthermore, reliance on investigator assessments, rather than blinded independent review, introduces subjectivity and potential bias. 

_Differences in follow-up_ 

HIMALAYA has a much longer follow-up time compared to IMbrave150 and REFLECT. The variability in follow-up duration across studies complicates direct comparisons of outcomes. The NMA did not fully adjust for these differences, which could impact the results' accuracy, particularly when assessing longer-term outcomes. 

_Use of informative priors_ 

The use of a published informative prior for the RE models that did not converge is a sound approach and improved model stability. However, the appropriateness of the informative priors is debatable, as their applicability to hepatocellular carcinoma-specific (NICE scope; Table 1) settings may be limited. The sensitivity of the results to the choice of priors introduces additional uncertainty, as different priors could yield varied outcomes. 

The impact of the model not converging with non-informative priors could have been delineated more clearly.

## **4 COST-EFFECTIVENESS** 

This section focuses on the economic evidence submitted by AstraZeneca and, additional information received in response to the EAG’s clarification questions. The EAG critically appraised the evidence submitted and examined the company’s electronic model. We provide a summary and critique of the company’s economic evidence, including the company’s systematic review(s), methods, and results (basecase, sensitivity and scenario analyses) as reported in the CS Document B using frameworks on best practices for reporting economic evaluation and economic modelling to assess the overall reporting quality and validity of these analyses. In the subsequent section, where possible, the EAG have addressed the concerns raised in the form of additional analyses undertaken, which concludes with the EAG basecase. 

The submission received by the EAG included: 

- A systematic review of the economic evidence 

- Methods used to undertake the economic analysis, the company’s base-case and sensitivity analysis results 

- Electronic version of the de novo Markov model built in Microsoft Excel 

## **4.1 EAG comment on company’s review of cost-effectiveness evidence** 

The company undertook systematic literature reviews (SLRs) to identify evidence on resource use, costs, and the cost-effectiveness of standard of care in patients with treatment-naïve advanced or unresectable HCC in the UK. Additionally, a systematic review was undertaken to identify studies that reported health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in the same population, also limited to the UK. The searches for both SLRs were undertaken in June 2024, with a date limit of 20 October 2021. The SLR 

methods in the company appendix refer to a previous, broader SLR (searches run May 2020, from database inception) and 1st update (searches run Oct 2021), which also sought HRQoL studies (see CS Document B, section B.3.1) and was not limited to the UK. 

82 



<!-- page 411 -->

Warwick Evidence EAG STA and HST Report Template post February 2022 

To obtain relevant studies, the company searched MEDLINE and Embase databases, as well as identifying records through searching UK HTA agencies via a database (INAHTA), relevant conferences, checking bibliographies of relevant SLRs, NMAs and economic evaluation. HTA bodies were not searched separately, which would have been ideal. Population terms in combination with disease terms and its stages, and economic terms were considered reasonable. 

In total, seven studies were considered relevant for the systematic review, five obtained from the database searches and two from supplementary searches. The company stated that no economic evaluation was identified that compared STRIDE to another relevant comparator as first-line treatments in adults with advanced or unresectable HCC. They identified previous appraisals of atezolizumab + bevacizumab, lenvatinib and sorafenib all of which included an economic model. The conduct of these economic analyses was reported in CS Document B, Table 32, pages 91-93. 

**EAG summary** : Because a geographic search filter for the United Kingdom was applied, searches will have likely missed relevant economic evaluations and HRQoL studies from other countries. Hence, it would have been beneficial to broaden the search by not limiting it to UK-based studies to potentially widen the evidence-base. 

## **4.2 Summary and critique of the company’s submitted economic evaluation by the EAG** 

The EAG reviewed AstraZeneca's economic evaluation model against NICE standards. A _de novo_ cost-effectiveness model was developed to assess the costeffectiveness of STRIDE in adult patients with advanced or unresectable HCC, in line with the HIMALAYA patient population, licence and decision problem for this submission. The EAG summarised the model structure and evaluated clinical 

evidence (e.g., efficacy, treatment discontinuation, mortality) and economic evidence (e.g., drug costs, health state resource use and costs, utilities). The EAG critiqued the methods and inputs used in the analysis.

## **4.2.2 Model structure** 

The company conducted a cost-effectiveness analysis using a partitioned survival model (PSM) to reflect disease progression and patient survival patterns in those treated with STRIDE and comparator therapies for advanced or unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The company stated that this model aligns with previous NICE evaluations, making it the most appropriate choice based on the available clinical data.[10, 14, 24] The PSM structure uses time-to-event data from the HIMALAYA study, focusing on overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS). The HIMALAYA trial provides five-year survival data. The company addressed uncertainties through consultations with UK experts on advanced or unresectable HCC. The model includes three health states: progression-free (PF), 

85 



<!-- page 414 -->

Warwick Evidence EAG STA and HST Report Template post February 2022 

post-progression (PD), and death. Figure 6 provides a simplified schematic of the model, illustrating the possible transitions between these health states. 

**==> picture [452 x 194] intentionally omitted <==**

**Figure 6: Simplified model schematic (Figure 22, CS Document B, page 89)** 

The company model starts with patients in a 'progression-free' state, receiving either STRIDE or a comparator treatment (atezolizumab + bevacizumab, sorafenib, lenvatinib). Patients may progress or die, and those with progressed disease may either remain alive with progression or die, with no improvement in health state. In the model, patients in the ‘progression-free’ and ‘progressed disease’ health states can be either on or off treatments. 

**EAG comment:** The EAG identified two concerns regarding the company's model structure. 

First, in the definition of health states, the model structure does not account for important subgroups within the "progression-free" and "progressed disease" health states. Specifically, there are two sub-states for each of these: "on treatment" and "off treatment." "On treatment" refers to patients who are still receiving the primary treatment (e.g., STRIDE), while "off treatment" refers to those who have discontinued primary treatment and are undergoing subsequent treatments. The costs associated with patients on primary treatment and those on subsequent 

treatments differ substantially. The EAG argues that collapsing these subgroups into single health states oversimplifies the illustrative model structure, especially when a considerable proportion of patients in the progression-free state transition to subsequent treatments. 

86 



<!-- page 415 -->

Warwick Evidence EAG STA and HST Report Template post February 2022 

Second, the company assumed that progression-free survival (PFS) serves as a proxy for time-to-treatment discontinuation (TTD) in treatments of atezolizumab + bevacizumab and lenvatinib. This implies that all patients in the progression-free state remain on primary treatment, while all patients in the progressed disease state receive subsequent therapies. The EAG contends that this approach introduces inconsistencies across treatments, which could lead to bias and ultimately weaken the robustness of the model. 

## **4.2.3 Population** 

The economic evaluation focuses on adults with advanced or unresectable HCC classified as BCLC stage B or C. The analysis is based on the HIMALAYA patient population, which aligns with the licensed indication for STRIDE. The evaluation specifically excludes patients eligible for locoregional therapy due to factors such as tumour burden, liver function, and vascular invasion.[28] The company quotes recent input from UK clinician experts to support this approach, emphasising that systemic therapy is only considered when locoregional options like SIRT are either not suitable or unavailable (see AstraZeneca, Data on File, HIMALAYA Clinician Validation Interviews, supplied in the CS reference pack). The evaluation also specifically excludes patients who have received prior systemic therapy. 

The clinical efficacy of STRIDE is examined demonstrated through subgroup analyses in terms of HCC aetiologies, ECOG performance status, and the presence of macrovascular invasion, among other factors. The company reported that the OS benefit of STRIDE versus sorafenib was consistent across most pre-specified subgroups, with HR estimates falling within the 95%CI of the overall population. Some variability occurred, particularly in the female subgroup and patients with HCV, where the 95%CI included one, indicating no significant difference in effectiveness. The company stated, in females, this was likely due to the small sample size (<100 per arm), while post-hoc analysis for HCV revealed imbalances. Despite this, OS benefit remained consistent across subgroups and at the primary DCO. The baseline characteristics used in the economic model are based on the HIMALAYA trial ( _see_ Table 25) and the company stated based on clinical expert feedback are deemed generally representative of patients in UK clinical practice (see AstraZeneca, Data on File, HIMALAYA Clinician Validation Interviews, supplied in the CS reference pack).

## **4.2.4 Interventions, comparators and subsequent treatments** 

## **Interventions** 

The intervention under review is durvalumab plus tremelimumab (STRIDE), consistent with the final scope. The HIMALAYA trial supports the approved dosing of STRIDE, where patients receive durvalumab (1,500 mg Q4W) and a single 300 mg dose of tremelimumab. STRIDE is administered until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity occurs, as per the European Medicines Agency.[9, 29] 

## **Comparators** 

The comparators include atezolizumab + bevacizumab, lenvatinib, and sorafenib, which the company states reflect current UK clinical practice for advanced or unresectable HCC, particularly for those ineligible for locoregional therapies. Atezolizumab + bevacizumab is the standard of care due to its superior efficacy over lenvatinib and sorafenib. Lenvatinib and sorafenib serve as alternative first-line therapies for patients for whom atezolizumab + bevacizumab is contraindicated or who prefer oral treatment. 

Other comparators, such as selective internal radiation therapy (SIRT) and best supportive care (BSC), are excluded by the company. The company states that SIRT is irrelevant to this analysis because it is classified as locoregional therapy, which is unsuitable for this patient population due to tumour burden or liver function. The rationale for excluding BSC is that, while essential for symptom management, it is only offered to patients who are ineligible for systemic treatment, rather than as an alternative to active therapy. 

## **Subsequent treatments** 

The company’s approach to subsequent treatments within the model ensures that once patients discontinue their primary treatments, including interventions and comparators, they do not receive the same treatment in later lines. Instead, patients transition to specific subsequent therapies based on their initial treatment. For instance, patients who receive STRIDE as their primary treatment may move on to ***, **********, or *********. All patients are assumed to receive BSC, either alone or in combination with other subsequent treatments, for the remainder of their lifetime. Since the model only accounts for first and second lines of therapy, it is assumed

## **4.2.5 Perspective, time horizon and discounting** 

The company adopted the perspective of the NHS and Personal Social Services (PSS) for costs and outcomes, following the NICE reference case. A lifetime time horizon of 40 years was selected to account for patient outcomes up to age 100 (it goes to age 103 according to company’s survival modelling). Based on the overall survival model employed in the base-case analysis, the company stated that this time horizon was deemed appropriate, as 4% of patients in the intervention arm are projected to survive beyond 20 years, ensuring the model captures all costs and QALYs across treatment arms. A one-week cycle length was used, aligning with the frequency of clinical events and treatment regimens. The company stated this 

90 



<!-- page 419 -->

Warwick Evidence EAG STA and HST Report Template post February 2022 

approach is consistent with the latest NICE evaluation in advanced HCC.[14] A halfcycle correction was applied. Costs and effects were discounted at 3.5% annually, as recommended by the NICE reference case. 

**EAG summary:** The perspective and discount rate used by the company are in line with the NICE 2022 recommendations and are appropriate to the decision problem. The time horizon of the model was 40 years. However, previous STAs for similar treatments have typically used shorter time horizons of 14 to 20 years.[10, 14] In its submission to CADTH for STRIDE, the company also opted for a 15-year time horizon.[80] The EAG submitted a clarification request to the company regarding the use of different time horizons in both the previous CADTH submission and the current one. However, the EAG found the company's response unconvincing. 

The EAG believes that a 20-year time horizon would sufficiently capture differences in costs and benefits of treatments, aligning with the NICE reference case. Additionally, adopting a 20-year time horizon would be consistent with previous STAs for advanced HCC treatments and is compatible with the advice of the EAG clinical advisors, especially given the age distribution of relevant UK patients. 

As described subsequently in this report, the EAG’s amendment to the modelling assumptions lead to  around 1% of people are projected to survive beyond 20 years. Given this, extending the time horizon to 40 years, compared to 20 years, is likely to have a negligible impact on the ICER. 

## **4.2.6 Overall survival, progression-free survival and time-totreatment discontinuation** 

## **Overall survival** 

The company conducted an overall survival (OS) analysis using individual patient data (IPD) from the HIMALAYA trial, with a median follow-up of 5 years for OS. Parametric survival models were applied to the Kaplan-Meier data for STRIDE and sorafenib. The proportional hazards assumption, evaluated through multiple statistical methods, was found to be violated. As a result, the company used independently fitted models for each treatment arm, rather than joint models, to minimise assumptions. The company used splines and knots for STRIDE and sorafenib. For comparator treatments, atezolizumab + bevacizumab and lenvatinib, 

91 



<!-- page 420 -->

Warwick Evidence EAG STA and HST Report Template post February 2022 

network meta-analysis (NMA)-derived hazard ratios (HRs) were applied to the sorafenib arm. However, proportional hazard violations for lenvatinib vs. sorafenib indicated potential bias, leading the company to apply a constant HR of one for OS, acknowledging lenvatinib’s non-inferiority to sorafenib in the REFLECT trial. For atezolizumab + bevacizumab, the absence of the proportional hazard violation 

allowed for the reliable use of the NMA-derived HR. Constant HRs were applied by the company for lenvatinib and atezolizumab + bevacizumab. See Figure 7 for the KM plots for STRIDE and sorafenib and parametric curves fitted.

## _**Lenvatinib and atezolizumab + bevacizumab**_ 

The company’s NMA uses HR inputs from three included studies (four interventions), irrespective of the proportional hazards violation. The NMA delivers hazard ratio estimates that are then used for modelling overall survival and progression-free survival over a lifetime for the comparators lenvatinib and atezolizumab + bevacizumab but not for STRIDE which is modelled independently on the IPD from HIMALAYA. 

The EAG have noted demographic differences between HIMALAYA and the UK population (age, gender mix, ethnicity and other factors that were not employed in stratification at randomisation). A problem of using IPD from HIMALAYA is that the population is not representative of that encountered in UK clinical practice.

The company use IPD for each arm of HIMALAYA to model OS for STRIDE and OS for sorafenib. The approach used to model OS for the comparators atezolizumab + bevacizumab and Lenvatinib is to apply NMA HRs to the sorafenib IPD. Two different approaches may lead to inconsistency. 

Similarly, the EAG for the atezolizumab + bevacizumab STA remarked that it is inappropriate to estimate the relative treatment effects of lenvatinib versus atezolizumab + bevacizumab using an HR from a random effects NMA, whilst estimating the effect of sorafenib versus atezolizumab + bevacizumab using armbased parametric survival model. 

The EAG for the atezolizumab + bevacizumab STA additionally considered that using HRs from NMAs in the context of an economic evaluation is inappropriate in order to estimate population mean benefit. 

The company sorafenib OS model is a spline 1-knot model. Applying a fixed HR (be it 1 or another value) to this model will generate another spline model. Thus, the survival models the company has generated for the comparators atezolizumab + bevacizumab and for lenvatinib are spline models. The base-case model for STRIDE is derived in a different way to the comparators, namely by generating a spline 1- knot model using HIMALAYA IPD. ## **Progression-free survival STRIDE; key secondary endpoint** 

The company assessed PFS for STRIDE and sorafenib using IPD from the HIMALAYA trial. The formal assessment of the proportional hazards assumption revealed a violation, based on visual inspection of KM curves, the log-log plot, Schoenfeld residuals plot, and Grambsch and Therneau test.[82-85] Due to this violation, the company opted to use independently fitted models for each treatment arm rather than joint models to minimise assumptions (see Figure 16). For PFS, the company applied splines and knots to the parametric survival models as follows: three knots for STRIDE and two knots for sorafenib. For comparators, atezolizumab + bevacizumab and lenvatinib, constant hazard ratios (HRs) were used. This approach was chosen to account for the observed proportional hazard assumption violation and ensure accurate modelling of PFS outcomes across the different treatments.

## _**The STRIDE Kaplan-Meier plot**_ 

The event for this analysis was defined as objective progression or death, whichever occurs first. 

Figure 6: Company submission Kaplan-Meier plot of HIMALAYA PFS results (primary analysis; FAS) (DCO: 27[th] August 2021) 

101 



<!-- page 430 -->

Warwick Evidence EAG STA and HST Report Template post February 2022 

**==> picture [451 x 260] intentionally omitted <==**

**Figure 17: Kaplan-Meier plot of HIMALAYA PFS results (obtained from CS Document B, Figure 6)** 

According to Figure 17 (CS Document B, Figure 6; DCO August 2021), within the first 12 months, 79.4% of STRIDE patients have already progressed, after which the incidence of progression greatly slows leading to a long flattish tail to the plot from about 16 to 18 months when only 14% remain at risk (86% already progressed) and extending to 41.8 months. The KM plot is apparently strongly influenced by the 14% of patients remaining at risk beyond approximately 17 months to 41 months that contributes about 58% of the total 41.8 months of observed PFS and most of any chosen modelled extrapolation to a lifetime horizon. 

As is characteristic of many PFS KM plots the company’s PFS plot has notable “bends” in trajectory reflecting the timing of visits to assess whether progression has occurred. Such plots obviously cannot accurately reflect “true” progression times (irrespective of how judged) which will be far more randomly distributed than implied by the “bends” due to imposed assessment times. The KM plot is compounded by a combination of assessment intervals plus actual progression times and is a combination of the two. 

“Standard” parametric models have consistent trajectory through time (i.e., are not characterised by multiple bends) and as such will deliver relatively poor AIC BIC values because they will not follow the bends in the observed plot. Such “bendy” 

102 



<!-- page 431 -->

Warwick Evidence EAG STA and HST Report Template post February 2022 

trends in observed KM can be more closely fitted using spline models with increasing number of knots that will tend to deliver improving AIC BIC values with increasing number of knots. However, close fitting to a bendy trajectory clearly will not reflect the reality of actual progression times because the event times of patients will be more randomly distributed than implied by the “observed” bendy plot which is 

compounded by assessment times and actual progression. In general, the closer the spline model is to the bendy PFS plot, the less likely it will reflect actual progression times and in extrapolation beyond 41.8 months of observation the more likely it will be influenced by the last bend(s) captured by the spline model’s knots or by the long flat tail of the KM from approximately 18 months. 

In brief, because of the uneven (bendy) trajectory of the observed data, it is unlikely that AIC BIC values will necessarily be meaningful in determining “a good” model of actual progression times (i.e. reflective of event times).

It was unclear to the EAG whether data from the DCO in Figure 6 or from a later DCO was used. The relevant part of CS Document B Figure 39 aligns observed hazard (shown as a dotted line) with the spline models’ hazard. In the EAG’s opinion, none of the spline hazard 

models shown fit particularly well after six months. For reasons explained above spline models although delivering favourable AIC BIC scores may risk over influence from the imposed visit times.

## **TTD for lenvatinib and atezolizumab + bevacizumab** 

The company found a lack of evidence for TTD of atezolizumab + bevacizumab or lenvatinib and assumed that PFS and TTD were equivalent for these interventions. 

The EAG comment: 

- A. lack of evidence does not seem a sound justification for the assumption made 

- B. the assertion that there is a lack of evidence for lenvatinib is incorrect 

- C. Previous TAs (TA551 lenvatinib vs sorafenib, and ID1655) have modelled TTD using IPD from the relevant trials and have modelled observed TTD where possible; TA666 used PFS as a proxy for TTD where data was not available, i.e., for Lenvatinib. Committee papers indicate that their approach was acceptable to committee. 

The use of PFS as a proxy for TTD of lenvatinib and for atezolizumab + bevacizumab means that the method used for STRIDE and sorafenib TTD (that is employing IPD from the HIMALAYA) differs from that used for lenvatinib and atezolizumab + bevacizumab, which the company models by applying the company’s interpretation of the anchored NMA HR output to the spline model of PFS for sorafenib. This may result in a non-alignment between modelled TTD (i.e., proxy PFS) and TTD (proxy PFS) seen in the relevant RCTs from which the HRs were

## _**Life-years gained (LYG) relative to time-on-treatment**_ 

The company’s KM data for discontinuation of STRIDE treatment extends to 3.5 years of observation. The AUC indicates that over 3.5 years about 0.9 life years were accumulated on STRIDE treatment. Over 3.5 years of observation the 

company’s KM plot for overall survival indicates that approximately 26% of patients remain alive, and the life years gained (estimated from AUC) over the 3.5-year time horizon was about 1.78 years. This gain was partly accumulated by patients while on STRIDE treatment and partly while alive but not on STRIDE treatment. From AUC estimates approximately 50% of the life years gained were while on STRIDE and 50% while off treatment. Thus, half of LYG seems due to a prolonged post-treatment effect of STRIDE and or secondary beneficial treatments received by patients who discontinued STRIDE. Over ten years (Figure 40) using the company’s Weibull model for discontinuation the percentage LYG off treatment increases to >50%.

There is doubt that analyses of HIMALAYA can be applicable to UK HCC population. 

The company used spline models for STRIDE OS and PFS, these predict a small proportion of patients unprogressed / “cured” after 40 years; the OS model seems influenced by a small subgroup of patients (14% of STRIDE population) that form a flat tail at the end of the KM plot. 

The company did an anchored NMA with input for three interventions (STRIDE, atezolizumab + bevacizumab, lenvatinib) relative to sorafenib. The NMA output for these comparisons delivered wide 95% credible intervals that indicate considerable imprecision in estimates that threaten the integrity of modelled extrapolations beyond observed data to the lifetime horizon of 40 years. 

The method for modelling OS and PFS of STRIDE (using IPD from HIMALAYA) differed from that for atezolizumab + bevacizumab and for lenvatinib (using NMA HR output applied to the spline model for sorafenib). 

The KM plot for TTD of STRIDE appeared influenced by visit times. The company found a lack of evidence about TTD of atezolizumab + bevacizumab and of lenvatinib interventions and so assumed PFS modelling for these could be used as proxy for TTD. There is evidence about TTD for lenvatinib in the public domain but this was not recognised by the company. The assumption of equivalence for PFS and TTD is difficult to justify and limited available evidence suggests the assumption is ill-founded.The assumption of equivalence for PFS and TTD is difficult to justify, and limited available evidence suggests the assumptions although potentially illfounded may be necessary from lack of alternative evidence. For example, although there is TTD data from TA666 this is redacted and unusable by the EAG. 

It is disappointing that lack of evidence resulted in the use of PFS as a proxy for TTD . This adds an extra-layer of uncertainty in the company’s cost-effectiveness analysis. Because of CIC redactions this data seems unavailable to both EAGs and to commercial companies making submissions to NICE. As a result, PFS has been used as a proxy out of necessity rather than choice.
